item.description: Here's everything you need to know injury-wise for Week 4 of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Week 4 is underway, and we're tracking all the injuries heading into the weekend.

Live injury updates

Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay expects wide receiver Puka Nacua to return in Week 4 against the Philadelphia Eagles. Nacua, who has missed the past two games with a hip and groin issue, said he is "taking it one day at a time."

"I'm getting my feet under me, hearing all the play calls," Nacua told reporters on Thursday. "It's not as foreign as it used to sound from Matthew Stafford, but he's definitely in full flow and rhythm. It's nice to be able to hear that play call in the huddle. I have to make sure I buckle my stuff up before so I can really focus on what he's saying."

While Nacua was listed as limited in practice, he said he took part in full on Thursday.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

Another wide receiver to keep an eye on is Justin Jefferson. The Minnesota Vikings star did not practice on Thursday with an ankle issue. Jefferson went down early in the Vikings' 23-16 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He underwent an MRI, which Monday revealed a sprain but no additional issues.

Head coach Kevin O'Connell said after the game that Jefferson was "close" to making it back into the contest, but just wasn't quite there.

Caleb Williams (hamstring) is looking like he will sit for another week, but could very well return in Week 5. Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson said that he knows who will start against the New York Jets, he just has not announced it yet. "We'll be in good shape for Sunday," he said as Tyson Bagent and Case Keenum, who started Week 4, are the two candidates to play. The Bears are also monitoring running back D'Andre Swift, who missed practice Thursday with a knee injury.

Other Week 4 injuries to monitor:

  • Jayden Daniels (elbow) has been ruled out of the Washington Commanders' London matchup against the Indianapolis Colts. The quarterback practiced this week in a limited capacity, wearing a brace on his left arm. He may potentially need surgery in the offseason, but the brace will provide protection for the remainder of this season.

  • The Eagles will likely be without wideout DeVonta Smith on Sunday night against the Rams. Smith has not practiced all week after suffering a hamstring injury on Monday night against the Bears. Smith leads the team with 19 receptions and 235 receiving yards through three games. With Smith likely out, along with A.J Brown, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon and the returning Zach Ertz will be Jalen Hurts' main targets.

  • Lamar Jackson (back) was dealing with "something small," which caused the Baltimore Ravens quarterback to miss Wednesday's practice. On Thursday, both Jackson and wide receiver Zay Flowers, who missed Week 2 a hamstring injury before returning last week, were upgraded to full participants.

  • It will be the Braelon Allen show with Jets running back Breece Hall ruled out with a quad injury suffered in Week 3. Allen has been getting most of the first-team reps in practice this week as the team prepares to face the Bears. "Nothing really changes for me in terms of preparation or my mindset, anything like that. I've always prepared to be in that position," Allen said.

  • A rib injury knocked San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Mike Evans out of Week 3. As the team prepares for the Denver Broncos, Evans remained out of practice on Thursday, but head coach Kyle Shanahan said the veteran "will make every attempt" to be on the field Sunday afternoon.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 4 Start 'Em, Sit 'Em: Justin Boone's lineup advice
item.description: Justin Boone helps you set those lineups for fantasy football in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Justin Boone provides a weekly look at undervalued fantasy players to consider starting this week and potential busts you might want to leave on your bench. 

For the rest of your lineup decisions, consult his Week 4 rankings. 

Starts

Tyler Shough, QB, Saints

vs. Falcons

Shough is off to an impressive start, posting the fourth-most fantasy points among quarterbacks so far. That includes very consistent production with weekly finishes as the QB6, QB8 and QB6 through three games. 

After fielding the fastest-paced offense last season, Kellen Moore has picked up where he left off. The Saints are nearly a full second quicker in neutral pace of play, which leads to plenty of volume for Shough and company. 

We're set up for a Monday night shootout, with a Falcons team that looked much more competitive with Michael Penix Jr. under center last week. Atlanta's defense is giving up the 12th-most fantasy points to passers and had to place its best cornerback A.J. Terrell on injured reserve. You can confidently project another QB1 result from Shough. 

Other QBs to start:

  • Jared Goff at Panthers – Speaking of corners heading to IR, Carolina just lost both Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson for at least the next four weeks and possibly longer. Even though we tend to avoid Goff when he's outdoors, we'll make an exception here in a game that's tied for the highest projected point total on the week at 51.5.

  • Bryce Young vs. Lions – Young is on the other side of that contest and facing a Lions defense that's been without several starters. Unsurprisingly, that's led to Detroit allowing the most fantasy points to opposing quarterbacks this year. Young is positioned well for his third top-12 finish on the season. 

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Cardinals

at Giants

Love is fresh off a breakout game against the 49ers, where he put up 109 scrimmage yards and a receiving touchdown on 26 touches. That was by far his strongest usage of the season (64% snap share) and a sign of things to come for the third overall pick. 

We might have even seen this happen sooner if it wasn't for his preseason ankle injury, but fantasy managers who drafted him in the third round aren't complaining now. 

Next up is a potential positive game script against a Giants defense that's given up the 10th-most fantasy points to running backs this season, including Javonte Williams (72 yards, two TDs), Kyren Williams (97 yards, one TD), Blake Corum (92 yards) and Tony Pollard (96 yards). Get ready for a big week from Love, who is a top-10 RB in my rest-of-season trade value charts.

Other RBs to start:

  • Aaron Jones Sr. vs. Dolphins – Jones, who turns 32 in December, can't hold up to massive workloads forever, but he should do well against a Miami team that's allowed the most fantasy points to running backs, including top-five finishes in each of the first three weeks. 

  • Braelon Allen at Bears – Breece Hall is sidelined, opening the door for the 22-year-old Allen, who's flashed on his limited touches. Chicago's defense has permitted at least 80 scrimmage yards to every starting RB its played. 

  • Jacory Croskey-Merritt vs. Colts (London) – Rachaad White is dealing with a shoulder injury that could keep him out this week. That may leave the recently signed Austin Ekeler and rookie Kaytron Allen as the only backups behind JCM. As I wrote about in my trade tips column, Bill is being underrated after a 48-yard TD was called back on an illegal formation penalty last week. I'm excited to see what he can do against a Colts defense that's the sixth-easiest matchup for RBs. 

Matthew Golden, WR, Packers

vs. Buccaneers

Golden is tied for the seventh-most targets per game through three weeks, just ahead of his teammate Christian Watson. While both players are performing well, Watson has received significantly more praise and sits as the WR3 overall in fantasy points per game. However, Golden isn't far behind at WR14. 

With the current state of Green Bay's offense, Watson and Golden are going to remain busy. The Packers have lost Jayden Reed for the season, Tucker Kraft is still working his way back to form after last year's ACL tear and the run game is non-existent. 

At the moment, Golden is looking like one of the best fantasy picks you could have made this summer. Expect his strong production to continue against Tampa's pass funnel defense. 

Other WRs to start:

  • Josh Downs at Commanders (London) – With Alec Pierce sidelined, the Colts have finally turned up the volume for Downs, who has 20 targets, 12 catches and 149 yards over the last two games. Now, he squares off with a Commanders secondary that's allowed the most fantasy points to receivers. 

  • Michael Wilson at Giants – After posting his best stat line of the young season (11-89-1 on 17 targets!), Wilson gets his easiest matchup so far in Week 4. The Giants defense has been responsible for a top-20 WR finish in each of the first three weeks and Wilson is next. 

  • Jameson Williams at Panthers – A high-scoring game against a defense that's missing its top two corners sounds like the perfect get-right spot for Williams. This will be a spike-week for the Lions' boom-or-bust wideout. 

Juwan Johnson, TE, Saints

at Falcons

Johnson has been an excellent late-round selection and an extremely consistent fantasy starter in the opening month. Among tight ends, he's fifth in receptions, sixth in yards and tied for first with three touchdowns. That's helped generate TE7, TE13 and TE5 weekly finishes. 

A friendly matchup with the Falcons awaits in Week 4. Atlanta is the seventh-most generous defense to fantasy tight ends, including allowing a league-high three touchdowns to the position through three games. 

Jordyn Tyson has one more week on IR and isn't immediately expected back, so Johnson will continue to be a strong fantasy TE1. 

Other TEs to start:

  • Kenyon Sadiq at Bears – Following his seven-catch, 105-yard, one-touchdown breakout last week, Sadiq has been limited in practice with a back injury. As long as he's healthy, he'll be a top-12 TE option, with Adonai Mitchell and Mason Taylor still week-to-week.  

  • Darren Waller vs. Lions – Waller gets to take on the same Detroit defense that was responsible for Sadiq's massive stat line in Week 3. Not only are the Lions giving up the most fantasy points to the position, they've allowed six touchdowns to tight ends in three weeks. If Jalen Coker is limited or ruled out, that would push Waller even higher up my rankings. 

Sits

Drake Maye, QB, Patriots

at Bills

During his rookie season, in the nine outings where Maye played at least 85% of the snaps, he never finished lower than QB17. Last year, we saw him combine that high floor with a high ceiling and he finished as the QB3 overall in fppg, while scoring less than 14 fantasy points only one time. 

This season, he's been under 13 fantasy points in all three outings and currently sits as the QB35. 

Yes, there have been injuries to A.J. Brown and the offensive line. The matchups have also been tougher (Seahawks, Steelers, Jaguars) after having an easier schedule in 2025. However, it's still hard to explain the disappearance of Maye's once high floor. 

Even against a softer opponent in the Bills, it's hard to trust Maye in your lineup until we see him turn this around. Though Buffalo allowed four TDs to Jared Goff, they held C.J. Stroud and Justin Herbert to QB15 and QB23 finishes, respectively.

I'm not dropping Maye, but I am sending him to my bench in the leagues where I have a decent streaming option. 

Other QBs to sit:

  • Justin Herbert at Seahawks – Herbert is also on the list of quarterbacks who have been massive disappointments in September. This doesn't look like a bounce-back week with Ladd McConkey's status uncertain and the Seahawks' defense waiting for them in Seattle. 

  • Bo Nix at 49ers – Nix finally stepped up for fantasy managers last week, in part thanks to a rushing touchdown. They all count though. We'll see if he can get the Broncos into scoring position as frequently against a 49ers defense allowing the eighth-fewest fantasy points to QBs. 

Omarion Hampton, RB, Chargers

at Seahawks

Hampton has been unspectacular in the early part of the season, saving his fantasy performances in the first two weeks by scoring touchdowns. That's important since his role in the passing game is limited and potentially shrinking. 

Keaton Mitchell and Kimani Vidal had their usage increase, resulting in Hampton only running a route on 16% of the dropbacks in Week 3. While I'm not concerned about his job security, it is worrisome that we might be talking about a three-man committee in an offense that's stumbled so far. 

The Seahawks aren't a defense to target either, since they're giving up the fifth-fewest points to runners. The schedule also doesn't relent for the next couple months with matchups against the Broncos, Chiefs, Rams, Texans and Ravens. 

Hampton might have to be started depending on your roster, but he's more of a TD-or-bust RB3 right now.  

Other RBs to sit:

  • Rhamondre Stevenson at Bills – Stevenson might be slightly undervalued in terms of his rest-of-season value, since his usage rebounded after fumbling in Week 2. Unfortunately, he's another ball-carrier sharing his backfield in a struggling offense. He's a TD-or-bust RB3 in a game where the Pats could fall behind quickly. 

  • Tony Pollard at Ravens – While the Ravens have given up solid stat lines to the likes of Jonathan Taylor and Javonte Williams, we can project the same for Pollard in a game the Titans will likely trail. Scoring opportunities are also few and far between for Tennessee.  

  • J.K. Dobbins at 49ers – Dobbins has been held to 36 yards, 36 yards and 53 yards during his first three appearances this season. He only caught one pass and has yet to visit the end zone. He's just a low-ceiling fantasy option, with RJ Harvey soaking up all the pass-catching work. 

Emeka Egbuka, WR, Buccaneers

vs. Packers

Through three weeks, Egbuka's numbers haven't been terrible, especially when you consider the overall state of the Bucs' offense. Stat lines of 5-63-0, 3-16-1 and 5-62-0 aren't going to destroy your chances of winning a fantasy week, but they aren't going to lead you to victory either. 

Now, he'll have to build on those performances without the help of Baker Mayfield for the next few weeks. Jalon Daniels is an intriguing rookie backup, but expecting him to improve this offense is wishful thinking. 

So even in a positive matchup with the Packers, I have Egbuka ranked as a volatile WR3/flex option. 

Other WRs to sit:

  • Ladd McConkey/Quentin Johnston at Seahawks – McConkey was seen walking around the locker room with a limp after being downgraded to DNP for Thursday's practice. Even if he suits up, the injury and matchup with the Seahawks is enough for me to bench him. Meanwhile, Johnston has been so bad this year that he would just be a risky WR3/flex option if McConkey sits out. Tre' Harris is an intriguing stash though. 

  • Rome Odunze vs. Jets – The Bears' passing game is being split four ways instead of three now that Kalif Raymond has a legitimate role. Odunze's average depth of target is nearly double his fellow receivers and he isn't getting many of the easy targets. That makes him a TD-or-bust WR4/flex. 

  • Xavier Worthy at Raiders – Worthy hasn't topped 25 yards this season. A big play is possible at any point, but he's a very dangerous flex swing with an extremely low floor for fantasy managers. 

Dalton Schultz, TE, Texans

vs. Cowboys

It turns out other defensive coordinators get to watch prior game film and after seeing Schultz catch 12 passes for 140 yards in Week 2, the Colts made it a priority to cover him last Sunday. The result was just three targets, three receptions and 30 yards. 

With Nico Collins expected to return this week, the volume scam for Schultz is over. The Cowboys have also held every tight end other than Isaiah Likely under 25 yards. 

While Schultz can still be started as a lower-end TE2 streamer, you should be able to find a better option.

Other TEs to sit:

  • Colston Loveland vs. Jets – Loveland isn't commanding the immense target share he had down the stretch last season. With the Bears being content to spread the ball around more, Loveland is just a risky TE2 until we see otherwise. New York's defense hasn't given up a touchdown to tight ends yet, with 44 yards being the highest output against it.  

  • Kyle Pitts Sr. at Saints – When Drake London is healthy, Pitts is an afterthought in the Falcons' passing attack. His stat lines of 0-0-0, 1-15-0 and 1-5-0 should have been reason enough for you to drop him this week.

item.title: Case Keenum is a nice story, but Bears should pivot to Tyson Bagent | Opinion
item.description: The 38-year-old third-stringer was spectacular in a win over the Eagles. But there are multiple reasons Case Keenum should return to the bench.
item.content:encoded:
As the 2026 NFL season enters October, perhaps there’s been no better story over the first few weeks than third-string quarterback Case Keenum leading the Chicago Bears to a resounding 27-7 defeat of the Philadelphia Eagles in front of a “Monday Night Football” audience on Sept. 28. It was the first regular-season game the 38-year-old journeyman had played in more than 1,000 days.

But if the Bears are smart, they won’t try to double down on the Keenum magic by asking him to perform an encore six days later.

As head coach Ben Johnson prepares the Bears to face the atypically frisky New York Jets at Soldier Field on Sunday afternoon, he isn’t saying whether Keenum or backup Tyson Bagent, who spent most of the week prior to the Eagles game in concussion protocol, will start. Johnson even seemed to leave the door open for blossoming starter Caleb Williams to play, though the hamstring injury he suffered in Week 2 is expected to keep him out for roughly a month.

“We've got three guys, and we'll work through the week and see where they're at,” Johnson said Wednesday.

“Whoever we feel like gives us the best chance to win.”

And while Keenum ripped through the Eagles defense for 247 yards and two TDs with his arm before scoring himself on a “sucker sneak” for a fourth-quarter exclamation point, there are simply too many good reasons for Johnson to pivot to Bagent against the Jets. So let’s count them:

Bears have already signaled preference for Tyson Bagent

You’re not supposed to lose your job because of injury in the NFL, though it definitely happens – just ask Drew Bledsoe, Trent Green, Trey Lance or countless others. But vaulting a nomadic QB3 who may be an ex-NFL player at just about any time over a highly regarded, young backup seems foolish.

“There was a reason why Tyson ended training camp as our number two quarterback,” Johnson said after beating the Eagles.

The coach also gushed about Bagent, an undrafted free agent in 2023 despite setting numerous NCAA and FCS passing records at Division II Shepherd University (West Virginia), when the Bears pre-emptively gave him a two-year, $10 million contract extension last summer.

"I've really been blown away by his approach,” Johnson, who knows a little something about quarterbacks and offense, said at the time.

“He does a tremendous job knowing what to do, how to do it and getting it done. … I think we actually have one of the best rooms in the NFL, certainly that I've been around in my career from top to bottom.”

Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor was nearly as complimentary this week.

“He's a guy that we've never felt like you have to worry about his mindset,” he said of Bagent. “He's one of the most locked in people I've ever been around.”

Tyson Bagent needs reps, for his own good and Bears

Bagent hasn’t started an NFL game since his rookie year, when he went 2-2 while subbing in for Justin Fields, and never for Johnson, who was hired last year. And while it’s tempting to go back to Keenum, getting Bagent sharpened and further experienced is probably the best play over the longer run – especially if Williams goes down again later this season.

Also? At some point, Bagent’s contract is going to expire (after the 2027 season actually). Yet he’s already shown enough to suggest he’s the kind of player another team might want to take a chance on as its long-term starter – in a similar vein as Jimmy Garoppolo or, just this year, Malik Willis. If Bagent gets more game action and excels – which seems fairly likely given what Keenum just put on tape while playing in Johnson’s system – then it becomes far more likely that the 26-year-old becomes a valuable asset that GM Ryan Poles could eventually spin off into draft capital at a time when it seems likely the Bears will no longer be perennially choosing players in the top 10.

“I have absolutely zero ego in this, and nobody's a bigger cheerleader and a fan of  Case Keenum than I am,” Bagent said Thursday.

“Yes, of course, it goes without being said that I would love to be in the game, love to make an impact for the team and love to make a difference when my number is called.”

The Ben Johnson factor

Chicago’s coach, perhaps the most highly regarded offensive mind in the league right now, just put another impressive bullet point on his résumé with Monday night’s win. And it’s important to note he had a full week to prepare a game plan tailored to Keenum – and his limitations. And the Eagles basically invited Keenum to beat them, instead clamping down on the Bears’ normally prolific ground game to the tune of 3.7 yards per carry – that success partly fueled because Keenum lacks the mobility of Bagent or Williams. And while Rome Odunze dropped a perfectly thrown Keenum pass for a TD, what turned into a spectacular 41-yard TD pass to Kalif Raymond later in the game was a complete bailout by Raymond – the wide receiver almost pirouetting to snatch a poorly thrown pass before taking it to the house.

KALIF RAYMOND TO THE HOUSE

📺: ESPN pic.twitter.com/JYrzzQ1Ol0

— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) September 29, 2026

Moving forward?

Though they’re only 1-2, the Jets are playing far better football – offensively and defensively – than the Eagles and just took Johnson’s former team, the still-explosive Detroit Lions, to the wire in Motown last weekend. The Bears will almost certainly benefit from putting Bagent into the lineup given his ability to contribute to the running game with his fresh legs, operate more effectively on rollouts and also stretch the field given his arm is much stronger than Keenum’s. And opening downfield windows for Johnson is typically deadly for the opposition.

Changing QBs creates another problem for Jets

Part of the reason for Keenum’s success was also that the Eagles really had no topical film to study of him operating Johnson’s offense – and preseason most definitely does not count. The same will apply to Bagent, who should now benefit from more than a full week of prep since he came back from the concussion, and maybe more so since his physical skill set should broaden Johnson’s play-calling options.

And if you don’t think teams struggle to beat unfamiliar backups? Consider that the six quarterbacks who have started games this season – despite not being their respective team’s Week 1 starter – are a collective 6-0. It’s another good reason to start Bagent, especially since the Jets have a much better idea how to defend Keenum than Philadelphia did.

And Keenum wants you to know the Bears will be fine, for now, with Williams out and that you should expect them to excel regardless of who’s in the lineup – maybe especially so with Bagent.

“It's not like we've been sitting on the couch and eating potato chips, or tortilla chips and queso and guac and salsa,” he said, referring to himself and Bagent.

“We've been working our tails off. That's part of this job, preparing. And when preparation meets the opportunity that's what it looks like. If his name's called, I expect the same, if not better. He's a baller.”

Sounds like Case closed.

item.title: Fantasy Football: Is Week 4 the last hope for these four polarizing players?
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen highlights four players who will be under the microscope in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
My wife and I have binged each season of "Shrinking" since it came out because nobody on the show gets to make an easy choice. You're not twisting my arm to put Harrison Ford on my screen. But how each character has to confront their issues, even in their light-hearted comedic way, is, ironically, therapeutic. One quote from Ford's character has stuck with me since he said it:

"You don't know whether your choice is right or wrong until you make it."

We're about a month into the fantasy football season. Some of what we've seen makes sense. But for a few of our players, all we've gotten is disappointment. The easy move is to cut them, but we keep waiting for the breakout that the data, or our gut, told us was coming. We won't know if holding is the right call until we make it. But we can define what "right" looks like.

Here's what we need to see from a few of this season's biggest disappointments to keep them around.

Marvin Harrison Jr., Cardinals

I was willing to lay all of Marvin Harrison Jr.'s shortcomings at Drew Petzing's feet. It was the playcalling. The former fourth-overall pick needed a scheme change. But the first three weeks of 2026 have brought us more of the same.

Every Marvin Harrison Jr. route run from Week 3 vs. the 49ers:

Some of my biggest notes:
- Routes are rounded, lacks suddenness
- Doesn't run as hard when he's not the primary read
- Creates little separation on the outside
- Best work came with deep in-breaking routes pic.twitter.com/Xx6QAojO1B

— Tommy Jaggi (@TommyJaggi) September 30, 2026

By this point, you know how I approach evaluating players. I'll be the first to admit assessing film isn't my strong suit. And while I agree with Tommy Jaggi's critique of Harrison Jr. above, let's say that you don't. Jacoby Brissett could have some culpability here. But the data says otherwise.

  • Target Rate (on the perimeter): 62.8% (Michael Wilson), 18.6% (Harrison)

  • Catch Rate: 66.7%, 50.0%

  • Yards per Route Run: 3.88, 1.82

I isolated the snaps where Brissett threw to the boundary, where Harrison has primarily operated (81.4% snap rate from the outside). Granted, we're working with a three-game sample. But there isn't a single efficiency metric that favors the Ohio State product. In fact, Trey McBride has generated half as many first downs as Harrison from the same alignment. And I'll let you figure out which WR has the only drop. Plus, going back to the commentary, Harrison's inability to create separation is something that shows up through the numbers.

Contested targets are where the defender is close by or right next to the receiver at the catch point. They make for great highlights, assuming our guys come down with them. But we'd like some layups. Harrison doesn't get those. At a 44.4% contested target rate, Arizona's WR2 has more than doubled the league average. Combined with a 17.8-yard aDOT, having just nine targets isn't a surprise. 

If you're still rostering Harrison, Week 4 is your last bastion. The Cardinals will face a Giants secondary below the league average in passing yards per game allowed to receivers, defensive EPA per play and pressure rate.

In short, it's an ideal situation.

However, let's make progress before we achieve perfection. While seeing Harrison in the end zone with the ball and a double-digit target rate above 15% would be a welcome sight. Balls thrown his way in the short area of the field would be even better. Anything to suggest his role isn't just to clear out space for Wilson or McBride would give me enough hope to hold on for at least one more week.

Omarion Hampton, Chargers

I'm not going to add to the number of think-pieces out there about the Chargers offense. I gave my two cents last week. But my focus was on the passing game. Unfortunately, their ground game hasn't been much better.

Omarion Hampton - Week 2 - every touch https://t.co/xz5CMdq8lmpic.twitter.com/bsVS5r618A

— Jacob Gibbs (@jagibbs_23) September 22, 2026

As the Chargers go, so does Omarion Hampton. His RB26, RB6, and RB40 finishes reflect the up-and-down nature of L.A.'s early-season returns. But a couple of things stick out from Jacob Gibbs' cutup of Hampton from Week 2 above.

First, if the hole was there, so was Hampton. Even as the gaps were closing, the second-year rusher was sticking his shoulder pads in for an extra yard or two. Said another way, his talent hasn't disappeared. If anything, he's (mostly) the same runner from '25.

  • Rushing Success Rate: 44.1% (2025 – Weeks 1-4, 17), 50.0% (2026)

  • Yards After Contact per Att.: 3.48, 3.00

  • Forced Missed Tackle Rate: 27.9%, 24.0%

Remember, we only got five full games with Hampton as the RB1. However, compared to full-season starters, Hampton's 27.9% forced missed tackle rate would've been behind only Bijan Robinson. Hampton would've been right next to both Lions' RBs in rushing success rate. The Chargers have a good rusher! However, fans have overstated the other takeaway, but it bears keeping in context.

  • Run Block Win Rate Rank: 31st (2025), 17th (2026)

  • Rate of Contact Behind the LOS: 58.1%, 52.0%

  • Yards Before Contact per Rush: 0.91, 0.86

By the letter (number?) of the law, the Chargers' offensive line has improved from last season. But that still leaves Hampton operating behind a sub-league-average run-blocking unit. With his offense in the bottom 10 for plays per game and yards per drive, he faces an uphill battle to pick up yards, and that's before considering Keaton Mitchell's workload.

Having to go through Seattle, Denver and Kansas City before the bye doesn't instill confidence. Ladd McConkey's foot injury makes things worse. But any consistency to the passing game would be a boon. Justin Herbert getting into a rhythm with his receivers, an increase in third-down conversions (35.1% conversion rate through three weeks), and generating explosives are all things we should be monitoring.

If we can see Hampton's environment improving, so will his results.

Jadarian Price, Seahawks

I have Jadarian Price in a league, and the platform we were using kept notifying me that Seattle was in the red zone multiple times on Sunday. The next message was supposed to be a message indicating Price scored a rushing TD. I never got one of those. I see why now.

JADARIAN PRICE FUMBLES!

Seahawks RB Jadarian Price puts the ball on the ground against the Commanders!#NFL#Seahawks#Commanders#F4Fpic.twitter.com/n0j8VaOt6L

— F4F (@F4F_Media) September 27, 2026

Price's two fumbles are tied for the most in the league among all RBs. To go with the wild day that was the Seahawks' trip to Maryland, the rookie's turnovers cost them the game. More importantly, the loss of trust in Price's ball-handling skills cut into his playing time.

After the fumble early in the first quarter, Price didn't see the field again until midway through the second. Enter: George Holani and Emanuel Wilson. Luckily, neither found the end zone. But based on their opportunity, they might have.

  • Rushing Share (Week 3): 53% (Wilson), 18% (Holani)

  • Route Rate: 28%, 28%

  • Goal-line Carry Rate: 67%, 33%

The carries from inside the 5-yard line for either backup are the most concerning part if you have Price. To date, he has one such carry. The Cardinals met him in the backfield. Price went nowhere. Across three contests, his two "backups" have nine.

Seattle's opened Zach Charbonnet's practice window, indicating a return is imminent. Worst-case scenario, he adds to the goal-line uncertainty for Price. But we do have time. 

Price's next three matchups (Chargers, 49ers and Broncos) are against defenses in the top half of the league in fantasy points allowed to RBs. Holding onto the ball would be the right step forward. Showcasing his power and burst to consolidate the backfield touches would be better.

However, if more of the same continues, at least we'll know what to expect when Charbonnet is back on the field.

David Montgomery, Texans

I wrote a "Worst Pick By Round" series during the offseason, highlighting historical profiles we should avoid and players who fit the mold for 2026. David Montgomery made the list. Apparently, he took that personally.

David Montgomery having a day!!! pic.twitter.com/2lsNUSmgUj

— Adam Rank (@adamrank) September 13, 2026

I was fretting over Cincinnati's back-and-forth game against the Bucs, so I wasn't paying attention to the game in realtime. But I did get the notifications of his touchdowns. I was ready to capitulate two quarters into the year. However, when I went under the hood, I got more worried for Montgomery.

  • Adj. Yards after Contact per Att.: 2.6

  • Forced Missed Tackle Rate: 15.0%

  • Rate of Contact Behind the LOS: 70.0%

For reference, Woody Marks in the same game had better … marks across the board. Of the 34 RBs with 10 or more carries in Week 1, Montgomery's success rate ranked 16th. His 3.0 YPC was just above MarShawn Lloyd's. And while Marks's involvement has oscillated each week, the full picture emphasizes my pre-draft concern about a fragile workload.

  • Snap Rate: 55.0% (Montgomery), 45.0% (Marks)

  • Short-Yardage Rushing Share: 48.0%, 52.0%

  • Two-Minute Snap Rate: 45.0%, 55.0%

I'm willing to entertain the idea that Nico Collins' absence has changed OC Nick Caley's game plans. Without Collins, I could see the need for more players with speed on the field to create big plays. So, Sunday will be Montgomery's first test.

Even with Dallas' defensive upgrade, a WR of Collins' caliber should stretch any defense, enabling more rushing lanes for Montgomery. Houston's run blocking is still an issue. But if Week 1 was how the Texans intend to run the offense, Montgomery should be back in the RB1 saddle with positive matchups against the Titans and Giants coming up. With signs he's still in control of the backfield, we can trust him as a mid-range RB2 in the short term.

item.title: Marcus Mariota to Start vs the Colts
item.description: An Old foe makes his return to face the Colts for the first time since 2019. Can the Colts beat Mariota for a 6th time?
item.content:encoded:
For the first time since Avengers: Endgame was the top grossing movie in the US (2019), the Colts will face off against Marcus Mariota at Quarterback. On Friday the Washington Commanders announced that starting QB Jaden Daniels would be out for a 2nd straight week with an elbow injury. Thus Mariota gets another start after leading a surprise upset victory over the reigning Super Bowl Champion Seahawks in Week 3.

Last week Mariota had 3 Passing TDs: one to RB Rachaad White, one to fellow former Tennessee Titan (albeit different eras) Treylon Burks, and one to former Mr Indiana Football Terry McLaurin.

He has yet to turn the ball over, and out of 32 QBs with 45+ Passing Attempts, Mariota ranks 11th in On Target Throw Rate at 77.3% (Daniel Jones is right behind him at 12th with 76.3%). And its not because Mariota has been dinking and dunking with short throws either, he ranks 7th in Average Depth of Throw with 8.5 showing a willingness to test a Defense vertically (stats per Sports Info Solutions).

The 32 year old former 2nd Overall Pick for the Tennessee Titans has a 2-5 record as a starter against the Colts from his 2015-2019 tenure with the AFC South rival to start his career. In those 7 career games he has racked up:

  • 143/217 Passing = 65.9% Completion %
  • 1,618 Passing Yards
  • 7.5 Yards Per Attempt
  • 9 Passing TDs
  • 6 INTs
  • 20 Sacks
  • 90.4 Passer Rating
  • 21 Carries
  • 96 Rushing Yards
  • 4.6 Yards Per Carry
  • 0 Rushing TDs
  • 4 Fumbles

But it has been 7 years since then, and in that time Marcus Mariota has bounced around the league. His NFL journey has had 4 different stops since he lost the starting job to Ryan Tannehill mid-2019 season:

  • The Las Vegas Raiders backup QB (2020-2021)
  • 13 Game Starter with the Atlanta Falcons (2022)
  • Backup QB for the Philadelphia Eagles (2023)
  • Backup QB with the Washington Commanders, 8 starts in 2025 with Daniels injured (2024-present)

Since leaving the Titans, Mariota has appeared in 43 games (22 starts) and recorded some solid stats as a journeyman:

  • 420/671 Passing = 62.6% Completion %
  • 4,966 Passing Yards
  • 7.4 Yards Per Attempts
  • 35 Passing TDs
  • 18 INTs
  • 52 Sacks
  • 91.3 Passer Rating
  • 189 Carries
  • 1,068 Rushing Yards
  • 5.7 Yards Per Carry
  • 8 Rushing TDs
  • 16 Fumbles

As both teams journey to London, England to face off at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, the Colts have an opportunity to beat an old foe once again and Mariota has a shot at redemption against one of his biggest obstacles from early in his career.

item.title: Bears vs. Jets: Keys to a Chicago victory
item.description: The Bears will once again start a backup QB. Our crew shares their keys to a Chicago victory.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears could be starting a third-straight different quarterback against the New York Jets on Sunday.

And for perhaps the first time in Bears history, that isn’t the largest concern.

Such is the Ben Johnson experience.

That isn’t to say it’s not a problem. It just isn’t the biggest problem.

Johnson has proved he can design a game plan that will be effective for about any defense and fit whatever players are available to him at the time.

So let’s get to the keys to the game for the Chicago Bears to beat the New York Jets on Sunday.

Sam: Rely on the ground game, get behind that offensive line and just grind out a win. The Jets’ pass defense will cause problems, but Chicago has the advantage on the ground. On defense, find a way to get after Geno Smith and don’t let Garrett Wilson beat you.

Lester: The Jets’ defense has been much improved this season, but that shouldn’t prevent the Bears from imposing their will in the running game. Regardless of which backup QB is playing, trying to replicate Monday’s quick pass game plan wouldn’t make sense. On defense, show blitz to confuse the pass protection, but drop off and cover because Geno Smith is completing 84.6% of his passes against the blitz this season.

Josh: I think Ben needs to keep doing Ben things, hunting explosives with relentless attention to the run game and shoving bodies around. Dennis Allen just made doubters look silly, and now he needs to show that it wasn’t a fluke. Take advantage of the loss of Hall and contest every catch.

Donald: So I’m going with the theory it is Tyson on Sunday. With that, the key for Tyson is to model himself after Case against the Eagles – quick and efficient passing. Don’t turn the ball over. Lean on the run game. With Swift on the report, I think the Bears will feature Monangai, and I think he can handle the load against the Jets.  As for the defense, we know Geno puts the ball in harm’s way. I see Muhammed and Thineman getting on the board with picks. And we will see another good DL line stack with Booker, Sweat, and motivated Dayo getting pressure. If the Bears win the turnover battle and BJ again dissects the opposing defense, the Bears will have another victory in their grasp.

Mongo Peanut: The Jets are better than they have been recently, and the Bears need to come in prepared. Still, the Bears are the more talented and complete team, even with Caleb sidelined. The key to the game is for the Bears to simply limit the mistakes. They have committed a lot of penalties and have executed poorly in the red zone thus far, having only scored TDs on 50% of trips, which is good for 21st in the league.
If the Bears clean those things up and play an efficient operation, they ought to win this one.

What are your keys to the game? Share them in the comments.

item.title: Browns and Steelers mismanaged the final seconds of the game
item.description: On Sunday, the Ravens and the Cowboys provided stark examples on how to handle, and how not to handle, the final seconds of a close game in light of the current kickoff rules.
item.content:encoded:
On Sunday, the Ravens and the Cowboys provided stark examples on how to handle, and how not to handle, the final seconds of a close game in light of the current kickoff rules.

The Steelers and the Browns apparently learned nothing from it.

After the Browns failed to work the clock down to the final few seconds before what became the game-winning field goal, 10 seconds remained.

Like the Cowboys in Rio, the Browns kicked into the end zone, giving the Steelers the ball at the 35. (A cutaway to Browns coach Todd Monken seemed to reveal his dismay.) It opened the door for the Steelers, who had a timeout in hand, to try to gain just enough yardage to allow for a field goal that would have forced overtime.

From the TV copy, it appeared that the Browns were playing the same kind of outside leverage that the Cowboys deployed when the Ravens, who had only seven seconds to work with, gained 27 yards and kicked the walk-off field goal. That gave the Steelers a shot at completing a pass in the middle of the field.

But the Steelers didn't call a play that would have entailed a quick throw for a moderate gain and a shot at a field goal.

Instead, quarterback Aaron Rodgers rolled to his right, looking to uncork a long throw. The pass, which came back to earth just inside the Cleveland 20, was intercepted. Game over.

Why not try for a 20- to 30-yard gain? Quick decision, quick throw. If it works, take the time out and try the field goal. If it doesn't, let Rodgers try to connect on another Thursday night miracle.

Coach Mike McCarthy (or Rodgers himself) inexplicably opted for a middle ground, with a long throw that, if it had connected, possibly would have allowed for a time out and a short field goal.

The decision made no sense. The Steelers could have had two shots — a shorter attempt to put them in field goal range for overtime and, if that failed (without an interception), a Hail Mary to win it.

The 2025 shift of the touchback point from the 30 to the 35 has significantly altered the available strategies for the final 10-15 seconds of a game. The Browns repeated the Cowboys' mistake by conceding the 35, and the Steelers failed to try to seize upon the very real possibility of using the final 10 seconds to gain enough ground to send it into overtime.

item.title: Week 4 NFL betting, odds: Picks against the spread, winners for every game from a blended AI model
item.description: We asked an AI model with four sets of NFL power ratings blended together to pick the against-the-spread winner of every Week 4 NFL game. Here are the results.
item.content:encoded:
Week 4 of the NFL season kicked off on Thursday night, as Deshaun Watson and the Cleveland Browns improved to 3-1 on the season with an impressive 27-24 win against Aaron Rodgers’ Pittsburgh Steelers as a three-point home underdog.

How will the rest of the weekend’s games play out?

We used a blended model with four NFL power ratings, including ESPN's FPI and FTN Fantasy's DVOA rankings, and asked Claude to simulate the final score of every Week 4 game and give a brief write-up of why the game would play out that way. We also asked it to list the against-the-spread winner and if the game went over or under the total.

Here are the results for every Week 4 game:

Indianapolis Colts (-4, 48.5) vs. Washington Commanders (in London)

The market has Indianapolis by four, but my ratings have it closer to a pick'em. Both defenses are bad: Indianapolis allows +19.2% DVOA and Washington +8.3%. Both teams give up about 30 points per game, so this should be high-scoring. The Colts' special teams (+9.4%) give them a slight edge on a neutral field, but Washington getting four points is the better value.

Projected score: Colts 26, Commanders 25

ATS winner: Commanders +4

O/U: Over

Tennessee Titans at Baltimore Ravens (-12, 42.5)

Baltimore's offense is third in DVOA (+28.1%) and scores 30.7 points per game. Tennessee is 0-3, scores 12.3 PPG and has one of the league's worst special teams units (-11.0%). The Ravens win comfortably, but the model's 11-point margin is half a point short of the spread, so the Titans cover only barely. The over is steadier: Baltimore's defense is only average, so Tennessee should reach 17 points.

Projected score: Ravens 28, Titans 17

SU winner: Ravens

ATS winner: Titans +12

New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills (-6.5, 48.5)

Buffalo's offense (+37.5% DVOA) should dominate a Patriots offense that ranks last (-29.9%) after a 35-6 loss at Jacksonville. New England's defense is good (eighth), and Buffalo's (22nd) just survived a minus-four turnover game, which keeps this from being a blowout. The model's 6.6-point margin lands just past the new number, so the Bills cover by a hair. Treat it as a lean, not a pick. New England scores only 12 per game, which keeps the total near 45, under 48.5.

Projected score: Bills 26, Patriots 19

SU winner: Bills

ATS winner: Bills -6.5

O/U: Under

Jacksonville Jaguars at Cincinnati Bengals (-2.5, 51.5)

This is a coin flip, and Jacksonville's defense tips it. The Jaguars rank second in DVOA (+43.1%) and allow just 12 points per game. Cincinnati is good (+18.8%, seventh) but allows 21 per game and is only favored on home field. Jacksonville plus 2.5 is solid value. The total of 51 is the highest on the slate, but one elite defense points to about 47.

Arizona Cardinals (-2.5, 44) at New York Giants

The market has Arizona favored, but its defense is 31st in DVOA (+21.9%) and allows 27 points per game. Chicago scores 29.7 per game and allows 17.7, and its offense is eighth in DVOA. The Bears beat Philadelphia 27-7 last week with Case Keenum at quarterback. The Jets just lost to Detroit and have poor special teams (-7.4%, 28th). The model projects a five-point Chicago win, covering -3.5. The Bears alone should score about 25, and the Jets get to 20, which clears 43.

Dallas has a top-five offense (+22.6% DVOA, 29.3 points per game) but a bad defense (27th). Houston is 0-3, though DVOA still ranks it 17th. My composite ratings give Dallas a slight edge, so the Cowboys' +3 is the value side. The model projects 49 total points, just over 48, which makes the over the thinnest lean on the board.

Green Bay is the clear pick with Baker Mayfield out. The Packers' defense is the main reason, even though their DVOA is a modest +12.8%. Tampa Bay's 20.7 points per game came with Mayfield, and a rookie making his first start should score less. Jalon Daniels' rushing ability and a simplified game plan around Emeka Egbuka and Bucky Irving help a little. The model's 4.4-point margin clears 3.5, but only by about a point, so it's a lean. item.title: T.J. Watt: Steelers made it too easy for Browns to go downfield at the end of the game
item.description: Steelers linebacker T.J.
item.content:encoded:
Steelers linebacker T.J. Watt had a sack, two tackles for loss, a pass deflection and two quarterback hits on Thursday night, but he was not happy with the defensive effort in the 27-24 loss to the Browns.

After the Steelers tied the game 24-24 with 1:42 remaining in the fourth quarter, the Browns went 36 yards on seven plays to move into range for the game-winning field goal. Watt said that led to the Steelers losing a game they should have won.

"To sit here and not be 3-1 isn't acceptable," Watt said, via Steelers.com. "Obviously, it's a long season, a lot left to go, but we just have to put it together. Even at the end of the game, it was way too easy [for the Browns] getting down the field and getting in [field goal] range. Just have to look at everything and move forward."

The Steelers' next three games are against teams with losing records -- the Colts, Buccaneers and Saints -- and then they have a rematch with the Browns. The schedule sets up for Pittsburgh to go on a run, but Watt knows the defense needs to play better.

item.title: Raiders-Chiefs Week 4: 5 things to watch
item.description: Can the Raiders pull off another upset to improve to 4-0?
item.content:encoded:
There is a huge game Sunday as the 3-00 Las Vegas Raiders host the 3-0 Kansas City Chiefs at Allegiant Stadium on Sunday. Kickoff is set for 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys for the Raiders to stay unbeaten:

Turnover magic:

A big reason why the Raiders are undefeated is how well their defense is creating turnovers. They have had had multiple takeaways in all three games (including four in the fourth quarter at New Orleans in Week 3) and have a league-high nine on the season. They are plus-five on turnover differential. That’s is a winning formula. It needs to keep up against the Chiefs.

Brock, Brock, Brock:

Raider’s star Brock Bowers showed his impact on this offense at New Orelans in his season debut. He had 10 catches for 116 cayrds and ccoach Klint Kubiak lined up in severeal different ways. Bwoers is an X Factor for this offense. The Riaders need to ride him to victory Sunday.

Stop Kelce:

While Bowers is a key for the Raiders’ offense, stopping Travis Kelce is a key for the Raiders’ defense. Kelce is re-energized and is having a big season so far. This guy is a noted Raiders’ killer, anyway. So, you know he will be up for this game. He can’t take over.

The crowd:

This is the biggest Raiders’ game at Allegiant Stadium since the Chargers’ game to end the 2021 season. Chiefs fans have famously taken over Allegiant Stadium every year since fans have been allowed inside for games. That can’t happen this week. This has to be a pro-home team crowd.

Third-down defense:

The Raiders allowed the Saints to convert on third down nine of 15 times in Week 3. That can’t happen against Patrick Mahomes, Kenneth Walker and Kelce.

item.title: Fantasy Football Matchups to Exploit in Week 4
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Ray Garvin breaks down key matchups in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
C.J. Stroud, QB, Houston Texans vs. Dallas Cowboys

C.J. Stroud has not been perfect through three weeks, but Houston has made one thing very clear: it wants to put the ball in his hands. Stroud has already attempted 120 passes. Only one quarterback in football has thrown it more. That volume has produced 794 passing yards, three touchdowns and no interceptions.

The bigger news this week is that Nico Collins looks like he is on track to return.

That is a game changer for an offense that has looked slow and lacked explosiveness without him. There might not be a wide receiver in football who means more to what his offense wants to do than Collins does for Houston. He gives Stroud a true downfield weapon, somebody who can win outside and a receiver who forces defenses to account for him on every snap.

Getting him back could not come at a better time.

Dallas has allowed 23.5 fantasy points per game to quarterbacks through three weeks, the third-highest mark in the league. Opposing quarterbacks have not needed to beat them with their legs either. Teams have consistently created explosive plays through the air and stressed this secondary.

This is the type of matchup where I want to bet on Stroud's passing volume finally turning into a bigger fantasy performance.

I have Stroud ranked as my QB11 with 18.7 projected fantasy points compared to QB17 in ECR. That puts him right back into the low-end QB1 conversation for me.

If you have been streaming quarterbacks or rotating through that second tier of options, Stroud is the guy I would be moving toward this week. Houston is already throwing the football at one of the highest rates in the league. Add Collins back into the mix against this Dallas secondary, and we may finally see this passing attack open up.

Aaron Jones Sr., RB, Minnesota Vikings vs. Miami Dolphins

There was some question entering the season about how this Minnesota backfield would shake out. We have our answer now. With Jordan Mason on injured reserve, Aaron Jones Sr. has taken control.

Jones has 52 carries for 203 yards and a touchdown through three games with another five catches for 34 yards. More importantly, over the last two weeks he has handled 40 carries and cleared 90 scrimmage yards in both games.

That is the type of workload I want before I even look at the opponent.

Then you get Miami.

The Dolphins have allowed 29.3 PPR points per game to running backs through three weeks, the third-highest mark in the league. Opposing backs have already totaled 293 rushing yards, three rushing touchdowns and another 95 yards through the air.

This is not one of those situations where I am pounding the table because my ranking is wildly different from consensus. I have Jones at RB15 and ECR has him at RB15.

What I like is how clean the setup is.

Jones has the workload, he has been productive with it and he gets a Miami defense that has been giving up fantasy production to the position.

I am starting him as a strong RB2 this week. If Minnesota controls the game and continues feeding Jones, the volume gives him access to an RB1 finish.

Jalen Coker, WR, Carolina Panthers vs. Detroit Lions

Jalen Coker is probably my favorite upside swing in this article. He is also the one we have to monitor closely because of the injury uncertainty.

Coker has caught 18 of 22 targets for 222 yards and two touchdowns through three games. He saw nine targets in each of the first two weeks before a quad injury shortened his Week 3.

If he is healthy enough to return to his normal role, the matchup is about as good as you could ask for.

Detroit has allowed 39.7 PPR points per game to wide receivers, the third-highest mark in the league. The Lions have also allowed the sixth-most yards per target and the ninth-most fantasy points per opportunity to perimeter receivers.

That fits what Coker has already been doing inside this Carolina offense.

He is not some random dart throw we are trying to talk ourselves into because the opponent looks good. The targets were already there. The production was already there. Detroit just gives him an opportunity to turn that volume into something much bigger.

I currently have Coker ranked as my WR20 with 10.9 projected half-PPR points compared to WR68 in ECR. That massive gap is almost entirely about his health status.

He missed Wednesday before returning to limited work Thursday, so the final practice report is important.

If Coker gets through the week cleanly and there is no indication that Carolina plans to restrict him, I am treating him as an upside WR2 against Detroit.

If we start hearing snap count, limited role or setback, then you move off of it. But if the quad cooperates, this is a smash spot.

Bhayshul Tuten, RB, Jacksonville Jaguars at Cincinnati Bengals

Bhayshul Tuten has quietly been one of the more dependable young running backs through three games.

Nothing about the production has been outrageous. That is actually part of why I like the profile.

He has 43 carries for 204 yards and two touchdowns with five catches for 36 more yards. Tuten has received at least 15 touches in every game and his rushing totals have landed between 65 and 73 yards each week. The workload has been remarkably steady.

Now he gets a Cincinnati defense that has not been a complete pushover against running backs, but teams have found room to run.

Opposing backs are averaging 4.5 yards per carry against the Bengals and have caught 18 of 20 targets through three games.

Tuten is giving us a stable workload with enough receiving usage to keep him involved even if the game script moves away from the run.

I have him ranked RB23 with 11.4 projected half-PPR points compared to RB19 in ECR.

Technically, I am lower than consensus, but a four-spot difference is not enough to scare me away from a player who has gotten at least 15 touches every week.

Sometimes we can get too caught up in whether a player is RB19 or RB23 when the actual lineup decision is much simpler.

Is he going to get the football enough to matter? Tuten has answered that question every week.

He is a flex for me in normal Yahoo leagues with enough touchdown equity to get right back into the RB2 range if Jacksonville gets into scoring position.

Jeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals at New York Giants

This is the Jeremiyah Love workload we have been waiting for. Week 3 felt different. Love handled 21 carries for 90 yards against San Francisco while Tyler Allgeier received only two carries. He also caught all five of his targets for 19 yards and a touchdown.

Twenty-six touches. A season-high 64% snap share. Now we have a role we can actually trust.

Through three games, Love has 41 carries for 160 yards and a touchdown with 10 catches on 12 targets for another 44 yards and a receiving score.

The rookie has been interesting from the beginning. The difference now is Arizona finally gave him a workload that puts him into normal redraft lineup decisions without us having to project a massive jump in usage.

The Giants have allowed 21.9 PPR points per game to running backs, the 11th-highest mark in the league. New York has given up 298 rushing yards to the position, along with 12 catches for 78 yards and two touchdowns.

I have Love ranked as my RB13 with 14.1 projected half-PPR points compared to RB9 in ECR. The model is a little more cautious than consensus. I am still starting him.

If Arizona gives Love anything close to the role we saw last week, he has already shown enough as a runner and receiver to support a strong RB2 outcome with legitimate RB1 upside.

The matchup is good. The workload is why I am buying it.
