item.title: Seahawks vs. Chargers, Week 4 preview: Can Seattle get back on track at home?
item.description: The Seahawks return home for a stretch of five games at Lumen Field over six weeks, starting with Jim Harbaugh’s 0-3 Chargers.
item.content:encoded:
After opening the season with two wins, the Seattle Seahawks enter Week 4 looking to bounce back from an unexpected 33-31 loss to the Washington Commanders. On the other side, the Los Angeles Chargers are still winless in 2026. They lost to the Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and Buffalo Bills, but the Chargers were in position to win their latest game after taking a 10-0 lead over Buffalo before eventually falling 24-16, despite forcing five turnovers.

The matchup will be played at Lumen Field in Seattle on Sunday, October 4, at 1:25 p.m. local time. It will be the first regular-season meeting between these teams since 2022, when the Seahawks defeated the Chargers 37-23 in Los Angeles.

For Seattle, this game is also an opportunity to prevent the loss in Washington from becoming the start of a negative stretch. The Seahawks committed three turnovers against the Commanders, and all three resulted in touchdowns, accounting for 20 of Washington’s 33 points. Seattle gained 437 yards compared to just 229 for Washington, but ultimately lost because it could not protect the football in the most important moments.

Can the Seahawks’ run game get back on track?

Perhaps the biggest question for Seattle entering this game is the running game. The Seahawks managed just 44 rushing yards against Washington after producing much better numbers during the first two weeks. The challenge now comes against a Chargers defense that has produced very different results from week to week.

Los Angeles allowed 116 rushing yards to Arizona in Week 1, then held Las Vegas to just 57 yards in Week 2 and Buffalo ran for 176 yards in Week 3, with James Cook accounting for 154 of them. Through three games, the Chargers are allowing about 116 rushing yards per game.

That means there is an opportunity for Seattle to try to re-establish its identity on the ground, but the matchup is not necessarily a simple one. Dalvin Tomlinson is an important piece of the interior defensive line, with Teair Tart and Jamaree Caldwell also there. Tomlinson might miss the game due to injury.

For Seattle, the goal will be to find a way to consistently gain yards without turning every run into a second- or third-and-long situation. After the struggles against Washington, establishing some offensive balance could also help take pressure off Sam Darnold.

The offensive line vs. the Chargers pass rush

The other major test for Seattle’s offense will come in pass protection. The Chargers have one of the more interesting pass-rush groups in the league, with Khalil Mack, Tuli Tuipulotu, and first-round rookie Akheem Mesidor giving them three players who can win from the edge.

Tuipulotu has already generated 12 pressures and two sacks through three games, while Mesidor has added five pressures and 1.5 sacks despite playing just 66 defensive snaps. Mack has also recorded two sacks this season.

The Chargers showed against Buffalo that they can create pressure without constantly sending extra rushers. Tuipulotu, in particular, was a problem for the Bills, finishing the game with 1.5 sacks and two quarterback hits.

That will be a major test for Seattle’s offensive line. Abe Lucas has been almost unrecognizable compared to the level we are accustomed to seeing from him this season, and this would be a good opportunity for him to get back to his usual level.

Grey Zabel will also need to rebound after a down game against Washington.

The Seahawks cannot afford to let the Chargers’ edge rushers consistently win early in the down. If Mack, Tuipulotu and Mesidor can create pressure without requiring additional help, Los Angeles can make life difficult for Darnold and limit the time available for Seattle’s deeper passing concepts.

Turnovers: the Chargers can take the ball away

There is an important similarity between these two teams entering this matchup: turnovers have already played a major role in their seasons.

Seattle turned the ball over three times against Washington, and all three turnovers became touchdowns.

The Chargers, meanwhile, just experienced almost the exact opposite situation. Against Buffalo, Los Angeles forced five turnovers — two interceptions and three fumble recoveries — but still lost.

That makes protecting the football particularly important for Seattle, especially for rookie running back Jadarian Price (assuming he plays after not practicing on Thursday). The Chargers have shown that their defense can create opportunities, and another game with multiple takeaways could give Los Angeles a path to victory even if the offense does not have a dominant performance.

Justin Herbert has given defenses opportunities

Justin Herbert remains the central figure of the Chargers’ offense, but there have been opportunities for opposing defenses to make plays against him this season.

Through three games, Herbert has thrown for 627 yards, three touchdowns and four interceptions, while taking eight sacks. More importantly for Seattle, his four interceptions do not tell the entire story. PFF has charted Herbert with seven turnover-worthy plays through his first three games.

That creates an interesting opportunity for Seattle’s defense. Herbert has already put the ball in harm’s way more often than his interception total suggests, and the Seahawks’ defense could be looking to turn those opportunities into actual takeaways.

Against Buffalo, Herbert finished with 226 passing yards, one touchdown and one interception. His interception came in the fourth quarter, when C.J. Gardner-Johnson undercut a throw intended for Marquez Valdes-Scantling near the goal line and returned it 41 yards.

Seattle’s pass rush vs. the Chargers offensive line

This matchup goes both ways. While the Chargers’ pass rush will test Seattle’s offensive line, the Seahawks’ front has a favorable opportunity against an offensive line that has had its share of problems through three weeks.

The Chargers’ interior has been particularly inconsistent. Cole Strange has allowed seven pressures through three games, while his PFF pass-blocking grade sits at just 25.6.

The unit has also struggled with penalties. Joe Alt was flagged four times against the Raiders in Week 2, and he was penalized again against Buffalo. That brought his season total to six penalties through three games, the most in the NFL.

That said, Alt’s season should not be reduced to those penalties. He had a strong performance against Buffalo and finished Week 3 with an 83.6 PFF grade, according to Chargers-focused reporting.

Still, the penalties are something Seattle can try to exploit. The Seahawks have the defensive line talent to make the Chargers play behind the chains, and the interior matchup against Strange could be particularly interesting.

Seattle’s pass rush will be particularly important here. Through three games, the Seahawks have generated seven sacks and 21 quarterback hits, with Leonard Williams and DeMarcus Lawrence leading the pressure production against Washington.

If Seattle can create pressure while maintaining its coverage integrity, there could be opportunities for the secondary to finally turn some of Herbert’s risky throws into turnovers.

Omarion Hampton vs. Seattle’s run defense

Los Angeles’ running game also deserves attention. Omarion Hampton has 193 rushing yards on 50 carries, averaging 3.9 yards per attempt, with two touchdowns. Against Buffalo, however, he was held to just 56 yards on 15 carries.

That will be another interesting test for Seattle’s defense. The Seahawks have allowed only 261 rushing yards through three games, an average of 87 per game.

The middle of Seattle’s defensive line has remained difficult to run through, but the edges gave Washington some opportunities last week. The Chargers could look to test those areas and force Seattle’s linebackers and safeties to make plays outside the tackles.

If Seattle can maintain its interior run defense while cleaning up some of the issues on the edges, it can force the Chargers into more obvious passing situations and allow the pass rush to become a bigger factor.

Ladd McConkey, Tre Harris, and the challenge for the secondary

In the passing game, Ladd McConkey (who didn’t practice on Thursday) has been the Chargers’ leading statistical target so far, with 12 receptions for 183 yards and a touchdown. Tre Harris has also emerged as an important part of the offense, with 10 receptions for 143 yards.

Quentin Johnston had his best game of the season against Buffalo in terms of involvement, although he also had a costly drop on third down. The combination of McConkey, Harris and Johnston gives Herbert several different options to attack the secondary.

For Seattle, that puts particular attention on the cornerbacks and how the defense handles different route concepts. Josh Jobe has an interception this season, but he has also given up two TDs in recent games and has struggled in several one-on-one situations.

The secondary will therefore be an important part of this matchup. Herbert has the arm talent to attack outside the numbers, and the Chargers have enough speed at receiver to turn a coverage mistake into an explosive play, particularly if Julian Love is unable to play.

A winless team that cannot be overlooked

The Chargers’ 0-3 record makes this look like a favorable matchup for Seattle on paper, but this could easily become a trap game. Los Angeles still has plenty of talent on both sides of the ball, along with a coaching staff capable of making adjustments.

The Chargers have been competitive in stretches of all three games. They led Buffalo 10-0 and were still ahead 13-10 entering the fourth quarter, while against Las Vegas, they had a chance to tie or take the lead late before Omarion Hampton’s fumble helped swing the game. Against Buffalo, the defense forced five turnovers and repeatedly gave the offense opportunities to take control.

That makes this an important game for Seattle not only because of what the Chargers have done so far, but because Los Angeles will be looking for its first opportunity to put together a complete performance. The Seahawks cannot afford to be the team against which the Chargers finally put everything together.

After the loss to Washington, Seattle has already seen what can happen when a team fails to capitalize on its advantages. The Chargers have enough talent, defensive playmakers and coaching to make this a difficult matchup if Seattle is not prepared from the opening snap.

Final Thoughts

The Seahawks and Chargers enter Week 4 in different situations, but with several similar questions. Seattle needs to clean up its turnover problem and find a way to get the running game back on track, while Los Angeles needs to turn its defensive production into points and wins. The Chargers have already shown that they can pressure quarterbacks and create turnovers, but their offense has not consistently capitalized on the opportunities created by the defense.

For Seattle, the priority should be getting back to the formula that produced the first two wins of the season: control the football, establish the run and let the defense dictate the pace of the game. The Chargers have players capable of changing the game at every level, from Mack, Tuipulotu, and Mesidor in the pass rush to Herbert and his receivers on offense.

The biggest difference could come down to which team is able to avoid giving the other extra possessions. Seattle already saw what three turnovers did against Washington. Los Angeles just showed that even five takeaways may not be enough if the offense cannot capitalize. In a matchup between two teams looking to correct very different problems, protecting the football and winning the line-of-scrimmage battles could decide the game.

item.title: The Deshaun Watson rehabilitation campaign is alive and disgusting
item.description: Deshaun Watson allegedly assaulting 27 women isn't 'adversity.’
item.content:encoded:
It was impossible to watch Thursday Night Football without being beaten over the head with veiled references to Deshaun Watson’s past. In what’s become one of the most disgusting rehabilitation campaigns in recent memory, Kirk Herbstreit, in particular, slobbered over Watson for the better part of the game, rebranding alleged sexual assault against 27 women as “past troubles” and turning the Browns’ recent success into a tale of overcoming adversity.

Coverage began on Thursday night with reporter Taylor Rooks having a sit-down interview with Watson, which never once directly mentioned the women he abused, instead vaguely referencing criticism of “Deshaun Watson the person,” as if his biggest crime was putting pineapple on pizza. We had to listen to Watson prattle on in platitudes about the struggles he’s pushed through, how he wants to be special, why he disagrees with people who criticize his character, and on several occasions he dropped jaw-dropping mentions of HIS need to forgive others. Yes, the man who allegedly abused 27 women is really needing to focus on forgiving the people who boo him, that’s his grand takeaway.

There’s no shortage of whitewashing past indiscretions of athletes, particularly when it comes to violence against women. It’s a predictable cycle of silence, followed by rehabilitation, then a return to business as usual. What makes the Watson situation unique is how announcers are trying to reduce his off-field actions and change the narrative to be about on-field performance. Herbstreit’s actions on Thursday Night Football were nothing short of vile, as he referenced fans booing Watson, his early struggles as the quarterback of the Browns, and now overcoming all that to lead them to victory.

No mention of Watson’s suspension, the backbreaking contract the team signed him to, the woman paid off to ensure their silence. If you tuned into a Browns game for the first time on Thursday, you would have thought Watson was a victim of irrational fan expectations, not that he leveraged the two-tier justice system to pay off the women he assaulted, rather than face any real punishment. That’s brass tacks: If Watson wasn’t a multi-millionaire, with the funds to pay off his accusers to the tune of $50M, at the very least he would have had to go through discovery, which could have led to evidence emerging that could have renewed criminal proceedings. Luckily for Watson, the system we have isn’t equal, and he was enabled through his NFL contracts to escape charges.

During the critical final drive of regulation, Herbstreit referred to Watson as “much maligned,” with Al Michaels chiming in “in capital letters,” as if to make light of the whole situation. This wasn’t simply the story of a quarterback playing bad football; he was a serial abuser who alienated fans of the Cleveland Browns when the organization decided to support him and insulate him, rather than cut him, take the hit, and move on. It was a perfect storm of incompetence that led us to this moment. Had the Browns not given Watson the worst quarterback contract in NFL history, which fully guaranteed his money — then he would have been cut for playing like ass two years ago, that’s it. Instead, he’s lingered on the back-end of the roster like a malignant tumor, and got the opportunity to start in the NFL again purely because he was marginally better than two other garbage options. It’s a bit like choosing to have meningitis, because the alternatives are hepatitis and rabies.

The Browns are winning football games. Watson is playing decently enough that the defense is able to carry the team. Sit down and watch him play the quarterback position, and it’s not as if Cleveland is benefiting from some individual brilliance. In fact, on the whole, Watson is mediocre, misses wide-open throws, and can’t actually drive to win a game. They beat the Buccaneers because Baker Mayfield has become a potato, the Panthers because they were missing five starters, and now the Steelers because Aaron Rodgers is washed. Good on them for winning the games in front of them, because that’s every team’s job — and the Browns defense is legitimately fantastic, but Watson isn’t the reason this team is winning; he’s just benefitting from the hard work of others.

In this world of identity broadcasting it’s not compelling to tell the true story. It’s not enticing to focus on defense, interview middle linebacker Carson Schwesinger, or a pass rusher like Jared Verse. Quarterbacks have reigned supreme forever, but Deshaun Watson deserves no praise, no focus, and he never will. Shame on everyone involved with Thursday Night Football for turning their broadcast into a chance to try to rehabilitate the image of a serial abuser.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 4 Fades: 3 players from Seahawks-Chargers may be worth benching
item.description: Matt Okada goes over players to avoid for fantasy football in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the fourth of seventeen weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until fantasy championships.

As a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

Without further ado, here is my list for Week 4 of the 2026 season.

Justin Herbert, QB, Chargers at Seahawks

This is Herbert's second appearance in this column in a span of three weeks, but he's the most relevant choice, considering how highly he was drafted and how many managers are still holding onto QB1 dreams. Listen, they may materialize eventually, though it's getting progressively less likely, but they're not materializing this week. Herbert has not yet hit 14 fantasy points in a game, after matchups with the Cardinals, Raiders and Bills. He's sporting a 73.4 passer rating and 59.1% completion rate through three weeks, and the Chargers offense still hasn't scored more than 16 points in a game. It certainly doesn't help that they're allowing the fourth-highest quick pressure rate in the league (pressures within 2.5 seconds from the snap), as the supposed-to-be-better offensive line ... has not been.

Now Herbert and Co. are headed to Seattle. The Seahawks have not yet allowed 200 passing yards to a quarterback, leading the league with 152 passing yards allowed per game, and four interceptions as well. They also specifically have the third-highest quick pressure rate in the league, behind the Vikings (and their absurd blitz rate) and the Falcons. Herbert is going to be forced to get rid of the football earlier than he'd like all game, and will be very hard-pressed to find any downfield production. He's not just outside starter range, he's outside the top 20 and might even be benchable in 2QB or Superflex leagues.

What to do ❓ Sit Herbert for just about anyone. You'd be better served dropping to streamers like Marcus Mariota, Daniel Jones, Jacoby Brissett or Geno Smith.

Omarion Hampton, RB, Chargers at Seahawks

Can you tell I'm not a fan of the Chargers' rudderless offense against the Seahawks' smothering defense? This one's admittedly much tougher than benching Herbert, as you probably drafted Omarion Hampton to be your RB1 somewhere in the first two rounds. Unfortunately, things have not trended well. He did have an excellent game with 115 scrimmage yards and a touchdown in Week 2, but he's also fumbled twice and lost significant work to Keaton Mitchell, particularly in the red zone (where Mitchell scored L.A.'s lone touchdown last week). In what should have been a decent Week 3 matchup against Buffalo, Hampton saw 15 carries to Mitchell's eight, but only outpaced him 56 to 52 in yards. Oh, and fullback Alec Ingold heavily outproduced him as a receiver.

And, once again, the Seahawks defense. They haven't allowed more than 12 fantasy points to any running back this season and held Jeremiyah Love to just six two weeks ago. They're allowing just 2.9 yards per carry to RBs (second-fewest in the league), haven't surrendered a single rushing touchdown and boast a league-best -0.43 EPA/carry against the position. They're also 7-point favorites, leaving the Chargers with an implied total of just 17.75 points ... which honestly feels high. No matter where you drafted Hampton, sacrificing points in your starting lineup out of stubbornness is a losing battle.

What to do ❓ Hampton can be played as a relatively high-floor FLEX, but he's outside my top 24 at running back. Do not expect RB1 or RB2 production, and if you can go with a higher-upside wide receiver in the FLEX instead, lean that way.

Jadarian Price, RB, Seahawks vs. Chargers

Three fades, three players from the same game?! I promise I'll diversify with the pass-catchers, but we need to address the reality with Seahawks rookie Jadarian Price. He's completely unplayable. After totaling just 11.3 fantasy points across the first two games, despite 27 touches, Price had just five carries and one catch in the loss to Washington last week, finishing with 0.7 fantasy points and fumbling for the second consecutive game. He played through a chest injury, and has been limited in practice this week, but is likely to play again in Week 4. And George Holani and Emanuel Wilson have been more involved than Price's managers would like to see either way. He's posted an absolutely brutal -0.54 EPA per carry, the lowest among qualified running backs, even below Packers’ MarShawn Lloyd.

And while Price has had very strong missed tackle and explosive run rates, he also sports the second-highest stuff rate in the league, behind only Woody Marks. Price is boom-bust and is not seeing enough volume to make the boom reliable. Now, Seattle has designated Zach Charbonnet to return to practice, spelling the imminent end of Price's role as the lead back. The Chargers' run defense has been one of their few bright spots this first month, but Price would be hard to trust against anyone. In fact, you may want to try trading him for anything better than a waiver pickup before he essentially loses all perceived value with Charbonnet's return.

What to do ❓ Bench Price for any reasonable starting RB or a wide variety of FLEX plays. Heck, I'd rather play Juwan Johnson as my FLEX.

Emeka Egbuka, WR, Bucs vs. Packers

Disclaimer up front: every once in a while, a bad-on-paper QB change creates a sort of strange chemistry-based phenomenon where one pass-catcher suddenly breaks out. We sort of saw this with Case Keenum and Luther Burden III on Monday night, as an example. So, it could be that undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels starts finding Egbuka downfield in ways Baker Mayfield had not been. But that feels very unlikely. Daniels was a six-year QB at Kansas, where his career highs were 2,531 passing yards and 22 touchdowns. And even though Mayfield had been borderline terrible before his dislocated thumb last week, expecting improvement from an undrafted rookie would be misplaced.

Meanwhile, Egbuka headlined my "Fallers" in the weekly Stock Report article on Monday. While he has been consistently alright for fantasy, Egbuka has not rediscovered his early-rookie-season upside since injuries to both him and Mayfield throughout the 2025 season. Egbuka has maxed out at five catches and 63 receiving yards, and his one touchdown came in a game where he had just three catches for 16 yards. It's been tough, especially given just how impressive his first five weeks as a rookie were, but until we see it again, Egbuka is hard to trust as a starting-caliber fantasy wideout.

What to do ❓ If you need a very low-upside FLEX, Egbuka is somewhat viable, even with the QB change. But he's incredibly risky and you're just as likely to get two points as 20. I'd aim to bench him until we see at least one game with Daniels.

Deebo Samuel Sr., WR, 49ers vs. Broncos

It feels like Deebo Samuel Sr. is going to be a popular play in Week 4, after his 15.4 points in Week 3 and amid Mike Evans' potential injury absence. But let's not get too carried away just yet. First, Samuel scored 14.0 of his 15.4 points on a single, once-in-a-season hook-and-ladder play last week. He didn't see a single target in the game, which brings his total over the last two weeks to three catches on four targets for 31 receiving yards ... and technically another 80 on the trick play. Keep in mind, Evans suffered his injury in the second quarter, and while Samuel did run the most routes among the wide receivers, he was out-targeted by Jacob Cowing and Jordan Watkins.

Then there's the opponent. While the Broncos were gashed by Davante Adams and Konata Mumpfield last week, they're much different receivers than Samuel. Denver has still held opposing wideouts to a 50.9% completion rate (second-lowest in the league) and just 22.9 fantasy points per game (11th-fewest). Brock Purdy and San Francisco will cobble together a productive day through their wide variety of unique weapons — à la George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey — and Samuel may have an impact play or two. But it's very hard to trust a receiver with a 13.6% target share and 6.0% air yards share.

What to do ❓ Like Egbuka, Samuel could be a decent FLEX play, but I would not trust him as a WR2 and would prefer receivers with more trustworthy involvement, like Stefon Diggs against Indy, Devaughn Vele against Atlanta or particularly Keenan Allen versus Washington.

Kenyon Sadiq, TE, Jets at Bears

I was tempted to return to Kyle Pitts Sr. or Colston Loveland (again), but at this point, at a shallow position, that feels too redundant. So I'm taking a much bigger risk and fading rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq after his breakout game in Week 3. Why? Largely because of the drop-off in matchup. Sadiq torched the Lions for 20.0 fantasy points, but the Lions have been by far the softest matchup for tight ends in all of fantasy. In fact, they've been the softest matchup for the position to start any season in living memory, allowing 28.5 fantasy points per game to tight ends as a whole. If you straight up removed Sadiq's performance, they would still have allowed more fantasy points than the next-softest matchup (the Commanders).

Meanwhile, the Bears have allowed fewer fantasy points to tight ends all season (18.8) than the Lions surrendered to Sadiq last week. They haven't faced great competition — T.J. Hockenson, Darren Waller, off-the-couch Zach Ertz — but the gap is still undeniably wide. Also, Chicago is 20th in passing yards allowed across all positions and has surrendered just three passing touchdowns, tied for fourth-fewest in the league. Sadiq is exciting and obviously flashed the talent that made him a first-round pick. But he also had just five catches for 38 yards on six targets through the first two weeks, before the run-in with Detroit. He's a good asset to have on your roster, but probably not in your starting lineup (at least for this week).

What to do ❓ Sadiq is outside my top 12 at tight end, and you probably weren't starting him before last week, so you should have a solid alternate. Juwan Johnson is tops on that list, but I'd also go with Dalton Schultz and Isaiah Likely, as well as Tucker Kraft, despite the early disappointment.

item.title: Ben Brown ‘ready to roll’ should Patriots call upon him against Bills
item.description: The Patriots are facing questions at right guard. Brown might be part of the answer.
item.content:encoded:
Entering 2026, right guard was supposed to be a position of strength for the New England Patriots. Mike Onwenu had been their best offensive linemen for several years now, and even with plenty of football under his belt has remained a top-tier if somewhat underrated blocker in the run and pass game.

However, three games into the season the outlook has changed dramatically. Onwenu suffered a fractured ankle in Week 2 against Pittsburgh, with his replacement — training camp free agency pickup Greg Van Roten — going down with an ankle injury one week later.

With both now on injured reserve, the Patriots are scrambling for answers at the spot. Looking at the roster, there are three candidates to fill Onwenu’s shoes now that Van Roten is out of the equation for at least four weeks: Ben Brown, Walter Rouse and Matt Pryor.

Brown entered training camp as the No. 4 interior lineman but was hampered by an ankle injury in preseason; Rouse was acquired in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings ahead of late-August’s roster cutdowns; Pryor was signed just this week to provide additional depth and experience. Who among them will emerge as the starter remains to be seen, but based on past performance in the system, Brown looks like a realistic candidate.

If indeed called upon, he vows to be ready.

“Physically, I feel great. I’m ready to roll however that might look,” he said earlier this week. “It’s just like Coach [Mike Vrabel] always says, ‘Prepare every week as a starter regardless of if you’re actually out there or not.’ That’s what we are intending, to be ready. And so, whatever is asked upon me, I’ll be ready for whatever.”

A rookie free agent in 2022, Brown made his way to New England via the Raiders practice squad in 2024. Since then, he has played 33 games with 14 starts — all of them at either left guard or center. In fact, only 11 of his 1,007 offensive snaps with the team have come at right guard.

And yet, Brown feels confident in his ability to play that role, in part because he did so during his college career at Ole Miss. Ultimately, though, his goal is to just help the team regardless of the role he is asked to play on game days.

“I want to do whatever I can to contribute, however that might look,” he said. “I just want to be ready for whenever my number’s called upon. Whenever that might be, because you never know in the NFL. It’s long seasons and a lot goes on in it. Best thing I can do for this football team is just be ready whenever my number’s called.”

item.title: Commanders vs. Colts injury report: Chig Okonkwo, Frankie Luvu will play

item.title: Can Kevin O’Connell’s 3-0 Vikings Survive the Dolphins Trap? Week 4 Preview
item.description: Vikings-Dolphins Week 4: Trap game or blowout? KOC, Kyler Murray, and Flores' defense under the microscope.
item.content:encoded:
The 3-0 Minnesota Vikings face a Miami Dolphins team in full rebuild mode, but as The Real Forno Show warns, this Week 4 matchup has trap game written all over it. — Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano sat down with Dolphins guy Kevin Fielder for the Week 4 preview, and this one is messier than a 7-point spread and actually it being double-digits. Miami, under Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley, is in an evaluation year. Not a tank. Fielder put it on Sullivan: “This is not going to be a rebuild in the sense that we’re gonna tear this down.” They brought in Malik Willis to reunite him with two people who already coached him in Green Bay. Early returns are mixed. Fielder was honest about it: “I think we’ll be talking about the Miami Dolphins needing a quarterback at some point in the next few years.”

De’Von Achane tore his ACL in Week 3, so Bobby Slowik has to rebuild the run game around Ollie Gordon and Jaylen Wright. The Vikings have their own questions. Kyler Murray has one full game in purple. Justin Jefferson had not practiced all week when we recorded. Tyler watched that debut and said, “I think he saw too much flash of color and decided not to” throw it into those windows. Fielder pushed back: “He’s just missing things down the field… there were explosive plays to be had.”

Brian Flores’ defense is going to test that Miami line. Fielder likes the interior: “Kadyn Proctor at left guard, Jonah Savaiinaea at right guard, Aaron Brewer at center, has played incredibly well.” The Vikings’ run game is still a work in progress with Josh Oliver out for the year and Aaron Jones always nicked up. Spread says comfortable. The tape says do not overlook them.

Key Points from the Episode:

  • The Dolphins are the NFL’s youngest roster but have been “oddly competitive” — pushing the Chiefs, 49ers, and Raiders
  • De’Von Achane’s ACL injury forces a schematic shift toward power-gap running
  • Chop Robinson, drafted to be a pass rusher, has struggled in year three — “he just has to figure something out”
  • Miami’s defense is 30th in EPA per play and 32nd in EPA per dropback, but 9th against the run
  • Brian Flores’ “blitz” numbers are inflated — his base is five rushers, which the NFL counts as a blitz complains Fielder
  • Kyler Murray’s misses against Tampa were reads, not accuracy: “He’s missing things that he should be taking”
  • If Justin Jefferson sits, Jordan Addison and Tai Felton take on larger roles
  • Donovan Jackson has been a revelation at left guard: “That guy is a baller. I was wrong,” Fielder conceded
  • Fielder called this the “quintessential trap game” — closer than fans expect
  • Dave Stefano invoked the 2018 Bills upset: “We were so much favored and we got our [back sides] handed to us”

item.title: Giants vs. Cardinals: Arizona offense poses challenges for New York
item.description: The Giants host the Cardinals in Week 4. How can the Giants’ defense slow down Arizona?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants will host the 1-2 Arizona Cardinals at 1 p.m. Sunday, with Arizona favored by 2.5 points and the Over/Under set at 44.5.

The Cardinals opened the season with a surprising 26-14 road victory over the Los Angeles Chargers, though Los Angeles has since shown itself to be a struggling team. Arizona followed that win with a lopsided 31-7 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in Week 2, but bounced back with a strong showing against the San Francisco 49ers in Week 3, falling 36-30 in a more competitive game, especially after trailing 23-6.

The Giants are 2-1, coming off an uninspiring 12-7 victory over the Tennessee Titans. Jameis Winston has struggled over the past two weeks, and he’ll face an Arizona defense that surrendered 297 passing yards and four touchdowns to Brock Purdy in Week 3, following a Week 2 performance in which Drew Lock threw for 235 yards and three touchdowns.

The seat is beginning to warm up for Winston. New York traded a 2027 fifth-round pick for J.J. McCarthy, raising an obvious question: How much longer will the Giants tolerate inconsistent quarterback play? Can New York’s defense continue giving the offense enough opportunities to win close games, as it did in Week 3?

Complementary football has long eluded the Giants. The special teams unit has been a bright spot, but the defense faces a major test against Arizona—especially after the injury to Brian Burns. Can New York’s defense hold up without one of its leaders against an Arizona team that’s shown more competency than many anticipated, despite their 1-2 record? Let’s look at the Cardinals’ personnel and statistics to answer that question.

The Cardinals’ offense

Over three games, the Cardinals rank 18th in points per game, averaging 21 points per game. The Giants are 28th in the NFL, averaging 15.3 points per game. The Cardinals rank 23rd in total yards, averaging 303 yards per game, while the Giants allow 271 yards per game, ranking 29th in the league. Arizona ranks 15th in third-down conversion rate (41%) and 20th in red-zone touchdown rate (55%).

The Cardinals average 210 passing yards per game (17th in the NFL) and 93 rushing yards per game (25th). However, running back Jeremiyah Love — who was selected in the top five — saw his role increase significantly against the 49ers. He had a 63% snap share after just 42% in Week 2.

Love suffered a high-ankle sprain in preseason Week 1, leading to heavy usage for Tyler Allgeier in the first two weeks of the season. Allgeier will have a role, but Mike LaFleur seems comfortable showcasing the talents of Love, who had 26 total touches in Week 3, which is what had TOTAL in his first two games.

Love has 160 yards on 41 carries (3.9 YPC), with one touchdown, 2.76 yards after contact, and five missed tackles forced. Allgeier has 24 carries for 70 yards (2.9 YPC), with 2.38 yards after contact and five missed tackles forced as well.

The Cardinals run a lot of DUO up front and want to displace at the point of attack in the run game. Paris Johnson Jr. starts at left tackle and Elijah Wilkinson is the starting right tackle. The latter has struggled as a run blocker, while the former continues to be one of the better young tackles in football. Isaac Seumalo and Isaiah Adams start on the interior — both bigger, more physical interior offensive linemen — and Hjalte Froholdt is their starting center.

The Giants have to expect a similar DUO blocking scheme that they faced against the Rams in Week 2 — New York surrendered 163 yards on the ground against Kyren Williams and Blake Corum. Expect Love’s role to be similar to Week 3, with Allgeier working in on short-yardage and to spell the talented young rookie.

The wide receiver situation in Arizona is interesting, to say the least. 2024 Top-five pick Marvin Harrison Jr. looks completely disinterested and has appeared this way through two coaching staffs. The Internet believes he could be traded. Here’s Mike LaFleur responding to a question about plays being designed for the disgruntled young receiver:

Harrison Jr. has four receptions on nine targets for 73 yards through three games, despite playing more than 70% of the snaps in each game. Tight end Trey McBride has been a target monster, leading the team with 31 targets and catching 26 for 211 yards and two touchdowns.

Michael Wilson continues to outshine Harrison Jr. The former Stanford Cardinal has been sensational with Jacoby Brissett at quarterback. Wilson averages 10.6 targets and 85.3 yards per game across the last 11 matchups; the Bengals’ Ja’Marr Chase averages 10 targets and 79.7 yards per game through that same span.

Wilson has 18 catches on 27 targets for 163 yards and a touchdown. New York will have its hands full with both Wilson and McBride. Kendrick Bourne is the third receiver, and he’s been efficient, catching 12 of 14 targets for 108 yards.

The matchup

Brissett is playing good football. He’s keeping the Cardinals’ offense on track with a quick, efficient passing attack that matches up well against the Giants. Brissett is completing 70% of his passes with 652 passing yards, four touchdowns, and just one interception. He has a 1.6% big-time throw rate and a 2.3% turnover-worthy play rate, and his receivers have dropped 4.7% of his passes, with 5.6 yards per attempt.

Brissett’s surface-level statistics check out with the more advanced analytics. The Arizona offense ranks 11th in the NFL in EPA (Expected Points Added) per play; they’re especially efficient in short EPA (7th in the NFL), while ranking 27th in deep EPA. The Cardinals, however, are dead last in explosive-play EPA.

Arizona is specifically good out of 11 and 13 personnel, recording the ninth-best EPA from the former and the third-best from the latter. Their 13 personnel package consists of McBride, Eliah Higgins, and Hunter Long. Tight end Tip Reiman is injured, which has affected the Cardinals’ ability to run effectively.

The Giants may look to dial up more pressure without star pass rusher Burns, but Brissett has done well against pressure. He is sixth in EPA when pressures, but 16th in EPA against the blitz. The Cardinals have used 11 personnel at a 62% rate, 12 personnel at a 12% rate, and 13 personnel at an 18% rate. Expect the Giants to align in nickel against 11 and stay mostly in base versus heavier personnel.

The addition of Jihad Ward — who is familiar with Dennard Wilson’s scheme — should lead to a different role for Kayvon Thibodeaux, who will be replacing Burns. There could be lighter fronts in passing situations with Ward, Abdul Carter, Thibodeaux, and Chauncey Golston.

New York ran middle-of-the-field closed often against Cam Ward and the Titans. The Giants may align a bit more in middle-of-the-field open against Brissett. New York should be getting Tae Banks back to help the secondary. Brissett has done well against single-high defenses, sporting the sixth-best EPA when facing single-high looks, although they’ve only seen single-high looks at a 26% rate (27th in the NFL).

The Cardinals rank 25th in EPA against middle-of-the-field open looks, and the Giants have struggled in split-safety looks. How Dennard Wilson balances his safety usage vs.the Cardinals will be interesting to gauge, and could be contingent on how well the Giants are doing up front against Love. New York ranks 31st in EPA when in a light box, with a 40.5% light box rate, which is a rate that ranks 23rd in the NFL.

The Giants currently blitz at a 22.5% rate, which ranks 26th in the NFL. The Cardinals weren’t blitzed much through their first three weeks — seeing just a 24.4% blitz rate, which ranks 28th in the NFL. Generating pressure — something the Giants have failed to do successfully — now without Burns may be a problem, and how Wilson looks to rectify the issue is yet another very interesting thing to observe during this matchup.

I expect Wilson to pick and choose his times to blitz, but we could see more aggression now that the Giants may be healthier in the secondary. The Giants currently rank LAST in generating pressure.

Final thoughts

The Cardinals are efficient with their quick game concepts, and they’ll look to mitigate the Giants’ ability to rush the passer. New York has failed to generate pressure, but the Cardinals have allowed a 31.7% pressure rate, ranking sixth most in the NFL. Lafleur is going to run a quick-hitting offense and attempt to replicate the quick-game success that they’ve seen. The Giants must be tighter with their coverage and pick their spots on when to blitz. This is a winnable game for both teams, but we’re about to learn A LOT about this 2-1 Giants team. The defense may, once again, have to pick up their end of the couch if the Giants want to go 3-1.

item.title: Dallas Cowboys: Reading Between the Line vs. Houston Texans
item.description: How do you think the Cowboys offensive line will play this week?
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we’re digging into the trenches, because that’s where the real action happens. We shine the spotlight on the Dallas Cowboys offensive line, who’s holding it down, who’s opening holes for the running backs, and who’s keeping Dak Prescott clean. Let’s get to it.

Trench Dashboard

Here are the Cowboys offensive line metrics for the 2026 season so far. 

Pass Block Win Rate – 50% 16th

Run Block Win Rate – 67% 31st

Pressure rate allowed – 28% 10th

Sacks allowed – 3 (2nd)

Last three week trend: Pass pro good, run blocking improving

The Pressure Point

Every opponent will look at the Cowboys offensive line and ask, where can we break it? Here’s what to watch for.

PRESSURE POINT: Terence Steele has a Will Anderson Jr. problem

There is no need to overcomplicate the biggest concern for Dallas this week. Will Anderson Jr. is playing outstanding football.

Against Indianapolis last week, Anderson produced nine pressures from only 32 pass-rush snaps. PFF credited him with three sacks and gave him a 93.3 pass-rush grade for the game. Official NFL statistics credit Anderson with 2.5 sacks in the game and four through three weeks.

Anderson was on the left side of its defensive front, meaning many of his snaps naturally bring him toward Dallas’ right tackle. Steele has already been the more concerning tackle in pass protection this season, while Tyler Guyton has taken a noticeable step forward on the opposite side.

Anderson can win in several ways. He is quick enough to race around the outside, but he also has the strength to drive a tackle backwards toward the quarterback.

PRESSURE POINT: Houston can squeeze the pocket from both directions

Stopping Anderson does not end the problem. Danielle Hunter is on the opposite edge. His start statistically has been quieter with four pressures and one sack, but this is a player who generated 92 pressures across the 2025 season. 

Houston also has Sheldon Rankins attacking through the middle. Rankins has six pressures and a 72.3 PFF pass-rush grade through three games. 

If Anderson pushes Steele backwards from one side while Hunter does the same from the other, Prescott normally has room to step forward. If Rankins is also winning through the middle, that escape route disappears. That is how Houston can create sacks without having to blitz heavily.

The good news is Dallas has allowed only three sacks through three games, so the protection has generally held up well despite Smith’s absence. Keeping that number low against this front would be one of the offensive line’s best performances of the season. 

Where to attack

Every defensive line has a weakness, here’s the Texans soft spots and where the Cowboys offensive line should attack. 

GREEN LIGHT: Run toward Danielle Hunter, not Will Anderson

Houston does not have an obvious weakness against the run. The Texans have allowed only 260 rushing yards through three games at 3.5 yards per carry, with opponents yet to reach 90 rushing yards in a game. But Dallas still has to run the football, the key is choosing where.

Anderson currently owns a 91.0 PFF run-defense grade. Running repeatedly toward him would be asking for trouble, Hunter is a different story.

His current 50.6 run-defense grade ranks 88th among qualifying edge defenders. That gives Dallas a target. When Hunter is lined up opposite Tyler Guyton, Dallas should test that side with Javonte Williams. Let Guyton use the strength he has shown as a run blocker and make Hunter repeatedly defend rather than rush Prescott.

Guyton’s development is particularly encouraging here. He currently carries a 79.6 PFF run-blocking grade, sixth among offensive tackles. That is strength against weakness. Dallas finally established a running game against Baltimore. It should not abandon it just because Houston has impressive season-long rushing numbers.

GREEN LIGHT: Attack Sheldon Rankins in the running game

There is another possible opening inside. Rankins has provided useful pass rush production, but his run defense has been significantly weaker. His current 41.5 PFF run-defense grade ranks 100th among qualifying interior defensive linemen. 

This is where Tyler Booker and Cooper Beebe should become important. Booker has been one of Dallas’ best run blockers this season. Through the available PFF data, his 78.6 run-blocking grade ranked ninth among guards. 

Dallas can put Booker and Beebe together on combination blocks against Houston’s interior defenders. That is exactly the type of physical football Dallas showed more of against Baltimore.

Houston is good against the run overall, so these yards will not necessarily come easily. But Dallas does not need five yards every time. Four yards on first down is useful because it keeps Anderson and Hunter guessing.

The Chaos Report

Here’s the Houston Texans defensive trends for this season at the defensive line.

Sack Total – 11 (3rd)

Pass Rush Win Rate – 42% 30th

Run Stop Win Rate – 31% 10th

QB Pressure Rate – 23% (26th)

Last three week trend: Pass rush trending up

Matchup of the week

Terence Steele vs. Will Anderson Jr.

This may be the most important individual offensive-line matchup Dallas has faced this season. Anderson is not simply playing well. He is currently one of the most disruptive defenders in football.

Steele struggled at times against Baltimore and was also responsible for a costly holding penalty that removed an important Dallas first down. If Steele handles Anderson himself, Dallas can leave tight ends in the passing game and allow running backs to release into routes.

If Steele needs constant help, Houston begins dictating what Dallas can do offensively. That is why this matchup affects much more than two players.

Best route to success: 

Stay out of third-and-long and make Houston’s edge rushers defend the entire playbook rather than simply hunt Prescott.

Injury Updates:

Nothing to add to the Cowboys, but Tyler Smith can officially return from injured reserve after this week. 

For Houston, Jadeveon Clowney and Mario Edwards Jr. are both questionable. Kayden McDonald went to IR with an ankle injury two weeks ago.

item.title: Eagles News: “This season can get turned around if Nick Sirianni has the right messaging and can push the right buttons”
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles news and links for 10/2/26.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

Whereas I felt like the onus was on the Eagles’ defense entering Week 3 against the Chicago Bears (and Vic Fangio’s group certainly failed that test), I feel like Week 4 is on Nick Sirianni. It’s important to see how the Eagles respond to their Monday night loss. On paper, they’re not in a great spot. The Rams are a tough opponent. The Eagles are going to be missing some key players. But this is a situation where the head coach needs to get his team to rally. I’m not even suggesting that the Eagles MUST win this game. But it will be disheartening if they’re not more competitive than they were against the Bears.

Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

Glass Half Full – Iggles Blitz

The NFC East isn’t loaded right now. Dallas has a terrific offense, but their defense remains a work in progress. Trading for CB Joey Porte Jr should help, but it won’t solve all their problems. Jameis Winston has struggled since taking over for Jaxson Dart in NY. Injuries are hurting that team. Washington has played better than anyone expected, but they lack talent and you just can’t trust them. This season can get turned around if Nick Sirianni has the right messaging and can push the right buttons. I believe the biggest problems are intangibles and those can usually be fixed. I’m not ignoring the tangible issues (poor safety play for instnace), but all 32 teams have weak spots. The Eagles can turn things around quickly if Sirianni can get this team to play smarter and tougher. The Eagles don’t have to win on Sunday to give me hope. I need to see them play good football. If the Rams happen to make an extra play or two and win, so be it. I just need to see major improvement from the Birds. That would help me to believe in them going forward.

Eagles-Rams Game Preview: 5 questions and answers with the Week 4 enemy – BGN

After two weeks on the road, the Philadelphia Eagles are returning to Lincoln Financial Field to host a familiar enemy: the Los Angeles Rams. In order to preview this Week 4 matchup, I reached out to our enemies over at Turf Show Times. The excellent Evan Craig kindly took the time took the time to answer my questions about this upcoming battle. Let’s take a look at the answers.

NFC East Mixtape Vol. 194: Week 4 Preview, Cowboys get Joey Porter Jr. – NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel

A new week is upon us in the NFC East and we have four games to rip through to prepare for it! The Philadelphia Eagles are set to take on the Los Angeles Rams and dropping a second straight game would certainly not be ideal. Meanwhile, the New York Giants will play the Arizona Cardinals in JJ McCarthy’s first game with the team. The Washington Commanders are across the pond in London to play the Indianapolis Colts and try to build on last week’s momentum. Stateside the Dallas Cowboys have a Texas State matchup against the Houston Texans and will take them on with a new player on the team as they just traded for Joey Porter Jr. on Wednesday night. RJ Ochoa and Brandon Lee Gowton discuss it all! You can see that we have a BRAND NEW NFC East Mixtape YouTube Channel so make sure to subscribe as the show will live here exclusively in video format. AND you can also listen to the show! On Blogging The Boys and/or Bleeding Green Nation podcast feeds as well as the SB Nation NFL Show feed!

5Qs, 5As with Bleeding Green Nation: How is Jalen Hurts faring with yet another new OC? – Turf Show Times

The Los Angeles Rams take on the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 4 for the fourth straight season. Los Angeles is searching not only for its first win over the Eagles since the 2020 campaign, but also for its first win over Philly with Nick Sirianni at the helm. Ahead of an important matchup between NFC contenders who suffered bad losses last week, I spoke with Brandon Gowton from Bleeding Green Nation to get the inside scoop on Jalen Hurts working with yet another new offensive coordinator, Vic Fangio’s defense and more.

NFL Expert Picks for Week 4 – SB Nation

The one game to really circle: Rams vs. Eagles. Here are two teams assumed to be the top of the NFC, but both have struggled to start the season and find themselves in need of a win. It’s seeming like one of these teams is going to miss expecations this season, and this game could definine that.

If Zack Baun misses Week 4? ‘Trot was born ready’ – NBCSP

With All-Pro Zack Baun likely sidelined with a concussion for Sunday’s game against the Rams, the Eagles are expected to turn to Jeremiah Trotter Jr. How ready is the young Axe Man? “Trot was born ready,” fellow linebacker Jihaad Campbell said. “Whether he’s got to play or not, at the end of the day, he always practices like a pro, he always takes notes and studies like a pro. He’ll be fine.” Trotter, 23, has technically started two NFL games before but both of those had little actual meaning. He started in Week 18 against the Giants in 2024 and Week 18 against the Commanders in 2025. This situation is a little bit different. The Eagles on Sunday afternoon are facing a desperate Rams team that has put up 480+ yards of offense in back-to-back weeks and are led by Matthew Stafford, Davante Adams, Puka Nacua and more — not to mention an offense that uses a ton of eye candy to constantly put linebackers in conflict. It’s not going to be easy on Sunday.

NFL Week 4 picks: Upset and score predictions, matchup breakdowns for every game – NFL.com

Why Gennaro picked the Eagles: Last Sunday night, Los Angeles blew a 16-0 halftime lead at Denver to drop back below .500 in a season that began with the Rams as prohibitive Super Bowl favorites. One night later, Philadelphia was blown out of Chicago by a Bears team that was forced to give Case Keenum his first start in 1,009 days. So, after a pair of nationally televised debacles, who’s in better position to bounce back? Well, the expected return of star WR Puka Nacua is certainly a boon to Sean McVay’s squad. But can the Rams coach exorcise his demons against the Eagles? McVay is 1-6 vs. Philadelphia, having dropped all four matchups against Nick Sirianni. Last season’s loss at Lincoln Financial Field was particularly painful: Not only did the Rams blow a 19-point third-quarter lead, but they had two fourth-quarter field goal attempts blocked, including a would-be game-winner from 44 yards out on the last snap of the contest. In addition to swatting that final kick, hulking DT Jordan Davis memorably scooped up the ball and galloped for an exclamation-point touchdown. But the big man’s triumphant rumble was easily the Eagles’ best run of the day, as the Rams held Saquon Barkley to just 55 total yards on 22 touches. That was a huge departure from Barkley’s previous two games against L.A., when he piled up 534(!) scrimmage yards. Philly’s had trouble getting a consistent ground attack going under new OC Sean Mannion, but Barkley did enjoy success against Chicago this past Monday night before the game got out of hand, potentially signaling a schematic breakthrough. In a matchup between two established powers that have yet to play up to their talent level this season, I’m far from bullish on the Eagles. But I anticipate Sirianni will rally the troops once again versus McVay, with the Birds feeling disrespected as home underdogs.

Bowen: Hey, I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but things aren’t going great for the Eagles. Just FYI – PHLY Eagles

Mannion is in just the third season of his coaching career. He was asked Thursday evening about second-half adjustments. “We get together as a staff, and we talk about the different looks that we’ve seen throughout the game, and basically try to chart a course for the second half,” Mannion said. He spoke of how coaches would say, “Hey, I want to get to this, I want to get to this.” He did not say anything about countering the opponent’s adjustments to what you are doing. Seems like they might want to discuss that, as well. Is this season – the last with Lane Johnson, apparently – going to end up being just a big “learning experience” for everyone? Growth toward some distant goal? That doesn’t suit where I think this roster is, overall. It certainly doesn’t suit where I think the fan base’s expectations are. If there is hope for Super Bowl contention in 2026, I’ll be surprised if it manifests itself against the Rams. Or even against the Jaguars in London, a week later. I think the patience of Eagles Nation is about to be tested. Severely.

NFL Week 4 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips – ESPN

Fantasy nugget: Eagles RB Saquon Barkley has been held under 10 fantasy points in three consecutive games for the first time in his career. He also has yet to surpass 15 rushing attempts in a game. The Rams’ defensive front ranks eighth in run stop win rate, so this could be another tough matchup for the Eagles’ offensive line and running game.

Kenny Moore II went from unsigned to teaching 8th grade. Now he has another NFL chance – The Athletic

Moore, a veteran defensive back and former Pro Bowler, started the football season teaching eighth-graders in Indianapolis. He missed training camp for the first time in a decade. Week 1 commenced with Moore still unsigned. Moore experienced the football player’s version of civilian life for the first time, complete with the emotions and vulnerabilities that come with it. While he waited to join a team, he taught a course on life and soft-skill development on Mondays. He played in a soccer league on Tuesday nights. He took photographs. He scrapbooked. The Eagles signed Moore to the practice squad last week. They elevated him to the 53-man roster this week. He could play Sunday against the Los Angeles Rams. It’s the end of what he described as a “roller-coaster” offseason. And it’s also part of a lesson plan that “Mr. Kenny” could use himself. “This past offseason, yes, it was abnormal, but it was still my favorite one,” Moore said. “It was still my best offseason.”

Rams vs. Eagles By the Numbers – PhiladelphiaEagles.com

In three games against the Rams as an Eagle, Saquon Barkley has posted 506 rushing yards (7.2 yards per carry) and four touchdowns. Barkley rushed for a franchise single-game record 255 yards in the 2024 regular-season matchup with the Rams. Barkley rushed for a franchise playoff single-game record 205 yards in the 2024 NFC Divisional Round win over the Rams.

The Eagles will provide details on sweeping tailgating changes today. Here’s what we know so far. – Inquirer

The Eagles are searching for ways to get back into the win column on Sunday when they take on the Los Angeles Rams, but there will be big things happening outside of Lincoln Financial Field as well. New guidelines for oversized vehicles from the Sports Complex Parking Venture are being implemented starting Sunday, changing the way Philly fans have tailgated for years. The organization, in partnership with the Eagles, is expected to hold a press conference on Friday morning to detail why the changes are being made. In advance of all that, here’s what to know about modifications coming to the South Philadelphia Sports Complex parking areas for Eagles home games.

item.title: Week 4 NFL picks against the spread, predictions for every game: Raiders ready for their biggest game in Las Vegas vs. Chiefs
item.description: The Chiefs and Raiders are both 3-0 heading into a big AFC West game.
item.content:encoded:
When Patrick Mahomes starts at quarterback, the Kansas City Chiefs are 13-2 against the Las Vegas Raiders. But the Raiders have changed.

It's hard to get used to the idea of the Raiders being good. They've been bad for so long that it's strange to think of them any other way, unless you're still watching old clips of Ken Stabler or Marcus Allen. However, there is no evidence that their 3-0 start is fraudulent. Even if there was some trepidation about getting behind the Raiders' 2-0 start, a 35-27 comeback win at New Orleans was pretty impressive.

The Raiders are ninth in DVOA, ranking 13th in offense, ninth in defense and fifth in special teams. They're 15th in EPA per play on offense and second in EPA per play allowed. There's a new coaching staff, the roster has been remade, and the early results are impressive.

The Chiefs are good, too, of course. Any worry about Mahomes being rusty coming off ACL surgery has faded away during a 3-0 start. The Chiefs aren't going anywhere.

But this is the biggest game the Raiders have had since moving to Las Vegas. Not that the Chiefs won't be ready, but this should have a playoff feel at Allegiant Stadium. It has been a long time since the Raiders could feel this confident in what they're building. Las Vegas is a sound football team and even if they lose to a strong Chiefs team, it seems unlikely they'll be blown out. Raiders +4.5 is the pick. It's time to find out how good they might be this season.

Here are the rest of my picks against the spread for Week 4 of the NFL season:

Commanders (+3.5) over Colts

The NFL's Sunday window opens early. Set your alarm for the first 9:30 a.m. Eastern start of the year, from London. There should be plenty of scoring in this one. The Colts had the worst defense in the NFL through two weeks (though it played well last week vs. Houston) and the Commanders are 31st in the NFL in points allowed. London games are usually a bit odd, and the Commanders can score even with Marcus Mariota at QB if Jayden Daniels doesn't return. I'll take the points.

Rams (-3) over Eagles

The Eagles are 2-1, but Monday night exposed them. They were dominated by the Bears. The first two games, they barely beat Washington and Tennessee, and now those middling performances look even worse after they got blasted in Chicago. We can say the Rams are 1-2, but are probably a bad defensive pass interference call away from being 2-1 with the one loss being the weird game in Australia. I have much more faith in them than Philadelphia.

Buccaneers (+3.5) over Packers

It is frightening to pick an 0-3 Buccaneers team with an undrafted rookie quarterback. But teams this season who are starting a QB other than their Week 1 starter are 6-0 this season, according to Josh Dubow of Associated Press. And it's very hard to pick the Packers as a road favorite. They have been awful this season. Can Bucs rookie QB Jalon Daniels just do enough to keep the Bucs close? We'll find out.

Bears (-3.5) over Jets

Maybe what we saw Monday night was the typical bump a team can get from its first game with a backup quarterback. But the Bears looked good with Case Keenum, and it's fair to credit Ben Johnson's coaching for that. The Jets could be without Breece Hall, Mason Taylor and Adonai Mitchell, three key skill-position players. New York hasn't been that bad, but here's a pick for the coaching matchup.

Patriots (+6.5) over Bills

The Patriots are another team that is hard to pick. They look bad. This also feels like a playoff game for them, even though it's only Week 4. If they fall to 1-3, three games behind the Bills, the chances of winning the division get very slim. If the Patriots have any hope at all of being a factor this season, you'll see it on Sunday.

Bet the New England Patriots to cover the spread at sportsbooks right now

Jaguars (+2.5) over Bengals

It's possible Jacksonville is the team we're not talking about enough. The Jaguars had one bad half against the Broncos. In the other five halves this season, the Jaguars have outscored their three opponents 79-19. The Bengals have looked pretty good to start the season as well, though a defensive letdown last week was disappointing. We might start talking more about the Jaguars after Week 4.

Titans (+11.5) over Ravens

It's hard to come up with a logical argument for the Titans, but bad teams cover the spread often in the NFL. If you play survivor, you understand this. Also, the Ravens are coming straight off a trip to Brazil. The Titans need any edge they can get.

Texans (-2.5) over Cowboys

I refuse to give up on the Texans. It looks like they'll have Nico Collins back this week, which the offense desperately needs. Also, like the Ravens, the Cowboys are coming straight back from Brazil, and unlike Baltimore they're playing on the road. The Cowboys also had a miserable loss last week that will be hard to shake off. This is the last time we're picking Houston if it loses this week. Maybe. We'll see.

Giants (+2) over Cardinals

Arizona has been pretty good. Still, it's surprising to see the Cardinals as a road favorite. We know why. The Giants offense isn't going to be fun to watch with Jameis Winston (spoiler alert: It's unlikely to be any better with J.J. McCarthy, if and when he gets his shot). But this line seems very disrespectful to a 2-1 Giants team that will play hard and is well-coached. Also, it's a team coming from the West to play one of those early East Coast starts.

Vikings (-10.5) over Dolphins

The Dolphins will cover a spread this season. Nobody goes 0-17 against the spread. I'm not sure it's this week though. The matchup of Brian Flores' Vikings defense against a Dolphins offense now without De'Von Achane seems treacherous. If Justin Jefferson doesn't play that does give the Dolphins a shot to keep it close. But it's too hard to take Miami right now.

49ers (-2.5) over Broncos

Are the 49ers the product of an easy schedule? Perhaps to some extent. The Rams had jet lag and the Dolphins and Cardinals aren't very good. But the 49ers have handled business and Brock Purdy is red hot. They've played better than every other team so far this season. The Broncos aren't a bad team, but the first halves (they've been a no-show in the first half for all three games) is a real problem. I'll go with the NFL's hottest team and hope they take on no more injuries before kickoff.

Chargers (+7) over Seahawks

The last time Jim Harbaugh had a losing season, not counting a truncated 2020 season, was 2008 at Stanford. This season could break that streak, though. The Chargers have been legitimately awful. Even a +4 turnover margin at Buffalo didn't lead to a win, or even covering a 7-point spread. And now they get a Seattle team coming off a loss. But there's no way the Chargers can be this bad all season. Right?

Lions (-3.5) over Panthers

The Lions will score points. That seems like a safe prediction. The Panthers have played one decent offense this season and gave up 59 points to Chicago. This week they put both starting cornerbacks, Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson, on injured reserve. Detroit is going to move the ball. Carolina can too. The Lions' defense is bad. But the Panthers' offensive line injuries are piling up. They're without both tackles and guard Damien Lewis is set to miss time, too, which helps the Lions. It's hard to trust Detroit's defense, but I think the Lions might score at will.

Bet the Detroit Lions to cover the spread at sportsbooks right now

Saints (-2.5) over Falcons

This isn't the best Monday night game, but it is interesting. Are the Falcons suddenly good now that they have competent quarterback play from Michael Penix Jr.? What do we make of the Saints? They are 1-2, but also won at Baltimore and nearly won at Detroit. I believe the Saints are the best team in that division, and what we saw from the Falcons in Week 3 says more about the Packers than Atlanta.

Last week: 5-11

Season to date: 20-29

item.title: Commanders rule out Jayden Daniels, confirm Marcus Mariota will start vs. Colts in London Week 4
item.description: The Commanders play the Colts in London in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
The Washington Commanders have officially ruled out injured quarterback Jayden Daniels for Week 4's international game against the Indianapolis Colts, head coach Dan Quinn confirmed to reporters Friday. Backup Marcus Mariota will start in his place.

Daniels traveled with the team to London and practiced in a limited fashion this week after suffering a dislocated elbow in his non-throwing arm in Week 2. The injury is to the same elbow that Daniels dislocated and reinjured just last season.

Though the team never gave a specific timetable for Daniels' return, the Commanders declined to place him on injured reserve, a sign they hoped he could return without missing four games. The injury initially raised fears of a long-term absence.

But Commanders general manager Adam Peters revealed last week that "surgery is not on the table." And NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Sunday that consultations with medical specialists concluded that Daniels is "expected back at three weeks or sooner."

Instead of surgery, Daniels will don an elbow brace to help avoid another dislocation. He shared Thursday that he's not concerned about a potential for reinjury once he's back on the field, saying, "That's what the brace is for. If I had that concern, I would have gotten surgery."

Washington is 1-2 following last week's upset win against the Seattle Seahawks. The Commanders have a chance to build on that success with upcoming games against the Colts and Giants before the schedule gets tougher in Weeks 6-9 with games against the 49ers, Eagles and Rams. They'd certainly like to have Daniels back sooner rather than later, but as Quinn said earlier this week, "We won't put him out there before he's ready."

Mariota played a clean game against the reigning Super Bowl champs in Week 3, completing 19-of-31 pass attempts for 183 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Now, he gets another opportunity against the Colts, who have allowed the fifth-most passing yards (828) and the fifth-highest passer rating (110.4) this season, per Pro Football Reference.
