item.title: Fantasy Football Usage Report: Matthew Golden feasting for pass-heavy Packers entering Week 4
item.description: Zachary Krueger takes a look at exciting and worrisome performances from Week 3 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Like many here at Rotoworld HQ, my optimism for Adonai Mitchell heading into Week 3 against the Lions was dashed when he popped up with a finger injury that sidelined him for what was shaping up to be a big game for the speedster. Fortunately, Jaylen Warren had a volume-heavy day, racking up 176 yards from scrimmage on 20 touches and 20.6 PPR points, which helped curb some of that disappointment regarding Mitchell.

Hoping for better results this week, below are some players who have caught my attention heading into our Week 4 matchups.

RotoPat’s Week 4 Fantasy Football Rankings
Ranking and evaluating all of Week 4’s top plays at quarterback, running back, receiver, tight end, kicker and defense.
  • Patrick Daugherty,

Running Backs

Kendre Miller (NO) vs. Raiders

Kendre Miller rushed four times for 14 yards in the Saints' Week 3 loss to the Raiders and caught two passes for another five yards on three targets. No, it wasn't a flashy performance, but I refuse to buy into either Ollie Gordon or Jaylen Wright after the season-ending injury to De'Von Achane (knee). With Travis Etienne (hamstring) heading to injured reserve, Miller should see a decent amount of opportunities for at least the next four weeks, which presents an interesting opportunity for fantasy managers to stash a player who is currently rostered in just 24 percent of Sleeper leagues.

Miller rushed for 9-30-1 in Week 1 against the Lions and is now poised to split work with Alvin Kamara, who has averaged a suboptimal 2.8 YPC on his 18 rush attempts this season. The door is open for Kamara to step into a high-volume role, but his struggles on the ground are hard to ignore. Even as a pass-catcher, Kamara's six receptions for 12 yards aren't enough to instill any real confidence in him going forward.

It's too early to assume Miller will leapfrog Kamara in touches as we enter Week 4's game against the Falcons, but Miller is a worthwhile stash playing in an offense that is averaging 27.0 points per game and currently ranks eighth in yards per game (382.7).

Jacory Croskey-Merritt (WSH) vs. Seahawks

After headlining the "encouraging" performances portion of this article following his Week 1 performance against the Eagles, Jacory Croskey-Merritt now finds himself on the more concerning side of things heading into Week 4 against the Colts. Croskey-Merritt's volume is the only thing keeping him somewhat on the fantasy radar at this point, because his production has left a lot to be desired. After rushing for 16-63-1 against the Eagles, JCM has totaled just 79 scoreless yards on 31 carries since Week 2 (2.5 YPC), and has just two catches for two yards.

Among 33 running backs with at least 30 carries on the season, Croskey-Merritt ranks 31st in both rushing success rate (38.0 percent) and missed tackles forced rate (8.5 percent), while his yards before contact per attempt ranks 27th (0.66 YBC/ATT). He faces a Colts defense that was pummeled on the ground by Derrick Henry and Kenneth Walker during the first two weeks of the season, but it limited David Montgomery to 11-33-0 in Week 3. JCM's lack of upside in the passing game also continues to limit his fantasy upside. Fantasy managers shouldn't consider him as anything more than a boom/bust RB3 when the Commanders take on the Colts in London.

Wide Receivers

Matthew Golden (GB) vs. Falcons

The Packers have struggled mightily on the ground through the first three weeks of the season. With Josh Jacobs suspended, the trio of MarShawn Lloyd, Chris Brooks, and Kaleb Johnson have netted a combined rushing line of 46-146-0 (3.2 YPC) with one lost fumble and a 35.6 percent rushing success rate. As a team, the Packers' 38.3 percent rushing success rate ranks 30th behind only the Dolphins and Vikings.

The Packers' struggles on the ground are no secret to head coach Matt LaFleur, as evidenced by their league-low 48 rush attempts. For perspective, the Titans' 64 rush attempts are the second-fewest in the league.

Second-year receiver Matthew Golden has benefitted from the Packers' decision to avoid running the ball. Golden has two games of 12-plus targets this season, and his 30 total targets are currently good for fifth-most among all receivers. Golden's 113 routes run rank sixth-highest among receivers, and his 26.5 percent targets per route rate (TPRR) is seventh-highest (min. 80 routes run).

He also ranks in the top 10 in air yards per target (13.9 AY/TGT).

All of this is to say that things have aligned perfectly for Golden and his fantasy managers thus far, and his early 15-253-1 receiving line has made him a nice value in drafts. He should have plenty of opportunities to put up another big week against the Buccaneers as the Packers look to avoid a 1-3 start to their season.

Chris Godwin (TB) vs. Vikings

It's been a rough start to the season for the Buccaneers. They're off to a 0-3 start, the offense is ranked 19th in scoring but 28th in yards per game, and now have to go the next few weeks without Baker Mayfield (thumb). Rookie UDFA Jalon Daniels, who earned the QB2 spot out of camp, will make the start in Week 4 against the Packers, which immediately downgrades all Bucs pass-catchers for the foreseeable future.

Unfortunately for Chris Godwin, he was already trending down after a third-straight disappointing game to start the season. Godwin has run 32 or more routes in every game this season, but has topped out at four targets in those games, and hasn't gone for more than 46 yards in a game. Among 48 receivers with at least 80 routes run this season, Godwin's 10.8 percent targets per route rate ranks 42nd, which is one spot lower than teammate Ted Hurst (14.1 percent TPRR).

Godwin's disappointing usage through three weeks would have had him as a risky WR3 for Week 4 if Mayfield were under center. Now, he'll be hard to trust as anything more than a low-end WR4 with an unknown entity under center in Daniels.

Week 4 Best And Worst WR, TE Matchups: Keenan Allen in a good spot, Makai Lemon could finally get going
Denny Carter breaks down slot and boundary matchups for wideouts and tight ends headed into Week 4
  • Denny Carter,

Tight Ends

Kenyon Sadiq (NYJ) vs. Lions

Rookie first-rounder Kenyon Sadiq had his breakout game in Week 3 against the Lions. The hyper-athletic tight end posted a 7-105-1 line on eight targets and ran a route on 83.3 percent of the passing-down snaps he appeared on. It's probably no coincidence that Sadiq's breakout came in a game Adonai Mitchell missed with a finger injury, and Mitchell has been a DNP in each of the Jets' first two practices this week.

Sadiq's big performance should warrant more opportunities with or without Mitchell being active, but with Mitchell trending toward missing a second-straight game, Sadiq could be primed for another high-volume day this week against the Bears.

Isaiah Likely (NYG) vs. Titans

Isaiah Likely looked every bit like the player fantasy managers hoped to see when he followed John Harbaugh to New York after spending four seasons with him in Baltimore. Likely caught all eight targets he saw for 78 yards and two touchdowns despite running just 23 routes.

Unfortunately, he's posted a forgettable 7-46-0 line on 15 targets over the last two weeks, and his 53 routes run over that span rank 15th among tight ends. To make matters worse, Jameis Winston has struggled mightily in his first two weeks of action, completing 25-of-49 passes for 229 yards, zero touchdowns and one interception while also taking five sacks. Winston's -0.307 EPA/play since Week 2 is the second-lowest in the league behind Atlanta's Cooper Rush.

The Giants have the second-lowest early-down pass rate (45.3 percent) since Week 2, and could continue to lean heavily on the run given their underwhelming quarterback situation. After a promising Week 1, Likely is looking increasingly harder to trust sans Jaxson Dart, and could be in line for another underwhelming performance in Week 4 against the Cardinals.

NOTE: Stats and information courtesy of PFF.com, RotoViz.com, ProFootballReference.com, NextGenStats.NFL.com, 4For4.com, FantasyPoints.com and RBSDM.com. All scoring is based on full-PPR leagues.

item.title: Fantasy Football Start/Sit Advice: What to do with Jameson Williams, Emeka Egbuka, more players in Week 4
item.description: Scott Pianowski plays traffic cop, sharing some lineup insight for fantasy football in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Start-sit decisions can be vexing for even the best of fantasy managers. If you need help setting your fantasy football lineups, Scott Pianowski offers some assistance with his Week 4 traffic report.

Green Light ✅

RB Bhayshul Tuten at Bengals: Tuten was in a job battle all summer, but he’s left Chris Rodriguez Jr. in the dust after three strong games. The Bengals talked up their defensive improvement before the year, but they’re still handing out 4.7 yards per carry. Tuten is pushing for set-and-forget status.

WR Josh Downs at Commanders: Downs is seeing more targets and additional downfield work in the absence of Alec Pierce, and Washington has given up the most WR fantasy points through three weeks. Downs has Circle of Trust privileges moving forward, and Keenan Allen is a reasonable spot start if you’re feeling an injury pinch. Note, the Colts-Commanders game is a 9:30 a.m. ET start in London this week.

QB Bryce Young vs. Lions: He lost his way at Cleveland, but can make amends against an injured and ineffective Detroit secondary (110.2 rating allowed). Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker (if healthy) are auto-starts, and TE Darren Waller also makes sense here. Islands in the stream, that is what we are.

WR Kalif Raymond vs. Jets: He’s done it for three straight weeks now, it’s time to accept that Raymond could have staying power. A lot of Raymond’s wins are coming on shorter, quickly-defined routes, the type of work we thought Luther Burden III might feast on for 2026. Be open-minded with Chicago’s surprise receiver.

WR Jameson Williams at Panthers: We accept most wide receivers live a boom-and-bust life, but the gaps are wider for Williams, who needs splash plays to cover his ADP. But the Lions will surely take some deep shots Sunday night, taking aim at a Carolina secondary that’s missing its two starting cornerbacks.

Yellow Light 😕

RB Ollie Gordon II at Vikings: Gordon piled up the volume after De’Von Achane got hurt last week, but he might have to share with Jaylen Wright this Sunday. Running lanes could be scarce up against Minnesota’s No. 1 ranked defense.

WR Malik Nabers vs. Cardinals: He’s probably not 100% healthy yet and the drop to Jameis Winston can’t be understated. But the Arizona secondary arrives just in time — the Cardinals rank 31st in pass defense DVOA. Give Nabers another week to make good.

RB Alvin Kamara vs. Falcons: While player development isn’t always linear, player decline almost always is — Kamara’s late-career dip makes sense. But with Travis Etienne Jr. now on IR, Kamara can hold fantasy value simply through projectable volume. Just remember to keep the light on for Kendre Miller, a legitimate sleeper in deeper pools.

RB Keaton Mitchell at Seahawks: At a modest 5-foot-8 and 191 pounds, Mitchell will never profile as a bell cow. And any date at Seattle is a tricky spot. But Mitchell continues to outplay Omarion Hampton, which means Mitchell has a good chance to earn double-digit touches per week moving forward.

Red Light 🚨

QB Drake Maye at Bills: There’s plenty of blame to go around for New England’s offensive collapse — OC Josh McDaniels isn’t helping the cause and the talent drop-off after A.J. Brown is significant. Maye’s pedigree and intelligence should be considered before a fantasy manager makes a rash decision, but the Patriots probably won’t get airborne again until Brown returns.

TE Kyle Pitts Sr. at Saints: Michael Penix Jr. has always had a smooth connection with Drake London, but it’s never translated to Pitts. The Saints have not covered tight ends well this year, but we still need a show-me game from Pitts before he returns to fantasy consideration.

WR Emeka Egbuka vs. Packers: It’s been a slow liftoff for the entire Tampa Bay passing game, and things could get worse with undrafted rookie QB Jalon Daniels forced to start. The Green Bay defense has been a downfield escort for three weeks, but Egbuka and Chris Godwin aren’t proactive starts at the moment.

WR Courtland Sutton at 49ers: I’m a longtime Sutton advocate, but he’s struggling to gain separation as he navigates his age-31 season. We also have to consider that Jaylen Waddle is the obvious target hog here, and QB Bo Nix has struggled to click with new play-caller Davis Webb. Even if you still believe in Sutton, make him play his way off your bench.

item.title: Mike McCarthy doesn't know whether the Joey Porter Jr. trade affected the team
item.description: The Steelers traded cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys less than 24 hours before their Week 4 game at Cleveland.
item.content:encoded:
The Steelers traded cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys less than 24 hours before their Week 4 game at Cleveland. After the 27-24 loss, coach Mike McCarthy was asked whether the timing of the move had a negative impact on the team.

"You know, I mean, that's really, you know, a question that's really specific to individuals, and I can't really speak on every individual," McCarthy said. "You know, the timing was, you know, was the night before a game, and, you know, I'm sure that's what the guys woke up to but, yeah, I mean, it's part of our business."

Earlier in the press conference, McCarthy revisited the intersection between business and football, as it played out throughout the Porter saga.

"You never hope business, you know, gets in the way of your preparation and playing, but, you know, it's the modern NFL," McCarthy said. "You know, it was a situation where, you know, it's been going on for some time. As an organization, we felt like this was the best thing for us and, you know, we wish Joey well, and, you know, I never really got a chance to coach Joey, but, you know, obviously, did some, you know, did some great things here, and we wish him the best in Dallas."

McCarthy added that there "was definitely a point" where he "definitely thought it was a possibility" that Porter would play for the Steelers against the Browns.

"We had a rep count in mind," McCarthy said, "so that's what we were working towards."

Quarterback Aaron Rodgers also got a question about the timing of the Porter trade and the potential impact on the team.

"You gotta ask the defensive guys," Rodgers said. "They're probably around him more often but, you know, I thought Joey might play this week, based on his practice stuff but, you know, we wish Joey well."

One defensive player wasn't surprised by the move. At the outset of the Thursday night broadcast, Kaylee Hartung said linebacker Patrick Queen knew that, when Porter didn't get on the bus with the team to Cleveland, "he wouldn't be in Pittsburgh when they came back."

Porter is now in Dallas. And it appears that he will indeed make his 2026 debut on Sunday, when the Cowboys face the Texans.

item.title: Deshaun Watson rallies Browns to a field goal in final seconds to beat the Steelers
item.description: The Steelers rallied after a bad first half against the Browns.
item.content:encoded:
A little more than a month ago, Cleveland Browns fans booed Deshaun Watson, and Watson shot back at the fans. It was the low point of a toxic relationship.

On Thursday night, Browns fans weren't booing.

Watson came through when it mattered as he did in each of the Browns' previous two games. After Aaron Rodgers and the Pittsburgh Steelers scored a touchdown and 2-point conversion to tie Thursday night's game in the final two minutes, Watson had a shot to make up for what to that point had been a rough second half.

Watson completed enough passes to get kicker Andre Szmyt close enough to try a 56-yard field goal, and he hit it with 10 seconds left to give the Browns a 27-24 win. Cleveland is 3-1 and in sole possession of first place in the AFC North, at least for a few days.

"It was electric. It was amazing. This is what it's all about," Watson told Amazon Prime Video after the game. "Nights like this, in Cleveland, in front of our home fans, getting them Ws, getting them wins, this is what it's all about."

In the Browns' second preseason game Watson struggled, was booed, then said it was disrespectful of Browns fans to do so. That seemed like it could be the end of a tumultuous relationship. But the Browns stuck with Watson, even though there were plenty of reasons to move on.

Now the Browns are 3-1, with three straight wins, and nobody is talking about benching Watson.

Browns dominate first half

The Steelers scored first, and then the Browns took over the rest of the half. 

Cleveland was moving the ball at will on Pittsburgh. Watson had what might have been the best half he has had with the Browns. He completed 14 of 17 passes for 181 yards and a touchdown in the first half. His 2-yard touchdown pass to tight end Harold Fannin Jr. gave the Browns a 21-7 lead. 

Watson was in control. He was spreading it around but mostly finding a talented pair of rookie receivers. Second-round draft pick Denzel Boston had 74 yards on three catches in the first half and first-round pick KC Concepcion had 58 yards on four catches.

Since the Browns' oft-maligned trade for Watson in 2022, the offense has rarely looked good. Cleveland has suffered through so many bad quarterbacks through the years, the first half had to be unrecognizable to Browns fans. 

Of course, the struggles of the Steelers' defense played its part in that. At one point Amazon Prime Video showed T.J. Watt making the unusual move of grabbing a headset from an assistant on the sideline and then was in a heated discussion with the coaches up in the press box. 

Getting picked apart by Watson was driving Watt and the Steelers mad. Pittsburgh's defense was much better in the second half.

Browns stall, Steelers get back in it

Watt tried to get the Steelers back in the game in the third quarter. He had a great play to strip Watson on a run-pass option and recovered the fumble himself. But his offense couldn't move the ball and punted after a sack. 

A great challenge by the Steelers' coaches in the fourth quarter got Pittsburgh back in the game. The Steelers got an interception downfield but there was clear defensive pass interference. Pittsburgh challenged, saying linebacker Jack Sawyer tipped Watson's pass. When a pass is tipped, there can be no pass interference afterward. The replay review showed the ball was tipped, so not only was the pass interference penalty wiped out but the interception stood. The Steelers drove down after that pick and scored their first touchdown since the first drive of the game, on a nice Rodgers pass to tight end Darnell Washington. The Steelers didn't get the 2-point conversion but trailed just 21-16.

The Browns finally got their first points of the second half on a field goal, pushing the lead to eight points. The Steelers punted quickly but downed a punt at the 1-yard line. Watson had Fannin wide open for what would have been a key first down but he missed him badly and Cleveland punted.

Rodgers had 3:32 to get the Steelers a touchdown and 2-point conversion. Rodgers immediately completed a couple of passes to get into Browns territory, and then another pass to DK Metcalf got Pittsburgh to the 12-yard line. Rodgers kept throwing jump balls to Washington and finally on fourth down they drew a penalty to keep the drive alive. The next play, tight end Pat Freiermuth caught a touchdown. The Steelers went for 2 and the tie, and after an offsides penalty Rodgers got in on a sneak to even up the game.

Watson moved the Browns into field-goal range, but took a sack that pushed Cleveland back a bit. Then he had a terrible third-down pass, and that left Szmyt to attempt a 56-yard field goal with 15 seconds left. Szmyt hit it.

Rodgers' ensuing desperate pass downfield was picked off and the Browns had the win.

"Just belief, hope, determination," Watson said, when asked on Amazon Prime Video what he sees in his teammates. "Those guys look at me and they want me to lead the ship. I just told them, 'Believe in me, do what I ask and I'm going to make a play when the opportunity comes.'"

The Browns are on a roll. Nobody expected Watson to be leading a first-place team after four weeks of the season.

item.title: Jalen Ramsey on Joey Porter Jr.: Unfortunate it didn't work out, but I'm happy for him
item.description: After a long, drawn out negotiation, the Steelers dealt cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys on Wednesday night.
item.content:encoded:
After a long, drawn out negotiation, the Steelers dealt cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to the Cowboys on Wednesday night.

Porter's now-former teammate Jalen Ramsey went through a similar situation with the Jaguars back in 2019, which ended with him being traded to the Rams.

After Thursday night's loss to the Rams, Ramsey told reporters that he felt like a big brother to Porter and wanted him to be a valued, important part of the Steelers going forward.

“It is very unfortunate that it didn’t work out,” Ramsey said, via Mark Kaboly of the Pat McAfee Show. “But at the same time, I am happy for him. I am happy that he is getting a fresh start. I wish him all the success in his NFL future. I think he is a stud, I really do. I think he is a top-five guy. People argue that he’s top 10, but I really think Joey is a good player, I really do.”

Ramsey also referenced his own story and compared it to Porter.

“It happens, and everybody moves on,” Ramsey said. “For me, I’ve been through it before. I was Joey before at one point. When I was 24, I was Joey. A little different; our situations were a little bit different. The exit was similar, potentially. It is what it is. I treat it as part of the NFL business. We held hope as long as we could that things would get done, but that’s part of it. That’s business. Guys have to do what’s best for them because the NFL is not for long. You have to do what is best for you, and you can’t be mad at a man wanting to do that.”

item.title: NFL Predictions: Will the Bears backup QB magic continue vs. the Jets?
item.description: The Bears will keep the Jets guessing about their quarterback, but will they keep the backup-QB magic going and win on Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
When the schedule was announced, most Chicago Bears fans penciled this one as a win, but that was before Caleb Williams suffered a grade 2 hamstring pull and before we saw how much better the New York Jets have looked. The Jets may be 1-2, but they played the Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions tough. It took overtime for the Packers to sneak by them in Week 2, and the Lions scored the go-ahead touchdown with 2: 25 left on the clock.

Thirty-six-year-old Geno Smith has been slinging it for New York, throwing for 783 yards through three games, 4 touchdowns, and no picks, with a league-leading 75.5 completion percentage.

Even if the Bears were at full strength, this one wouldn’t be the gimme many thought, but that said, I like the Bears to win; regardless of who is playing quarterback.

Head coach Ben Johnson isn’t going to tip his hand, as he wants to keep the Jets guessing. On the Amazon Prime Video Thursday Night postgame show, James Palmer said that Caleb Williams has been living in the trainer’s room to try to get his hamstring right but is still likely out. He also said the Bears seem to be leaning towards Bagent to start on Sunday.

ESPN’s Adam Schefter speculated it’ll be Bagent, and while he made it clear it wasn’t a report (just his opinion), he went on to list several reasons he believes it’ll be Bagent.

I’ve been on the Tyson train since Ben Johnson spoke after the Monday night game. It just makes sense given that he’s the backup, Ben has said he believes Bagent is good enough to be a starter in the league, and he’s one of the best-paid number twos in the NFL. And besides, that Keenum moment was magic, so why tempt fate?

Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Bears as a 3.5-point favorite, and I think they’ll win by at least a touchdown. The weather is expected to be nice in Chicago, so I expect Ben’s offense to be humming, which is why I like the 42.5 over to hit too.

item.title: NFL predictions: Houston Texans run it back against the Dallas Cowboys
item.description: Reasons to bet the Texans win this week
item.content:encoded:
How are we here again? Your Houston Texans are 0-3. The offense, full of weapons, is struggling to put more than 18 points per game on the board and suddenly, this is a must-win match up against the Oklahoma South Cowboys.

Fanduel ‘s odds currently have the Texans down by 3. Will Kaimi Fairbairn take that bet and kick H-Town to their first win of 2026? Hopefully it won’t come to that. However, the betting site’s first prop bet has the Texans opening drive ending in a field goal as a more likely outcome than a touchdown.

Texans fan and BRB faithful Sarlegant pointed out a recent Seth Payne video the other day where former H-Town defender Payne unpacks some Texans truths. After listening to head coach Demeco Ryans discuss the coaching staff, play calling and some other nifty tidbits in the video,, there is hope for Battle Red Nation!

If you’re unfamiliar with Seth Payne, despite his humorous self-deprecation, he holds a very unique place in local Texans coverage. As a former player, highly intelligent student of the game and passionate Texans fan, Payne has unique access and insights into the organization, coaching, schemes and on-field results. When he breaks things down, you’ll likely learn something new, and chuckle more than once along the way.

Reason for hope: the offense gets Nico Collins and Ed Ingram back this week. Dallas pulled off a newsworthy trade with the Pittsburgh Steelers this week to secure cornerback Joey Porter Jr., who may start this weekend. Cowboy fans think that’s fantastic. Texans fans remember Collins facing Porter in the playoffs last season.

Prediction One: Nico Collins scores on Joey Porter Jr.

While Collins did not have a stellar outing in the Texans 30-6 blowout of the Steelers in last season’s wild card, Nico is a “put the team on your back and win” kind of player. Sitting on the sidelines, watching his teammates struggle to move the ball and score points has him chomping at the bit. With Tank Dell still out, Jayden Higgins on IR and the tight ends serving as o-linemen, Collins will get quarterback C.J. Stroud’s attention early and often. Expect him to step up.

Prediction Two: Will Anderson Jr. has 3 sack game.

Much has been said about the “players only” meeting led by Anderson Jr. last week. While not every player on the defense seemed to respond against the Indianapolis Colts, it’s very clear Anderson Jr. is on a mission to win a Super Bowl, even if he has to do it all by himself.

Dak Prescott has been sacked 3 times so far in 2026, but he’s yet to face a defense like Houston’s. With the need to hold the ball a little longer, his desire to scramble will rise. Derek Stingley Jr. had 2 breakups and an interception the last time these teams met and Prescott will remember. And with that memory, he opens himself up to pressure from Danielle Hunter, Sheldon Rankins, Jadeveon Clowney and Anderson Jr.

Reason for hope: Despite Ryans’ recent insistence that offensive coordinator Nick Caley will continue to call the plays, Ryans low-key admits things are not working as they should. How does this play out heading into this weekend’s game? Hopefully other voices (Stroud, QB coach Jerry Shuplinski, Ryans) will speak into the play calling. This offense has the talent to perform, just not the way Caley seems to think they should.

On paper the Cowboys seem like the better team so far in 2026. But they’ve not stood toe-to-toe with a team like Josh Allen’s Buffalo Bills. Houston has, and nearly won.

Prediction Three: Dallas Cowboys 19 Houston Texans 31

The Texans are due for a breakout game. H-town football fanship is perpetually sailing through rough seas, but for every trough between waves, there’s a crest to keep us all hoping for more. The offense seems to suddenly click, the defense contributes a touchdown, and Dare Ogunbowale will reignite the special teams. Not only will the Texans take their first win of 2026, they’ll beat the spread doing it.

item.title: Carolina Panthers 2026 fan mailbag: Injuries, play call balance, practice squad rules, and more!
item.description: Answering all your questions in this week’s fan mailbag!
item.content:encoded:
Hello CSR! Welcome to Brian Answers, part two of your weekly Panthers fan mailbag for everyone! We’re coming off a rough Sunday, but its a new week, the Panthers are playing in prime time, and they have a ton of injuries to figure out. Let’s dive in to all your questions!

Brazilian Panther: Okay Brian, with almost a month of football so far, tell us two players on the Panthers that disappointed you the most so far and two others that surprised you on the positive side of things.

I find it hard to get into early grades on players only 3 games in, but I will give it a try. I’ve been most surprised by Tommy Tremble and Darren Waller at the tight end position. This position was considered to be a need all throughout the off-season, but these two have been showing out so far as reliable pass catching targets which I really did not expect going into the season. Obviously Waller has shown more touchdown production, but they both have carved out reliable roles in the passing game in a tight end room that I think many considered one of the worst in the NFL on paper.

As far as disappointments, I think its hard not to point to Derrick Brown as one of them. I think he’ll find his way once again, but he’s definitely played below expectation in these first 3 games. I’d also say Robert Hunt at right guard, for the money they are paying him he hasn’t been a top tier guard so far.

Brice Guild: We have had to call on a lot of depth players already this season. Give me your take on the the performance and quality of play we have seen from them.

Lee Hunter is certainly playing well enough to justify having a 4th round pick play significant snaps at corner. I would also give Zakee Wheatley props as he’s been graded pretty highly at safety. I mentioned the tight ends already so I won’t rehash that, but on offense Brycen Tremayne is still continuing to show he can play as a wide receiver when called upon.

Coach_K: which cornerback are you looking forward to step up or perhaps sign?

I don’t know if Carolina will sign a cornerback in the next couple of days, I think they just end up sticking with what they have. This is a great opportunity for Corey Thornton to step up from the practice squad after playing some really meaningful snaps as a UDFA last season before being knocked out due to injury. I think he makes a lot of sense to take some snaps when they need to pull Will Lee off the field or rotate at the nickel position. Thornton showed he can play wherever they need him to, and Sunday would really allow him to build on his rookie season.

DBelt: What have you noticed about the difference in the offense with Brad Idzik calling plays, for better or worse?

The aggression on offense is definitely up a notch from last season. I like them taking more deep shots down the field, but it really shot them in the foot going for it on 4th down against the Browns and trying to get intermediate completions instead of just getting the sticks. We’ll see if they can level it out, but I do enjoy the idea behind the aggression.

CasualFanAlso: What impact, if any, has the performance of the OL had on the timeline for the return of Moton and Ekwonu? I know the team will want to be “cautious”.

I don’t expect them to move the timelines up at all, as sad as that may be to read. Taylor Moton’s blood clots aren’t something you can rush and Ikem Ekwonu is still going to be lucky if he plays at all this season. Both will return when it makes sense.

schrodingersblackcat: You’re Brad Idzik. How do you address the offense’s struggling ground game? How do you distribute the workload between Chuba and Dillon and whoever else we have in the backfield? What is an acceptable YPC? How do you improve the O Line’s ability to establish a credible run threat early in the game?

I don’t really know to be honest. They might be missing their starting left guard and right tackle this week, so that’s already going to be a handicap. My best guess is one cut rushes that don’t take long to develop, and have the back just hit the hole fast. Maybe mix in some presnap motion to get the linebackers moving prior to the snap. More RPOs could also work as an extension of the run game since Bryce Young is so comfortable with those.

carolinajerry: Brain, Panthers Nation is panicking. Fans are spiraling. Please instill some good ol’ Panthers optimistic delusion into us and save our sanity. Will we be ok?

The optimist in me says that the Panthers probably should have won that football game on Sunday, they just missed some easy turnovers and made mental mistakes, combined with some questionable 4th down decisions in a game where defense was ruling. These are all correctable mistakes, and they aren’t facing a mobile quartertback this week which ultimately cost them a lot of points on defense in weeks 1 and 3. There’s actually a strong chance they can rebound against the Lions if they clean up their own mistakes and force Detroit into a few of their own. And being 2-2 going into a much needed bye week wouldn’t be a bad position to be in at all.

Dcangio09: What happened to Derrick Browns strength, anchor and power. I haven’t seen him get repeatedly blown off the line this consistently since his 1st couple years.

This is one of those few questions where I don’t really know what to say. Its been quite concerning how much of a drop off we’ve seen, both on the field and as far as dumb penalties and mental mistakes. I’m sure the offenses have schemed around him because he’s one of the best in the game, maybe they will play Cam Jackson more to try and take some of those double teams off of him.

DannyLimes: How surprised will you be on a scale of 1 to 43.25 (where 1 is not surprised and 43.25 is a surprised as you could possibly be about something) when we beat the Detroit Lions? What is the main reason for this surprise or lack there of?

I actually wouldn’t be all that surprised if the Panthers pulled out a win, so maybe a 28? The Panthers actually match up fairly well against the Lions offensively, if they can control the pass rush a bit. Defensively, the biggest killer for them has been quarterbacks escaping the pocket and extending plays and I don’t see that happening with Jared Goff. This could be a game where Ejiro Evero breaks out some new looks to throw off the offensive gameplan with new personnel due to injury. And its at home. Being unpredictable could really work to their benefit.

celticgreen86: With Damien Lewis not out a few weeks, what changes do you anticipate to the OL which will now lose its best player to date?

The Panthers clearly liked Corey Bullock quite a bit when they claimed him on waivers during roster cutdowns. So I think he’s just going to step right in and play, which will be interesting to watch. What they do at tackle should Monroe Freeling be unable to play might be more interesting.

sgtx: What questions should we be asking that we haven’t ?

I miss the food questions.

Aggressively_avg2: Based off games played, and the fact we literally could have had Pat Surtain, Jaycee Horn has to go down as a bust, right?

Nope. Jaycee Horn has been one of the best at his position, and these same injuries could have befallen Surtain if he were put in the same position. Horn didn’t enter the league with injury concerns. Players getting hurt just happens.

Chef: Hey, Brian! Lots and lots of doom and gloom after the Browns debacle. Give me something that no one is talking about that should age well as the season progresses. Position groups, individual players, coaches, ect are all on the table. I need some silver linings, thanks.

The Panthers special teams unit is one of the best in the league, and that’s building on what the unit did last season. Their kickoff unit is excellent. They’ve had some snafus with muffed punts but the coverage unit is definitely in the conversation for top of the league, and Ryan Fitzgerald is doing a darn good job with the dirty kickoffs.

GooseCreek: Okay, Brian. I see where OLB Cam Gill has been resigned onto the Practice Squad after a previous stint on this squad. During that prior tenure he was promoted in a standard game day elevation. Players on the PS can be the designee for such promotions three times during the current season. So, here’s your question… Is Cam Gill available for two more game day elevations since he has one on the books OR Is Cam Gill available for three more game day elevations since he has been resigned after earlier being cut from the roster? In other words, is he a considered a player returning to the PS or did his being cut make him the equivalent of a new player being hired onto the PS?

No, Cam Gill would need to have signed to a new team for his elevation counter to reset. He did not sign to a new team’s practice squad. This is likely a rule to prevent teams from just arbitrarily cutting guys from the PS and then re-signing them to reset the counter.

JakeNCVA: Hey Brian! Can or should the Panthers keep running 40 pass to 20 run plays a game — that is about what it has averaged out to for the past three games. People seemed to love it the first 2 games and not as much this past game with the Browns (48 pass plays to 23 run plays)

I think they want to be more balanced, but they need the rushing game to actually produce consistently to keep the offense on schedule. That really hasn’t been happening. They should try to run the ball more but they can’t be continuing to struggle to get 3-4 yards and expect the balance thing to work.

That’s all for this week, Panthers fans. Enjoy SNF, and KEEP POUNDING!

item.title: The morning after: The Steelers is the Steelers
item.description: The Steelers is the Steelers.
item.content:encoded:
Trade Joey Porter Jr. and lose to the Cleveland Browns in a 24-hour span. This is the new normal for the Pittsburgh Steelers.

And I say “new normal,” but it’s not exactly new, is it? The Steelers haven’t beaten the Browns in Cleveland since Ben Roethlisberger’s final season in the NFL back in 2021, and they’ve made a habit of trading top players at key positions without any sort of backup plan in place.

They did it with Diontae Johnson in 2023 and didn’t find an adequate No. 2 for George Pickens. They then traded Pickens in 2025, didn’t find a good No. 2 to put opposite DK Metcalf, and Pickens went on to be an All-Pro. Now, they’ve dealt Porter and their secondary was immediately exposed by Deshaun Watson and the Browns.

This isn’t the team from the 2000s where their defense was the best in the league for a six-year span and the offense was being led by a young star at the position. At some point, they stopped being the big brother that would give the Browns a noogie twice a year. Instead, they are the brother that is past their prime and still clinging to his glory days at a high school reunion. At some point, it’s time to take off the letterman jacket and class ring and leave your hometown.

The Steelers haven’t done that, though, and it doesn’t feel like they ever will. Not with this owner, at least. Rather than being a team that consistently competes for Super Bowls like they did 15-20 years ago, now they trade players they don’t want to pay and lose to the Browns every year. Because that’s who they are now. Draft a good player, player showcases high-end talent, trade player away, try trading for another player to replace the player you just traded. The whole “Browns is the Browns” joke is certainly rich coming from any Steelers fan who still says it, because at this point, the Steelers is the Steelers, and this is their identity.

But hey, that 2008 season was special, wasn’t it? It’s the morning after game day, and it’s time for the Steelers to change how they do business.

Aaron Rodgers miscues

Aaron Rodgers had several misses that severely impacted the outcome. In the third quarter, he had DK Metcalf wide open for what would have been the easiest deep touchdown pass of his career. He didn’t see it and instead checked it down to Ben Skowronek.

On the final play of the game for the Steelers, Rodgers had Metcalf open again. This time, it would have been an easy completion to put the Steelers at the 35-yard line for what would have been a 52-yard field goal for Chris Boswell to try and send the game into overtime. Instead, he forces a ball to Roman Wilson that gets picked off and seals the game.

Pressure on Rodgers puts hard cap on Steelers offense

The Browns found a specific defense that worked and just ran it into the ground all night. Per Sumer Sports, Cleveland played one-high safety on 80 percent of looks, which usually coincided with pressure getting to Rodgers. They rushed five on roughly one third of snaps, and the Steelers couldn’t figure out a counter for what the Browns were doing for most of the night. There were sacks where Rodgers held the ball for quite a bit, but that had a lot to do with the Steelers’ receivers complete inability to generate separation against man coverage. The Steelers don’t have consistent man-beaters, and that’s something that defenses can certainly hone in on throughout the year.

Atrocious tackling and coverage

The lack of ability to take down a ball carrier was abhorrent. Cole Holcomb and Rayshawn Jenkins both riffed on bringing down Jaleel McLaughlin on the Browns’ first touchdown of the night. Payton Wilson and Patrick Queen both had dreadful nights when it came to bringing down ball carriers, and there were whiffs on potential sacks. It was a largely bad game from the defense, especially in the first half when the Browns scored 21 unanswered points.

Additionally, coverage was terrible. Daylen Everette was torched multiple times, including a 60-yard bomb to Denzel Boston that set up a Browns touchdown, and a slant while playing outside leverage while Cleveland was deep in its own territory. If only they had a high-quality young cornerback on their roster.

Other notes

  • T.J. Watt continues looking like his old self. He finished with a forced fumble, a fumble recovery, and a sack.
  • Jalen Ramsey needs moved to safety permanently and Brandin Echols should take the nickel spot. The current safety rotation just isn’t getting it done.
  • The offense needs to run through Jaylen Warren. On money downs, and short yardage situations, he needs to be the guy.
  • I’m officially at Defcon 3 with Chris Boswell. If he makes his first kick of the night, we are having a very different conversation right now.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!

item.description: Las Vegas represents a potential get-right game for Kansas City’s defensive line.
item.content:encoded:
Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face. It’s a quote made famous by Mike Tyson, and it applies in all aspects of life.

Especially football.

Imagine you’re standing in your backyard playing catch with your 7-year-old son. It’s easy to throw a pass 10 yards away. No pressure, right? But what if there’s someone in front of your child? Suddenly the throw becomes more difficult. Now imagine a 290-pound grown man sprinting toward you at full speed as you’re attempting to make the throw.

Yeah, good luck.

That’s the life of an NFL quarterback. Every. Single. Week. It sounds miserable. It’s no wonder fewer than 20 people in the world can do this job at a high level at any given time.

Applying that pressure on opposing quarterbacks is the goal of every defensive coordinator in the league. Don’t let the opposing quarterback get comfortable. Get him off his spot. Throw him off of his rhythm. We hear this every single week. It’s easier said than done.

But when you do it, it’s special. It’s what made the Seattle Seahawks’ defense stand out a year ago. It felt like a new player was getting after the quarterback on every single play. That defensive line came at opposing offenses in waves. It was constant, relentless pressure.

It’s the kind of thing every team in the league hopes to replicate. The Kansas City Chiefs are no different.

After the first week of the season, it felt like Kansas City might be on its way to a better year in that regard. The defensive line made Denver Broncos quarterback Bo Nix look uncomfortable from the very first snap. Steve Spagnuolo was in his bag. The results were hard to argue.

Chiefs defenders had three sacks and five quarterback hits in that season-opener against Nix and the Broncos. This same defense has zero sacks and five quarterback hits over the past two weeks… combined.

Wait, what? Why? How? Didn’t this team just spend millions on a new nose tackle and multiple top-50 selections on defensive linemen? And aren’t they spending $50 million against the cap on two other defensive linemen?

Yupp. They are. The results should be better. But they aren’t. Not yet, at least.

What’s gone wrong? Let’s dive into the numbers, shall we?

*Stats courtesy of Dynatize & Pro Football Reference

So, yeah, it’s a bit all over the place. The Chiefs blitzed the Broncos, and Denver responded by getting the ball out of Nix’s hands as quickly as possible. It resulted in a ton of dump-offs and a lower pressure rate, but the Chiefs’ blitzes paid off with a few sacks.

The blitz rate dropped over the past couple of weeks. The pressure rate did increase ever so slightly, but the Chiefs’ ability to finish plays in the backfield all but disappeared.

It’s strange. It’s hard to explain. It needs to change.

This is a good week to get things back on track. Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins is the first true pocket passer the Chiefs have faced all season. He’s been sacked five times and hit 10 times over the past two weeks against the New Orleans Saints and Los Angeles Chargers, and he could be without starting right guard Jackson Powers-Johnson this week. Powers-Johnson has missed practice each of the past two days with a groin issue. His replacement would seem to be Caleb Rogers, a player with six career starts.

That sound you hear is defensive tackles Chris Jones and Peter Woods licking their chops.

This was already a relatively advantageous matchup for the Chiefs’ defensive line, and it looks like it’s getting better. Brandon Thorn of Establish The Run ranked the Chiefs’ defensive line vs. the Raiders’ offensive line as the fifth-biggest mismatch in the league this week. He has the Raiders rated as the 21st “best” offensive line in the league. The Chiefs rate as the fifth-best defensive line.

That’s a lot of faith in a group that hasn’t produced. There are reasons why smart individuals like Thron still have so much belief in a group that’s failed to produce a sack over the past two weeks. It’s entirely possible the Chiefs’ defensive game plan focused on stopping the run against the Indianapolis Colts. At times, it looked like they played more of a contain rush against quarterback Malik Willis to force him to win from the pocket. It’s also possible safety Chamarri Conner’s absence has forced Steve Spagnuolo to run a more vanilla game plan on the back end of the defense in recent weeks. Throw in a nagging calf injury for Jones, and you’ve got a formula for limited pass-rush production.

That’s all fine and dandy. But eventually this unit has to start putting pressure on the opposing quarterback again. This would be a good week for it to start.

item.title: Miami Dolphins vs. Minnesota Vikings: Three reasons the Dolphins can win, lose in Week 4
item.description: You know the meme with the lady who says nah, then maybe, but then nah… yeah. That.
item.content:encoded:
The Miami Dolphins show signs of life.  They hung with the Kansas City Chiefs for most of the game and could have been in contention for a win without penalties, mistakes, and other issues young teams need to clean up.  This week, the Dolphins face the 3-0 Vikings, making Miami the 2nd team in NFL history and the 1st since 1986 to have their first 4 opponents go undefeated (hat tip to Urthling).  Talk about a brutal schedule.  Maybe we could have foreseen the Chiefs and Niners, but the Raiders and Vikings are a surprising 3-0.  Anyway, this game is not without its own glimmers of hope.

Reasons for hope

Miami’s offense is showing some potential

The Chiefs’ defense generally doesn’t get much media attention because all the focus is on quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the offense.  But their defense is top 5 or top 10 in total yards allowed (4th), passing yards allowed (6th), rushing yards allowed (10th), and in scoring defense (3rd).  Miami was expected to struggle offensively, despite being at home.  It was supposed to be even worse when they lost Achane to injury.  However, the Dolphins managed 329 yards of offense, including some explosive plays, and for the first time this season, they didn’t have a single 3-and-out… unless you wanna count the 3-play drive to end the game when it didn’t matter.  They moved the ball without Douglas and Achane for all or most of the game.  Now, it wasn’t all sunshine and rainbows.  The Dolphins had 2 drives that ended in a turnover on downs.  They also fumbled in scoring territory where at least a field goal was likely.  The offense committed several penalties that set them back, and this team isn’t capable of consistently overcoming that.  But they made progress and should keep developing as the season moves forward.

Minnesota’s offense is bad

Despite everything I just wrote, the Dolphins’ offense is still bad.  At least in terms of scoring.  They are averaging 12 PPG and haven’t gotten over 13 points in any game.  But in terms of yardage, they aren’t the worst.  Their opponent this week IS the worst offense in this regard.  The Vikings are dead last in total yards at 715, passing yards at 411, and are just above the Dolphins in rushing yards at 304 (tied for 16th; Miami is 20th at 295).  The Vikings score more than the Dolphins, averaging 23.7 PPG.  But they have faced the Bears (7th in scoring defense), Bucs (23rd in scoring defense), and the Packers (30th in scoring defense).  The Dolphins have faced the Chiefs (3rd), 49ers (5th), and Raiders (8th).  The Dolphins have faced the 6th, 10th, and 14th best passing defenses.  The Vikings have faced the 11th-, 12th-, and 13th-best passing defenses. The Dolphins have faced the 10th, 15th, and 20th best run defenses.  The Vikings have faced the 2nd, 21st, and 28th best run defenses.  I could make other comparisons, like opponents’ pressure percentages and so on, but I think you can smell what The Earl is cooking here.  As bad as the Dolphins offense has been, the Vikings have been similarly bad.  If there was ever a game for a struggling secondary to have a chance…

Miami’s defense is also showing some potential

So far, the Dolphins have faced some tough offenses.  They got their feet wet against the Raiders and Ashton Jeanty.  They faced the juggernaut 49ers and their arsenal of weapons, then came home to face off against Mahomes and the league’s leading rusher.  The Dolphins have faced the 2nd- and 3rd-ranked teams in scoring offenses this season.  The Niners are averaging 32.7 PPG while the two AFCW teams are tied at 29.3.  That is a LOT of scoring.  Yet in Week 3, they held the Chiefs to 17 points until a late drive pushed them to 24.  The Chiefs and Niners are tied for 6th in passing yards.  I discussed the issues with the total number of incompletions Miami allowed, but they have faced tough opponents. 

In the last two games, the Dolphins have allowed less than 100 yards rushing, including just 88 total yards to the Chiefs, who have the league’s top rusher.  They limited him to 70 yards on 18 carries – 3.9 YPC – including a 22-yard run.  Meaning they held him to 48 yards on the other 17 carries – 2.8 YPC.  That’s solid work against a guy who went over 100 yards in the previous 2 games.  The Chiefs said they wanted to lighten his workload, but the other RB went 6 for 17. The passing defense still needs work, but instead of Purdy or Mahomes, they get the Murray/Wentz combo that is averaging 137 passing yards per game.  Something will have to give here. 

The rookies are also stepping up.  Miami also saw rookie CB Chris Johnson go untargeted by Mahomes all game. Rookie LB Jacob Rodriguez is tied for 7th in the league in combined tackles at 28 and has 3 TFLs, which is tied for 17th with several players.  That is solid considering he doesn’t get sacks added to that total.  He also generated a turnover this week with the INT and is now the leading favorite to win defensive rookie of the year.  The Dolphins still haven’t recorded a sack but did manage to generate 8 pressures in this game (per PFR).  Miami’s 3 previous opponents have lower-end pressure percentages, but now face Murray, who is pressured about as much as we have seen Willis get pressured.  Could this be the game for the defense to get things right, build some confidence, and start to turn this ship around?

Reasons for Concern

Vikings still have weapons

As fun as it is to discuss the Vikings’ potential offensive ineptitude, they still have a dynamic WR duo in Justin Jefferson (who may not play) and Jordan Addison, plus a good receiving TE in TJ Hockenson.  They have Aaron Jones at RB, who is currently 12th in the league with 203 yards.  Despite the emerging potential from the pass defense, they have still not forced more than 6 incompletions in the last 2 games.  Part of that is a lack of pressure, and part of that is softer coverage.  If either or both of those issues show up, the Vikings have more than enough talent on offense to make the Dolphins pay. 

The Vikings have also faced circumstances that could explain a lack of offensive production.  They scored 39 points at home in week 1 but lost their starting QB in the 1st quarter.  That generally puts a damper on the offense, even if the backup is good.  That backup then had to travel to face a good Chicago team in week 2, the one top-ten scoring defense they have faced.  Then they had to travel to Tampa Bay to face the 6th-ranked defense in yards allowed.  One home game with injury issues and 2 road games.  Now the Vikings have their starter back and will be playing at home against a defense that allows 80.3% of opponents’ passes to be completed and allows 28.7 PPG.  Maybe the Vikings offense is the one that can help the Dolphins defense turn their ship around.  Or maybe the Dolphins defense is the one for the Vikings offense to turn their ship around.

On the road again

The Dolphins are singing like Willie because they travel to face an opponent for the 3rd time in 4 games.  Road games in the NFL are tough for anyone and even more so for a struggling team.  The Vikings are more than a TD favorite, and ESPN’s matchup predictor gives Minnesota an 83.1% chance to win.  For an offense that has struggled with pre-snap issues, they now have to go play in a raucous environment where noise will be a factor.  Miami committed 8 penalties in week 1 and 7 penalties in week 2.  In each game, 6 of those penalties were offensive.  This issue can rear its ugly head again this week, and this offense cannot afford to get behind the sticks and in unfavorable down-and-distance situations because…

Vikings defense and the Brian Flores factor

I saved the worst for last because this has the potential to unravel any of the hope I mentioned.  We’ll start with Flores.  Everyone is aware of the history between Vikings DC Brian Flores and the Dolphins organization.  Most of the particulars involved are no longer with Miami – only 2 players from the Flores era are still on the roster: Austin Jackson and Zach Sieler.  That doesn’t mean Flores does not still hold animosity to the organization that derailed his head coaching career.  Now he gets his first chance to call a game against THAT team AND that team is struggling mightily amidst a rebuild.  You think he doesn’t wanna stick it to the Dolphins in what should be an easy middle finger game for him?  He has had this game circled for as long as possible.  Why will this be an easy middle finger game? 

For as bad as the Vikings offense has been, the Vikings defense has been great.  The Vikings are currently 12th in total yards allowed, 4th in rushing yards allowed, and 2nd in points allowed.  The Vikings have actually allowed more passing yards than the Dolphins, but we all know about the bend-don’t break style of Flores’ defense.  Where it gets scary is protecting the QB.  The Vikings blitz more than any other team, at a rate of 66.4%.  The next closest team is Chicago at 39.8%.  That’s nearly 2/3 of the time.  And it works because the Vikings are tops in the league in pressure percentage at 40.3%.  The second-place team is Las Vegas at 36.3%, and we remember how that game went.  The Chiefs blitz at a higher rate than most but only get pressure 20.2% of the time. 

The Vikings not only blitz and disrupt the passing game, but they also get home.  The Vikings lead the league with 14 sacks.  They rank 4th in hurry percentage at 17.2% and tie for 1st with 23 hurries.  If the ball does come out, they get the ball carrier to the ground.  They are 2nd in missed tackles with only 7 (Miami is actually good here, tied for 6th with 12).  When they aren’t getting to the QB or getting ball carriers to the ground, they are turning the ball over.  They are 5th in turnover percentage at 16.2%.  They are tied for 1st with 4 INTs and have forced 2 fumbles.  They have the lowest passer rating allowed at 67.7 and allow a TD on only 2.6% of attempts.  That’s a long-winded way of saying this defense can put opposing offenses in a bind, let alone one still struggling to find its footing.  And even more so with a spurned, vindictive ex-HC licking his chops to make it as ugly as possible.  The Dolphins will enter this game without their best weapon in Achane and their best receiver in Douglas possibly out.  The Dolphins’ defense may have a chance to make a statement.  The Dolphins offense may be in the part of hell that burns blue.

I said what I said

I foresee this being a slog-fest of a football game with very little scoring on either side.  I would bet on the Vikings offense to score against Miami’s defense rather than the other way around.  However, if there is one silver lining for the offense, it’s Malik Willis as a rushing threat.  They have only faced one QB this season with true rushing prowess, and that was Caleb Williams. He went 5 for 42 in that game.  If Slowik can use Willis strategically in the run game to force the Vikings to play more conservatively, the Dolphins will have a chance.  Regardless, it would be nice if one side of the ball could finally have a breakout game.

item.title: Bills fans’ Week 4 rooting interests: One more week before the rules start to change
item.description: One more week for strength of schedule, strength of victory, and a little AFC chaos before the rules start to change.
item.content:encoded:
Three weeks down, and so far our rooting interests have been pretty easy to figure out. 

The Buffalo Bills should win. The rest of the AFC East should lose. Teams Buffalo has beaten should win, because strength of victory is our friend. Teams still waiting on the Bills’ schedule can win, too, because strength of schedule may eventually matter. 

And, when none of that applies, we can always fall back on one of my favorite rules: Bad AFC teams should win enough games to stay away from the really good draft picks, while bad NFC teams are welcome to lose as often as they would like and collect them instead. 

But we’re getting close to the point where things change. 

After this weekend, four games will be in the books. That’s still early, but it’s also roughly a quarter of the regular season. Beginning next week, we’re going to have to start paying a little more attention to the top of the AFC standings. Strength of schedule is nice. Making the road to the No. 1 seed a little less crowded is nicer. 

For one more week, though, we’ll mostly stick with the rules that got us here. 

_____________________________________________________________________________- 

AFC East 

New England Patriots at Buffalo Bills 

Root for: Buffalo Bills 

This one needs no explanation. But the win will mean more than a much more pleasant Monday for Bills Mafia. It’s Buffalo’s first AFC East game of the season. New England is 1-2. Not going to lie – watching the Patriots return to reality has been fun. Let’s remind them who the real “Beast of the East” is. Go Bills! 

New York Jets at Chicago Bears 

Root for: Chicago Bears 

This one checks two boxes. The Jets are the Jets, which means we want them to lose. The Bears are also on Buffalo’s schedule later this season, which means a Chicago win helps the strength-of-schedule side of things. No overthinking required. 

Miami Dolphins at Minnesota Vikings 

Root for: Minnesota Vikings 

Miami loses? Good. A future Buffalo opponent wins? Also good. 

The Vikings are 3-0, but they’re safely tucked away in the NFC, so their undefeated record isn’t standing between Buffalo and anything we want. Let Minnesota keep winning while Miami keeps doing the opposite. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

Rest of the AFC 

Pittsburgh Steelers at Cleveland Browns 

Root for: Cleveland Browns 

This is a weird place to start because the entire AFC North is 2-1. There isn’t a bottom-feeder available for us to adopt, and there isn’t a clear division leader for us to knock down. 

So, we’ll take Cleveland. If the Browns eventually turn into a legitimate AFC threat, we’ll adjust. For now, putting another loss on Pittsburgh works just fine, and we don’t have a strength-of-schedule reason to prefer either one. 

Indianapolis Colts at Washington Commanders 

Root for: Washington Commanders 

Here’s an easy one. Neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule, and Indianapolis is in the AFC. Give the AFC team another loss and let Washington take the win. It doesn’t do much for Buffalo, but not every game has to. 

Dallas Cowboys at Houston Texans 

Root for: Houston Texans 

Houston is 0-3, which isn’t exactly helping Buffalo’s strength of victory after the Bills beat the Texans in Week 1. A Texans win gives Buffalo’s strength of victory a boost and gets Houston away from the bottom of the standings and, eventually, the very top of the draft. That’s two reasons to temporarily become Texans fans. 

So, come on, Houston. Do something useful. 

Tennessee Titans at Baltimore Ravens 

Root for: Baltimore Ravens 

Enjoy this one, because I suspect this answer might be different pretty soon.Baltimore is on Buffalo’s schedule and Tennessee isn’t, so under our early-season rules, we’re rooting for the Ravens and the strength-of-schedule bump. 

But Baltimore is already 2-1 and very much part of the AFC conversation. Once we get through this week, teams hanging around the top of the conference aren’t going to keep getting our support just because Buffalo plays them eventually. 

Jacksonville Jaguars at Cincinnati Bengals 

Root for: Cincinnati Bengals 

There isn’t much direct Buffalo benefit available here. Both teams are 2-1, neither is on Buffalo’s schedule, and they’re both in the AFC. 

So, this is mostly a pick-your-poison game. Jacksonville currently leads the AFC South, while Cincinnati is stuck in that ridiculous four-way 2-1 tie in the AFC North. We’ll take Cincinnati and put a loss on a division leader. We’re getting close enough to the point where that starts mattering. 

Kansas City Chiefs at Las Vegas Raiders 

Root for: Las Vegas Raiders 

And here is where our rules collide headfirst. 

Kansas City is 3-0. Las Vegas is 3-0. Both are sitting right beside Buffalo at the top of the AFC, and the Raiders are also on Buffalo’s schedule in Week 6 – a full six weeks before the Bills can handle their own business with the Chiefs. 

So we’re taking Las Vegas and handing Kansas City its first loss. 

Los Angeles Chargers at Seattle Seahawks 

Root for: Los Angeles Chargers 

Please win a football game, Chargers. 

Buffalo just beat Los Angeles, but that put the Chargers at 0-3. That’s not particularly helpful for the strength-of-victory column. A Chargers win gives that number a boost and, as a bonus, moves an AFC team away from the premium draft picks. Seattle can take the loss and move a little closer to them instead. 

This is exactly what our weird little rule system was built for. 

Denver Broncos at San Francisco 49ers 

Root for: Denver Broncos 

This one is mostly about strength of schedule. 

Denver is a future Buffalo opponent, so every Broncos win makes the Bills’ schedule a little stronger. They’re 2-1, which is worth keeping an eye on in the AFC, but we’re not quite ready to start rooting against every AFC team with a winning record.  

Plus, a Denver win coupled with our hopeful Kansas City loss keeps the AFC West crowded at the top. Let them spend all their time and energy fighting with each other. Maybe by the time they remember Buffalo is over here, they won’t have much fight left for us. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

NFC 

Arizona Cardinals at New York Giants 

Root for: Arizona Cardinals 

Neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule, so we’re heading to the draft-pick portion of the program. The Giants are 2-1. Arizona is 1-2. Let the Cardinals get back toward the middle while the Giants take the loss. We’re not trying to hand premium draft capital to NFC teams that don’t need our help getting better. 

Los Angeles Rams at Philadelphia Eagles 

Root for: Los Angeles Rams 

Meet next week’s opponent. 

Buffalo heads to Los Angeles in Week 5, so we’d like the Rams to look a little better before the Bills get there. A Rams win improves Buffalo’s strength of schedule now and could become a strength-of-victory boost later if Buffalo handles its own business. 

Besides, at 1-2, Los Angeles could use the help. 

Green Bay Packers at Tampa Bay Buccaneers 

Root for: Green Bay Packers 

The Packers are on Buffalo’s schedule. The Buccaneers aren’t. That’s enough for now. Green Bay doesn’t show up until December but wins count the same whether we collect them for the strength-of-schedule pile before or after we meet. 

Detroit Lions at Carolina Panthers 

Root for: Detroit Lions 

Buffalo already beat Detroit, so we know the drill. Every Lions win from here makes that Week 2 victory look a little better. Carolina doesn’t appear on Buffalo’s schedule and can happily absorb the loss. Strength of victory wins this one. 

Atlanta Falcons at New Orleans Saints 

Root for: Whoever you want 

We’ve found it. The game where I can’t come up with a particularly convincing reason to care. Neither team is on Buffalo’s schedule. Both are in the NFC. Both are 1-2. 

If we’re going strictly by the draft-capital rule, somebody has to win, so flip a coin and hope the other one gets closer to stealing a good draft pick from an AFC team. Or use this game to make dinner. That’s probably the better option. 

_____________________________________________________________________________

We’re still early enough that most of this is tiebreaker housekeeping. Buffalo’s wins over Houston, Detroit, and Los Angeles get more valuable when those teams win, and future opponents piling up victories can help the Bills down the road. 

But the grace period is almost over. 

Once Week 4 is finished, we’ll have enough of a season to start looking harder at the AFC standings. If Kansas City, Baltimore, Las Vegas, or somebody else starts separating from the pack, we’re not going to keep cheering for them just because they happen to appear somewhere on Buffalo’s schedule. 

At some point, the simplest rooting interest becomes the most important one: Everybody between Buffalo and the No. 1 seed needs to lose. 

We’re just about there.  Go Bills!

item.title: Where the 49ers have surprised the most through three weeks
item.description: The Niners have been rolling on offense, and one unit is standing out.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are off to a hot 3-0 start to the 2026 season, securing wins over the Los Angeles Rams, Miami Dolphins, and Arizona Cardinals.

So far, it’s been their offense that’s been the story, as the 49ers have excelled behind Brock Purdy, playing mistake-free football and ranking first in the NFL (by far) in EPA per play. Their passing offense has especially come out strong, as Purdy looks like an MVP candidate, but we’re also slowly starting to see the run game built out with Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black.

It isn’t a surprise that the 49ers offense has looked good. Many have under Kyle Shanahan, but this unit has looked quite elite through three weeks, and it isn’t just Purdy and the skill position players.

The offensive line has also played quite well, holding up in pass protection, while the run blocking is also starting to play out. According to Ben Baldwin’s formula, which takes into account PFF grades, blown block percentage, and pass-block win rate, the 49ers rank first in the NFL in pass protection rankings currently.

They lead the NFL in both PFF grades and blown block percentage through three weeks, and they also haven’t given up a sack. What has the coaching staff seen from that unit so far?

“I think they’ve been really good,” offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak said. “We knew who four out of the five would be, I think, in general, but as far as the guard competition, we felt really good. Whoever ended up starting was going to be the right guy and play good for us. These guys have done a heck of a job through three weeks. Obviously, no sacks, but I look at that as a team stat too.

“It has a lot to do with, obviously, the O-Line, our tight ends, our backs, our quarterback, our receivers being in the right place. There’s been a little bit of luck involved. Brock’s made some great plays of making people miss. So, it’s really a team stat. It has to do with our offense being efficient and staying on track, and so far so good. Hope to keep that going.”

The 49ers are also bringing back that efficiency in the run game after struggling last season. So far, they’re averaging 5.1 yards per carry as a team, with Christian McCaffrey up at 4.7 yards per carry on 35 attempts. What has been the key to being more efficient there?

“I felt like we were really efficient running the ball, staying out of long passing situations, second and long, third and long,” Kubiak added. “In this game, it felt like maybe in the second half we got that going a little bit more. Anytime you can be efficient on first down running the ball, it’s going to help. I always talk about staying out of obvious passing situations where the D-Line can tee off, where a play caller might change up their coverages. It just gets harder when you’re in those situations, so the more efficient we can be.

“I’ve been real happy with our backs. They’ve had some good runs, but there’s been hard runs that get us four, five, six yards that maybe were blocked for three that keep us on track, get us to second and four and then maybe third and two and we have a better chance of staying on the field. Then you look at the second half last week, Christian [McCaffrey] had a 12-yard run in the fourth quarter. That’s what we’re talking about. Those just efficient grinder runs that keep you on the field and let you keep calling plays, so hopefully we keep that going.”

So far, when it comes to protection, Jake Brendel has allowed just one pressure through 163 pass-blocking reps. Dominick Puni has given up just two, while Connor Colby and Colton McKivitz have given up four each, and Trent Williams has allowed five.

The 49ers offensive line was a strength last season as well, but the run game never really got going. Now, that unit is looking like a strength again this season, and they’re near the top of the NFL in a couple of metrics so far.

item.title: Signs point to Tyson Bagent for the Bears on Sunday
item.description: As Bears coach Ben Johnson prepares for a reunion with fellow former Lions coordinator Aaron Glenn, Johnson is doing his best to keep Glenn and the Jets in the dark about who the starting quarterback will be.
item.content:encoded:
As Bears coach Ben Johnson prepares for a reunion with fellow former Lions coordinator Aaron Glenn, Johnson is doing his best to keep Glenn and the Jets in the dark about who the starting quarterback will be.

It's one of the benefits of having injury issues complicate the most important position in pro football. The uncertainty can be weaponized, in the hopes of preventing the next opponent from knowing who they'll face.

Johnson is trying his damnedest to keep the plans for Week 4 secret. Through two full practice days in advance of the game against the Jets, he has largely succeeded.

That said, it's hard to keep the many people who are present for practice from saying something to someone who is trying to find out who's getting the work. As we hear it, Tyson Bagent (not Case Keenum) has gotten the first-team reps so far this week.

This obviously points to Bagent as the starter in place of Caleb Williams, who continues to recover from a hamstring injury.

It makes sense. Bagent earned the backup role. He entered the Week 2 game against the Vikings in the fourth quarter and nearly pulled off a last-second win.

Keenum got the Monday night start because he was available to prepare for the game against the Eagles at a time when Bagent was in the concussion protocol. By the time Bagent was cleared, the hay was in the barn with Keenum.

The question of whether a coach can keep the identity of his starting quarterback a secret is separate from whether the league should allow it. It creates another chunk of inside information that could be mishandled by those who know the truth.

Presumably, the Bears will make an announcement today. Or maybe they won't. The rules don't require it.

And if it's Bagent, the Bears can say they necessarily made the announcement by not updating their depth chart. Bagent is No. 2, Keenum is No. 3. Both are healthy. Common sense points to Bagent.

If he's indeed getting all of the practice reps, that only reinforces it.
