item.title: Five Good Texans Questions with Blogging the Boys
item.description: We catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys for five questions
item.content:encoded:
Like the Olympics, the battle with the interstate rivals comes every four years. It is never a disappointment because someone in the state is getting bragging rights. Fortunately, we have some consistency here at five questions and so I get to catch up with David Halprin of Blogging the Boys yet again. It was good catching up with him again. Like the Texans, the Cowboys suffered a disappointing loss late and that is where our conversation hegan.

Battle Red Blog: The Cowboys are obviously coming off a tough loss overseas to the Ravens. Are you concerned about a hangover?

David Haprin: At this point, I’m concerned about everything Dallas Cowboys. Well, maybe not their ability to throw the ball on offense, but outside of that, nothing has been really solid in Dallas. In the Ravens game, the biggest cause of the loss was HC Brian Schottenheimer, something he has admitted himself. His play-calling in certain situations was abysmal and he knows it. In a weird way, if you look at a lot of things that happened in that game, the Cowboys played pretty well, especially considering the amount of injuries they have on defense. They got their run game going, their defense had some splash plays that kept them in the game, but mistakes on the field, and especially along the sideline, really cost them. They were in position to beat the Ravens, and beat them pretty handily. But they threw it all away. Will there be a hangover from that? Maybe, one never knows with this team. 

BRB: The Cowboys offense has always been able to move the ball and score points. Are there any new wrinkles that fans from outside of Cowboys Nation might not be expecting?

DH: I wouldn’t say much has changed since that part of the team went virtually untouched from last season. From the coaches, to the starters, even to some of the backups, it is a unit with a high continuity level. They will do what they do. They love to run Javonte Williams between the tackles. They will give a lot of eye candy pre-snap, and they use movement blocking from their offensive line in the run game in diverse ways, but essentially what they want is Williams chewing up yards between the tackles. 

That allows them the freedom to use their passing game, which is the star of the show in Dallas. Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens are the best thing Dallas has going for them. Outside of his playoff issues, Prescott is a stats machine. Lamb and Pickens can be used all over the field. Pickens is thought of as a deep ball, contested-catch specialist, but the Cowboys will throw a short slant to him also. Lamb can be used everywhere, even on screens. Backing them up are TE Jake Ferguson and WR3 Ryan Flournoy. As long as their offensive line holds up, they will score points.

BRB: Obviously the Cowboys defense has been more shaky. What is the key for them getting back on track?

DH: I mean, at this point, we are just hoping for performances where they hold the team in the game so the offense can win it. That usually means making a few splash plays in a game to create a turnover, a fourth-down stop, or something that gives the offense the ball in decent position. They don’t have a good pass rush, that is one of their problems. They are okay creating pressure, but they don’t get sacks. Mobile QBs also really hurt them. They are also not great against the run, although they did a decent job of keeping Derrick Henry in check last Sunday. 

Their biggest problem right now is the injuries in the secondary. The Cowboys defense has suffered an inordinate amount of injuries recently, with a large cluster in the secondary. We almost ran out of bodies back there against the Ravens. Rookie linebacker Jaishawn Barham and rookie safety Caleb Downs have been the best players on that side of the ball. The Cowboys need some of their veterans, like Quinnen Williams, Rashan Gary and a few others to start playing up to their abilities to get close to back on track. 

BRB: Are there any key injuries that could have a significant impact on the game on Sunday?

DH: Short answer – absolutely. Long answer – on offense, we are still without our best lineman in G Tyler Smith, but sub T.J. Bass has been great. On defense:

Starting CB Cobie Durant has been out, and will likely miss this week, too.

Starting LB DeMarvion Overshown has been out but it is possible he suits up this week.

Starting S Malik Hooker has been out but he could also be back this week. 

Starting S Jalen Thompson was hurt in the Ravens game and is likely going to IR.

Top backup CB Shavon Revel was hurt in the Ravens game and his status is unknown.

Top backup S P.J. Locke has been put on IR.

Backup DT Jonathan Bullard might go to IR.

BRB: How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending?

DH: Honestly, I am so unsure this week. The Cowboys are Jekyll and Hyde, sometimes in the same game. We just never know how they will play. But it is early in the season and I am still an optimist, so I am going to take the Cowboys for the win, but it is going to be a close one. The Cowboys offense will move the ball, even against really good defenses they can usually generate some points, but their defense can make the most mediocre of offenses look all-world. In the end, I’m betting, speaking of prop bets, on the trio of Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. They will lead Dallas to a squeaker of a win. 

We wanted to thank David again for taking the time to answer our questions and for being so easy to work with again after four long seasons. We want to wish David and the Cowboys the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck begins on Monday morning.

item.title: From Andre the Giant to Tacko Fall: The case for using a 7-footer to block field goals
item.description: Decades ago, Washington floated the idea of bringing in Andre the Giant to block field goals. Now, the idea has been floated again, this time with 7-foot-7 Tacko Fall.
item.content:encoded:
In spring of 1975, Washington coach George Allen hatched a plan to keep his NFL team in the headlines in the dead of the offseason. 

Allen spread word that he was interested in signing professional wrestling behemoth Andre the Giant and developing him into a specialist at swatting field goals and extra points out of the air.

Washington quarterback Joe Theismann recalls being asked to pose for publicity photos beside Andre at a press luncheon organized by the team that July. The most famous photo features the 7-foot, more-than-400-pound wrestling icon effortlessly cradling Theisman like a toddler. Said Theismann with a laugh, "I've never been around another human being that large in my life."

The way Theismann remembers it, Allen's pursuit of Andre was more marketing ploy than serious courtship. There was never a tryout, Theismann said, nor a contract offer. Andre's drawing power barnstorming the country as professional wrestling's ultimate attraction brought him far more money than he ever could have earned in those days from playing NFL football.

"George Allen was the ultimate promoter," Theismann told Yahoo Sports. "Back in the 1970s, you didn't have football 24-7-365 like you do now. When the season ended, there was a time when there was a lull, but George always wanted to find creative ways to keep the Washington Redskins' name front of mind."

An idea that started as a harebrained publicity stunt half a century ago has since resurfaced as a radically unconventional strategic proposal. A former NFL assistant coach and director of football analytics posted to social media earlier this week encouraging teams to give 7-foot-7 former NBA center Tacko Fall a tryout as a field goal block specialist.

The notion of deploying someone like Fall in this role first struck Ryan Paganetti nine years ago when he was part of Doug Pederson's Philadelphia Eagles coaching staff. A fellow coach in a special teams meeting emphasized the potential for interior rushers to block a field goal if they're able to generate two yards of push and get their hands up. That made Paganetti wonder how much more disruptive that interior rush could be if it cleared space for a long-armed, bouncy-legged 7-footer with a basketball background. 

Since NFL rules prohibit defenders from lining up directly over the long snapper on field-goal or extra-point attempts, Paganetti proposes putting two interior defensive linemen on one guard and tasking them with driving him backward as far as possible. Then Fall or another similarly gigantic human would rush into the lane they've created, extend his arms and attempt to time his jump to meet the kick. 

The concept was zany enough that Paganetti didn't dare mention it as a 27-year-old Eagles assistant linebackers coach just a few years out of Dartmouth. As the economics major-turned-football analytics savant says now, "You can't walk into the head coach's or GM's office and suggest something that would sound bats**** crazy. Then they just laugh at you and you have no credibility for the rest of your career."

What Paganetti wisely did instead was bide his time while waiting for technology to come along that enabled him to quantify his idea. Gradually, he became more comfortable pitching colleagues on the notion of 7-footers as special teams weapons. 

Trusted friends across the industry were receptive. One special teams coordinator who worked with Paganetti was not. 

"I will literally freak the f— out if you bring that up to [the head coach or general manager]," Paganetti recalls the special teams coordinator telling him. "I don't want to have to worry about coaching that s***." 

Now in his first year working as an independent football analytics and strategy consultant after previous stints with the Eagles, Jaguars and Raiders, Paganetti decided the timing was right to go public with his idea. 

"Could the tallest player in NBA Combine history change the outcome of a Super Bowl?" Paganetti wrote to begin a 593-word X post on Tuesday evening. 

That post now has more than one million views. 

"If you want to be innovative, you have to be willing to think outside the box," Paganetti said, "and you have to be willing to be laughed at." 

1 in 4 games decided by a field goal or less

The tallest NFL player ever deployed as a field-goal block weapon seldom rushed the kicker from the line of scrimmage. 

In 1969, Kansas City Chiefs coach Hank Stram would position 6-foot-10 rookie tight end Morris Stroud under the goal posts and have him try to time his leap to deflect the ball as it approached the crossbar. 

The NFL quickly intervened and banned Stroud's goaltending tactic before the former Clark Atlanta University basketball player blocked a single NFL kick. The rulebook now bans players from leaping up to bat away a kick as it passes over the crossbar and grants permission to the referee to award three points for that "palpably unfair act."

The best current demonstration that height can be an advantage when blocking field goals in the NFL is Calais Campbell, the long, nimble 6-foot-8, 307-pound defensive end who has swatted 10 kicks out of the air since 2009. Campbell has earned the freedom from special teams coordinators to dictate where he lines up on any field-goal block try because of his unique blend of reach, strength and innate sense for where the path of the ball might be.

Campbell's height is an outlier among pass-rush specialists because of his unique ability to maximize the advantages of his extraordinary length while still moving explosively and getting low enough not to sacrifice leverage. Most athletes 6-8 or taller would be fighting against physics because their center of gravity is so much higher than the average 6-4, 310-pound offensive lineman.

Those issues help explain why no NFL team has experimented with a 7-footer as a field goal blocker before. That player would almost certainly have to be a specialist who could not be counted on to contribute in other ways.

It's Paganetti's contention that a 7-foot-7 giant like Fall would be worth rostering if he could be developed into a special teams weapon. Roughly one-in-four NFL games are decided by three points or fewer. A team significantly increasing its field-goal block rate from the standard 1.9% could be worth an extra victory or two. Then there's the potential intimidation factor, which could also reduce accuracy and prove meaningful. 

"It's definitely worth the last spot on a 53-man roster if a guy can do this at a high rate," Paganetti said. "Honestly, it's probably worth like the 30th roster spot." 

What combination of height, reach and vertical jump would a 7-footer need to strike fear into NFL kickers? The best way to quantify that comes from a sports technology company founded in Denmark by golf-enthusiast brothers Klaus Eldrup-Jørgensen and Morten Eldrup-Jørgensen, along with radar engineer Fredrik Tuxen. 

Harnessing Tuxen's expertise in using Doppler radar to track bullets and missiles, the founders of TrackMan created a reliable way to reconstruct the trajectory, velocity and movement of a golf ball. Then TrackMan began applying its precision tracking system to other sports. The Chicago Bears became the first NFL team to use TrackMan in 2019 when evaluating kickers to replace Cody Parkey. Now, special teams coaches from all 32 NFL teams receive TrackMan data reports on kickers and punters at events like the NFL Scouting Combine.

The average ball height on NFL field-goal attempts after seven yards is just shy of 12 feet, according to Simon Mathiesen, head of TrackMan's football operations. About 80% of NFL field-goal attempts are 11-13 feet off the ground after seven yards, Mathiesen said. Seven yards is the relevant data point in Mathiesen's eyes because NFL kickers tend to kick from eight yards behind the line of scrimmage and field-goal defenses typically generate one yard of push. 

At the 2019 NBA Draft combine, Fall stood 7-7 in shoes with a standing reach of 10 feet, 2½ inches. Throw in a reported 26.5-inch vertical leap, admittedly without a helmet and football gear to weigh him down, and Fall would clear the 12-foot mark with ease.

"Theoretically, I think it's worth exploring," said Mathiesen, a former All-American kicker at Division II Northwest Missouri State. "If I were a GM, I think I'd look for the most athletic 7-footer I can find and test him out in the preseason. Is that more valuable in a preseason game than a sixth-string receiver? I certainly think so." 

Paganetti gently pushes back against the TrackMan estimate that the field-goal block unit typically generates only one yard of push. He argues that the interior rush often pushes the offensive line back two yards — and that such a push should happen more often if the defenders driving the guard backward don't have to worry about jumping or getting their hands up. 

NFL player tracking data has the ability to measure how far backward a guard is typically driven on a double-team rush, but Paganetti has not found time to study that yet. If he's right that the push is often two yards instead of just one, that would mean that the ball is crossing that spot about 10 feet off the ground instead of nearly 12. 

"I feel very good saying that 12 feet is way too high," Paganetti said. "I don't think there's actually been a single block where any player was 12 feet high. I'm not even sure there's been a single block where any player was 11 feet high. The rush is getting more movement than that."

It has been tried

In July 2025, someone actually dabbled with Paganetti's concept before he had the chance. 

University of Florida special teams coach Joe Houston received permission to have 7-9 men's basketball walk-on Olivier Rioux participate in practice and attempt to block some kicks from Gators kicker Hunter Smith.

The experiment didn't last long. Houston eventually scrapped it, reportedly because Rioux's vertical was just 11 inches and even with his extra-long reach, the former world's tallest teenager was unable to block any kicks. 

"They were a little disappointed," Florida men's basketball coach Todd Golden told the Associated Press.

By then, so many of Paganetti's friends knew about his obsession with this idea that he received a half-dozen texts containing links to articles about this experiment. Paganetti loved to see Florida giving the concept a try, but he said he wishes he could talk to Houston or former Florida head coach Billy Napier about some of the nuances that went unreported. 

"It's unclear if they basically just messed around with him standing at the line of scrimmage, or if they actually had more of a plan," Paganetti said. 

Yahoo Sports also sought further clarity from Napier and Houston, both of whom have since left Florida and moved on to other jobs. Houston is the best person to speak with, Napier said via a James Madison football spokesperson. An LSU football spokesperson did not return multiple messages seeking comment from Houston.

To Paganetti, finding the right 7-footer is as important as having a savvy scheme. He argues NFL teams would need to target someone with the ball skills and coordination to be able to time their jump and the girth and toughness to be able to withstand a hit. The 7-footer can't be so athletic that he's NBA-caliber, yet also can't be such a plodding stiff that he can't make explosive movements.

In other words, Tacko Fall. The 7-foot-7 center last appeared in an NBA regular-season game as a member of the Cleveland Cavaliers on December 30, 2021. He has since played professional basketball in China, where he has twice led the league in blocked shots. Fall received an invitation to training camp with the Philadelphia 76ers but is a long shot to make the roster.

It's unclear if Fall would have any interest in donning a football helmet and shoulder pads. Even if he did, some in football circles are unconvinced that his presence would prove disruptive for field-goal kicking operations.

"If NFL teams decided to start signing former 7-foot-plus basketball players specially to block field goals, I don't believe it would significantly change the percentage of blocked kicks," said retired former NFL kicker Nick Novak, now a private kicking coach and showcase host in the San Diego area. 

Height over the line of scrimmage was always a major point of emphasis for Novak during his playing days when preparing for teams with proven field-goal block specialists. Special teams coaches would position him as close as five yards from the crossbar, forcing him to either clear it or risk the ball ricocheting back at him. Nowadays, Novak's pupils use TrackMan to measure the trajectory of their kicks. 

"A great operation combined with great blocking from the field-goal protection team prevents penetration up the middle and pressure off the edge," Novak said. "You don't want a kicker changing his normal ball or trajectory because there happens to be a 7-footer on the other side."

Count former NFL special teams coach Gary Zauner among those who are skeptical that any team will ever roster a 7-footer as a field-goal block specialist. Zauner questioned if such a player would get a hand on enough kicks to prove worthy of taking up a roster spot. The former Vikings, Ravens and Cardinals special teams coach also pointed out that an astute team could kick from nine yards behind the line of scrimmage instead of eight if it sought to lessen the threat of an on-rushing 7-footer.

"Devin Hester caused me to lose sleep," Zauner said. "I don't think this would cause me to lose any sleep."

Theismann isn't as quick to dismiss Paganetti's idea as Zauner is. For decades, the former Washington quarterback has wondered what sort of impact Andre the Giant might have made if Allen were serious about pursuing him, if it wasn't just a publicity stunt. Now, Theismann wonders if Victor Wembanyama's presence on a field-goal block unit would be as terrifying for kickers as him lurking near the rim is for opposing guards attacking off the dribble.

"I would love to see it happen just because of my curiosity," Theismann said. "Certainly people would be talking about it."

item.title: Brian Schottenheimer: Great start for Joey Porter Jr., we'll see about Sunday
item.description: Cornerback Joey Porter Jr. was traded to the Cowboys late on Wednesday night and went through his first practice with the team on Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Cornerback Joey Porter Jr. was traded to the Cowboys late on Wednesday night and went through his first practice with the team on Thursday.

Porter did not practice all summer because of what was called a back injury and had been on the injury report in Pittsburgh during the season due to that injury or conditioning needs related to his long absence. He was not on the Cowboys' injury report for any reason, which has led to thoughts that he will be on the field for Dallas when they face the Texans on Sunday.

During a Friday appearance on 105.3 The Fan, Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said the team is still working out whether Porter will make his debut this weekend.

“We’ll see how he moves around today, see if he’s sore today," Schottenheimer said, via Jon Machota of TheAthletic.com. "But I thought it was a great start yesterday. Really, really pleased with not just what I saw on the field, but really just the way he attacked his preparation and in learning the system. The big thing that will drive this is his ability to communicate with Caleb Downs and some of the safeties and things like that as we get ready to finish the prep.”

Schottenheimer called the deal for Porter a sign the Cowboys are in "win-now mode" and that suggests we'll be seeing the newest Cowboy on the field sooner rather than later.

item.title: Lions vs. Panthers preview, prediction: On Paper
item.description: Our stats-heavy Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers preview and prediction for Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions and Carolina Panthers face off on Sunday night in a litmus test game for both franchises. Though the Panthers are 1-2 and the Lions are 2-1, both teams are very much considered a competitor for their respective divisions, and both are looking for a defining win to silence some of the doubters.

The Lions are currently 3.5-point favorites according to FanDuel Sportsbook, but this one could be even closer than that. Let’s break down the matchup in this week’s On Paper statistical breakdown, preview, and prediction of Detroit Lions vs. Carolina Panthers

Note: We are throwing away all 2025 data. Everything listed below represents 2026 only, unless otherwise stated.

Lions pass offense (12th) vs. Panthers pass defense (16th)

Through the first three weeks of the season, I expressed a healthy amount of optimism for the Lions’ passing attack given the incredible consistency they’ve shown over the last three years. They’ve rewarded that trust with one of the most efficient passing attacks in football thus far. Through three weeks, the Lions rank:

  • Third in passer rating (116.1)
  • 10th in yards per attempt (7.4)
  • Sixth in dropback EPA (0.286)
  • Fifth in success rate (53.2%)

Behind Jared Goff, this remains a top-10 passing attack that’s on the border of a top-five unit. The one thing they have been missing thus far is explosive plays. Through three games, the Lions have just nine passes of 20 yards or more, ranking 14th in the league. In each of the last four seasons, they’ve finished top-five in that statistical category. But teams are playing deep-shells against them and Detroit hasn’t found a way to pierce that coverage. Goff has just three passing attempts with 20 or more air yards (one completion), which is tied with Sam Darnold for the least in the NFL.

The good news is that pass protection has been stellar so far for Detroit. Goff has faced a pressure rate of 32.2% (seventh lowest), has a sack rate of 6.0% (15th), while the offense line ranks second in pass-block win rate (60%), but 20th in PFF pass blocking grade.

It’s hard to get a firm grasp on the Panthers’ pass defense. In Week 1, the Bears’ offense was just all over them, but they held their next two opponents relatively in check—although neither are the most explosive passing attacks in football. Through three weeks, the stats are inconclusive:

  • Sixth in passer rating allowed (79.0)
  • Sixth in yards per attempt (6.1)
  • 11th in dropback EPA (0.004)
  • 18th in success rate (46.8%)

The first two data points are promising, but the last two may fall closer to reality given that the Panthers have faced two mediocre-at-best passing offenses—and have mostly seen the damage done on the ground .

The main talking point about the Panthers’ passing defense has been the loss of their two starting cornerbacks this week. Both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn were placed on IR this week, leaving Will Lee and Akayleb Evans to step in. Admittedly, both players have flashed at time and won’t be pushovers, but they still represent significant downgrades.

Carolina’s pass rush is better on paper than in practice thus far. Free agent defensive end addition Jaelan Phillips (12 pressures, 2.0 sacks) is an outstanding player, as is veteran defensive tackle Derrick Brown (six pressures), yet the overall stats for Carolina’s pass rush are underwhelming. They’re just 21st in pressure rate (24.2%), 19th in sack rate (6.0%), and 23rd in time to pressure (2.70 sec.).

Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. The Panthers tend to lean heavy on zone and deep coverage—again trying to take away the explosives. So I expect St. Brown to eat over the middle, especially against less-experienced cornerbacks.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. The only way I see the Lions losing this matchup is if the Panthers’ pass rush lives up to its billing finally. Carolina does like to send the extra heat, but Detroit proved they could handle it last week with Goff playing nearly perfect football against the blitz. I’m not sure how the Panthers’ reserve secondary will hold up against the Lions receivers, but it certainly seems like a favorable matchup.

Lions run offense (2nd) vs. Panthers run defense (23rd)

With the sample sizes so small, I am trying to pull back my optimism of the Lions’ rushing attack, but the early signs are very promising. I want to completely throw out Week 2, because of the injuries the Lions were dealing with on the offensive line, but that’s not completely fair.

Still, even with that stinker of a game—in which the Lions also had to abandon the run—the Lions rushing efficiency metrics are optimistic. They rank:

  • Ninth in yards per carry (4.4)
  • 15th in rush EPA (-0.082)
  • Fifth in rush success rate (48.1%)

The only reason for Detroit’s low ranking in EPA is the lack of truly explosive plays. While the Lions have 11 rushes of 10+ yards (t-sixth most), they only have a single run over 20 yards to help skew the data this year.

But the offensive line stats are stellar in the run game. Detroit ranks fifth in PFF run blocking grade (70.6), fifth in adjusted line yards, and fourth in rushing yards before contact per rush (2.06).

This week, you’ve likely heard how bad the Panthers’ run defense is, and to an extent, that is true. However, it’s likely better than you think it is. Their season ranks are:

  • 32nd in yards per carry allowed (5.7)
  • 18th in rush EPA (-0.090)
  • Ninth in success rate (35.6%)

Those last two data points required some extra research, and I discovered the following. For one, the Panthers have been disproportionately impacted by quarterback runs through three games. Of their 580 rushing yards allowed, 25% of that yardage was damage done by mobile quarterbacks. That won’t be an issue this week. They’ve also given up a ton of big rushing plays—allowing five (most) rushes of 20+ yards. In between those splash plays, the Panthers have actually been okay. Not good, but okay.

But one thing they haven’t done well is create negative plays: Carolina sports the second-lowest “stuffed rate” (rushes of 0 yards or less) in football with 8.9%.

Player to watch: Devin Lloyd. Expected to be back after missing a game, Lloyd is the quarterback of the Panthers’ defense. Entering his fifth year and first with the Panthers, Lloyd brings a reputation of being a great all-around linebacker but specifically a stout run defender. He ranked 11th in PFF run defense grade in 2025 (85.2) and ninth in 2024 (84.2).

Advantage: Lions +1.5. This could—and should—be the week the Lions break out a long run. And while I expect the Panthers run defense to be stouter than the numbers suggest, Detroit also has one of the best rushing attacks in football right now, and I don’t think the Panthers are equipped to stop them for four quarters.

Panthers pass offense (15th) vs. Lions pass defense (26th)

Okay, now the bad news.

Bryce Young appears to be taking Year 4 by the horns, and is off to a very strong start. Thus far, the Panthers passing attack ranks:

  • 16th in passer rating (95.6%)
  • Eighth in yards per attempt (7.7)
  • 14th in dropback EPA (0.130)
  • 23rd in success rate (44.2%)

Okay, so it’s not the most efficient passing attack in football despite ranking first in passing yards per game.

The fact of the matter is this is a passing offense that is probably below average on a play-to-play basis, but is capable of an explosive play at any moment. This is highlighted by the fact that Carolina ranks just 28th in completion percentage (59.0), but has produced more 20+ yard passing plays (13) than anyone through three games.

Pass protection has been a pretty big issue, with the Panthers allowing a league-high 43.6% pressure rate and seeing that pressure arrive at 2.52 seconds (fifth fastest). They rank 25th in pass block win rate (47%) and 21st in PFF pass blocking grade (63.0). Their ace in the hole, however, is Young’s mobility. He’s done an expert job at managing the pocket and avoiding sacks. Despite allowing the highest pressure rate in football, Carolina’s sack rate is just 5.4%, good for 12th best.

Something to keep an eye on this week is the availability of Jalen Coker. He leads the Panthers in catches (18), yards (222) and receiving touchdowns (2), but is dealing with a quad injury. He sounded optimistic about his chances to play, but the Panthers have a Week 5 bye, so they could play it safe with their top receiver.

Deep breaths. Brave faces.

The Lions pass defense has been terrible. There is no putting lipstick on this pig. The stats can’t really be bent in any sort of positive direction. Detroit ranks:

  • 27th in passer rating allowed (110.2)
  • 24th in yards per attempt (7.9)
  • 29th in dropback EPA (0.245)
  • 29th in success rate (53.2%)

It’s ugly out there, folks.

I’d like to say it’s just the explosive plays (16 20+ yard passes allowed, 32nd) that are killing them, but the bottom-four success rate suggests the problems run far deeper. Coverage is clearly the biggest problem, with the Lions sporting the 22nd-best PFF coverage grade (53.7).

If there is hope, it’s in the Lions’ pass rush. Detroit ranks 10th in pressure rate (39.0%), second in time to pressure (2.46 sec.), and second in sacks (12). Their success in getting to the quarterback only makes their struggles everywhere else that much more frustrating.

Player to watch: Tetairoa McMillan. Last year’s Offensive Rookie of the Year is off to a decent Year 2. Most notably for this week, of the Panthers’ 13 passing plays of 20+ yards, he has four of them. His size (6-foot-5, 212) should be a problem for Detroit’s relatively short secondary.

Advantage: Panthers +2.5. Because Carolina is inconsistent from down-to-down, I do think the Lions will have opportunities to get off the field early and often. But the explosive play matchup here is a potential nightmare, and I won’t feel comfortable on any third-and-longs.

Panthers run offense (21st) vs. Lions run defense (29th)

It’s been a pretty slow start for the Panthers’ running game after finishing 2025 around the middle of the pack. Through three weeks, the Panthers rank:

  • 11th in yards per carry (4.3)
  • 23rd in rush EPA (-0.193)
  • 24th in rush success rate (35.7%)

There’s nothing flashy or splashy about the Panthers’ running game, as their longest run by a running back this season is just 16 yards. And while Young has been elusive in the pocket, he doesn’t tuck and run very often—he has just three rushing attempts all season.

The offensive line has been part of the problem, and it’ll be without its best piece this week with left guard Damien Lewis expected to be out. The Panthers do rank 10th in adjusted line yards this year and 10th in PFF run blocking grade (66.3), but 28th in run block win rate (71%). They do a good job avoiding negative plays, allowing a stuffed percentage of just 11.9%, sixth best in the league.

The jury is still out on the Lions’ run defense. While they were good in both Weeks 1 and 3, those rushing attacks have proven to be two of the least effective run offenses thus far this season. The Bills game looms large, but that is also the most efficient rushing attack in football right now, so we’ve got some odd and confusing data to parse through.

The season-long data doesn’t provide much clarity, either:

  • 21st in yards per carry allowed (4.4)
  • 31st in rush EPA (0.045)
  • 18th in success rate (40.6)

Without a doubt, the Bills performance (0.330 EPA, 58.6% success rate) is dragging them down, but I’m not entirely sure we can just toss it out. It’s just too early to tell.

Player to watch: Christian Izien. One of the biggest changes in performances between Weeks 2 and 3 was the play of strong safety Christian Izien. Detroit struggled to be gap sound on the perimeter against the Bills, but Izien was fantastic in run support against the Jets, tallying three tackles for loss. If Izien can replicate that performance, Detroit’s run defense could take another step toward legitimacy.

Advantage: Draw. I just don’t have enough data to feel any sort of way about Detroit’s run defense, but the Panthers run offense isn’t scary enough for me to give them an advantage.

Last week’s prediction

On Paper moves to 3-0 on the season and 2-1 against the spread after Detroit narrowly covered against the Jets last week. I still feel pretty dang good about my 24-20 prediction given how close New York actually was in that game. However, I underestimated Detroit’s ability to bounce back in run defense after the Bills game, and I certainly didn’t give Gibbs and a healthy offensive line enough credit. Detroit’s ability to control the line of scrimmage last week should bode well moving forward.

In the comment section, we had our very first perfect prediction of the season. task0778 nailed it perfectly with their 31-24 Lions prediction. Here is your prize, task. Please feel free to share it with Brad Holmes.

This week’s prediction

Detroit comes out with a +0.5 advantage, which feels perfect for this. The Lions are likely a better team in at least two of these matchups, maybe three. But they are so vulnerable in pass defense that the Panthers can—and probably will—keep this game close via explosive plays through the air. Still, with some serious inconsistencies from Young and company, Detroit should still walk away winners on Sunday night. Lions 37, Panthers 31.

item.title: 3 Titans who need to be way better vs. Ravens in Week 4
item.description: The Tennessee Titans need the following three players to be better versus the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans will play against Derrick Henry, Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens in Week 4. The winless Titans need to be significantly better than they’ve been if they hope to execute an upset. We’ve identified three veteran players the team needs big-time performances from.

QB Cam Ward

It obviously starts with quarterback Cam Ward. Believe it or not, the sophomore No. 1 overall pick did some good things versus the New York Giants in Week 2, including leading a possession where he completed 8-of-8 passing attempts and threw a touchdown. But Ward made two glaring red-zone errors that cost the Titans 14 points in a five-point defeat.

The fanbase is beginning to sour on Ward. Sunday’s showdown with the Ravens will be his 21st career start. The Titans can’t admit defeat on a top-pick quarterback this quickly, but progress needs to start becoming evident.

DE Jermaine Johnson II

The offseason trade that sent T’Vondre Sweat to the New York Jets for defensive end Jermaine Johnson II is starting to age terribly. Sweat has made an instant impact in East Rutherford. Meanwhile Johnson doesn’t have his first sack with the Titans.

All the advanced metrics (Pro Football Focus) say Johnson has been Tennessee’s least efficient pass rusher. Playing against Lamar Jackson and this Ravens offensive line is always a challenge. The Titans need way more from Johnson.

CB Alontae Taylor

PFF has Titans cornerback Alontae Taylor allowing 13 receptions on 15 targets for 116 yards. That’s a completion percentage of 86.7%. He also doesn’t have an interception or a pass breakup yet.

Taylor has been serviceable on tape, but the Titans need more from their $19 million per year cornerback. Ravens wide receiver Zay Flowers has been excellent through three weeks. Taylor will probably draw the coverage assignment on Flowers.

The Daily Slop 2 October 2026

Colts vs. Commanders, NFL London preview: ESPN experts on key players, matchups and predictions

What’s the biggest thing we’ve learned about this team that we didn’t know coming into the season?

Stephen Holder: It’s taking longer than hoped for some of the new additions on defense to make an impact. The Colts changed five of their 11 starting players on defense this season, and that has proven to be a difficult transition. Whether it all works as designed is still an open question as we are just three games into the season.

John Keim: Their run defense is excellent. Washington had hoped it would improve in this area, but that was the case each of the last two years as well but it never materialised. From 2024-25, the Commanders ranked 30th in rushing yards allowed and 26th in yards per carry. But the defensive line — Javon Kinlaw, Tim Settle and Daron Payne — has been excellent and the linebackers speed has been a big factor as well. Odafe Oweh earned a big contract because he can rush the passer, but he’s been terrific at setting the edge.

What’s the biggest concern around the team heading into this game?

SH: The Colts were yielding a historic amount of yardage in their first two games, leaving them statistically as the worst defense in the NFL. The 417.3 yards per game the Colts are allowing, on average, from opponents is well below the NFL average of 329.5. While the Colts made noticeable strides in their win against Houston last Sunday, it remains to seen whether they can sustain that momentum.

JK: Health. But we already covered that above. Their depth will continue to be tested until more starters return over the next couple weeks. That’s obvious so let’s take a look at something else: the pass coverage. Indianapolis does not have a dynamic passing attack — quarterback Daniel Jones ranks 18th in number of pass attempts of 15 air yards or more and only has a 56.6 passer rating on such throws. But the Commanders’ weakness has been coverage; they’ve allowed the sixth most passing yards and the second most passing touchdowns.

Where do you think Sunday’s game will be won and lost?

JK: I’ll say the ground game. The Colts have two outstanding corners in Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward to contend with Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs. But they rank 28th in yards per carry allowed. The Commanders have remained devoted to running — with the fourth most attempts despite being only 16th in yards per carry. But they will stick with it, using both Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White. If Washington’s defense has been excellent vs. the run, with 27 of 64 carries going for two yards or less — but if the Commanders continue stopping the run they must have better lane discipline when rushing Jones.

This gives Washington a way to control the game without asking Marcus Mariota to carry the offense. Establishing the run early will force Indianapolis to commit extra defenders to the box and create opportunities for Terry McLaurin, Stefon Diggs, and the tight ends.

Secondary: Indianapolis allows 276 passing yards per game, 30th in the NFL, and has zero interceptions through three games. The Commanders are averaging 182 passing yards per game against three top-10 passing defenses. They have the personnel to take advantage of this, and those players must show up.

Terry McLaurin has 141 receiving yards, while Stefon Diggs already has three touchdowns. If Indianapolis focuses too heavily on one of them, Washington has another established target who can win a matchup: Antonio Williams.

Commanders own the turnover battle

A to Z Sports

The Colts defense is giving up everything

Indianapolis has started poorly. The Colts don’t do anything redeeming on either side of the ball. They are a much worse team than Seattle & the worst team the Commanders have played all season.

The numbers are staggering:

  • The Colts are giving up 30.3 points per game, 29th in the league
  • They are surrendering 417 yards per game, dead last
  • Opponents are getting 6.5 yards per play against Indianapolis, worst in the league
  • Teams are running for 4.9 yards per carry against the Colts, 29th in the league
  • They’re giving up 141.3 rush yards per game (29th) & 276 pass yards per game (30th)

Mariota just beat the league’s best defense. Do I think he could put up 300-plus yards against a defense surrendering an average of 417 per game? Yes. He had a good day passing in the rain against Seattle. I wonder how he’d do with a clean track against this god-awful defense.

This could be a big day for the running back room. This could be a big day for Mariota on the ground. And it’s not just one faulty area for Indianapolis. Run defense, pass defense, yards per play: pick your poison. The Colts are in the bottom three in all categories.

The Colts offense isn’t saving them either

Even if Mariota is not what he was last week, say he’s shaky, doesn’t like the food over there, or the climate is weird for him, whatever. Indianapolis’ offense is still bad too. The Colts are 25th in pass yards per game & only 15th in rush yards per game. They carry a -1.7 turnover margin.

The only redeeming quality about the Colts? They are not getting penalized. They lead the league in fewest penalties per game at five. That’s it. That and their kicker make his kicks, because they can’t get in the end zone and can’t generate enough yards to threaten with Jonathan Taylor in the red zone.

You go through the roster, and you’re circling maybe three dudes: Josh Downs, Jonathan Taylor, & Tyler Warren. The Seahawks had 12 players you had to circle. Your coach is in the film room, yelling at you to buckle up and draw circles all over the board. Against the Colts, you’re circling three.

Jayden Daniels not concerned about reinjury risk: ‘That’s what the brace is for’

Jayden Daniels didn’t need to hear the full question to know what he was being asked.

Does it change how you throw the ball at — “Nope,” he responded.

How about handing the ball off? “Nope.”

It doesn’t make any difference? “Nope.”

He has been through this once before, unfortunately, having first injured the elbow last November.

Daniels appeared much like he did pre-injury: throwing without any obvious discomfort and playing without hesitation.

The one obvious change was the large accessory on his left arm.

Daniels says he is not worried about a potential reinjury when he plays.

“That’s what the brace is for,” he said. “If I had concerns, I would’ve gotten surgery. … You have those conversations with the people that I need to have those conversations with, and if the surgery needed to be ASAP, then I got to do what’s best for me. Commanders notebook: There is intrigue in London beyond who starts at quarterback

David Blough & Marcus Mariota shine in Commanders win over Seahawks

The Seahawks have the best defense in the NFL and are coached by Mike Macdonald, who has been the best defensive play-caller in the NFL for the last few seasons. For offensive coordinator David Blough, coaching just his third game as a play-caller with a back up quarterback, it was a tough task. Sports Illustrated

Three Games In, Washington Is Already Trying to Change What Defenses Think They Know

One of the more ambiguous things about the 2026 Washington Commanders was new offensive coordinator David Blough’s scheme and how he planned to use said offense. Three weeks in, Blough realizes the Colts now have a luxury the Eagles, Cowboys, and Seahawks didn’t: film to study before the they meet on Sunday.

“Over the first couple weeks, we’ve dove a lot into our own self-scout because we know there’s only three weeks of information that the Colts are getting to look at on our offense,” Blough said. “And so, how do we predict what they’re seeing, and how do we kind of adapt to that hopefully before they catch on? So, you know, it’s always a chess match, and we got a lot of respect for this team, this head coach, defensive coordinator that we’re going up against this week, and we want to stay ahead of that curve as well.”

While three games is not enough for opposing teams to truly know what David Blough’s offense will become, it is enough for them to start developing a scouting report. That means the Colts have more information on the Commanders than any other team they’ve faced this season. Blough’s job now is making sure the picture the Colts studied all week isn’t exactly the one they see Sunday.

Mike Sainristil is running out of time with Washington Commanders

If they don’t feel comfortable that Sainristil can turn it around, they have options available in house. One option is to promote Fred Davis II, a 6-foot-1, 200-pound rookie who last played college football at Northwestern and impressed in training camp and preseason. Another option is Terrell Smith, a fourth-year veteran out of Minnesota, who played for the Chicago Bears from 2023 to 2025 and has starting experience; however, he hasn’t [been on the field] for the Bears since 2024 because he tore his patellar tendon in the 2025 preseason. If Washington opts to go outside the organization, they could sign a veteran cornerback like Tre’Davious White, Mike Hilton, or Adoree Jackson. Yet through three weeks, the best options may already be within the organization. Though Washington was not one of the primary teams in the mix, a trade for a cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is officially off the table after instead landing in the NFC East with the Dallas Cowboys parting with draft capital ahead of week four.

All in all, Sainristil still has the talent he flashed as a rookie, but he needs to build confidence in his craft and clarify his role in the defensive scheme. However, the non-negotiable thing he must address is his perceived lack of effort, which shows up on tape for everyone to see.

Amik Robertson is a fantastic tool for Daronte Jones’ defense

When Robertson was brought in, the assumption was that he would play in the nickel position as Trey Amos and Mike Sainristil would stay on the outside. However, Amos is yet to make his season debut and Sainristil has seen his snaps get cut after frustrating outings during the first two weeks of the season.

In their place, Robertson has lit up the stat sheet with the most PBUs among cornerbacks in the league, one forced fumble and 17 total tackles. Throughout most of Week 3, Robertson was tasked with Jaxon Smith-Njigba who is one of the best receivers in the league regardless of who’s covering him. During the first half of the game, Robertson was thrown at four times allowing only one reception, 20 total yards and already had four PBUs.

Robertson fits particularly well in this defensive scheme because of his ability to originally line up in man coverage then make a hard sprint to the quarterback. This flexibility from players is exactly what Daronte Jones asks of his players.

Washington Post (paywall)

Amik Robertson nearly gave up on the NFL. The Commanders are glad he didn’t

There aren’t many NFL cornerbacks playing better than Robertson this season. He allowed just 5.2 yards per target through Week 3 — 13th among cornerbacks who’ve been targeted at least 10 times, according to the stats site Pro Football Reference. He doesn’t have any interceptions, but he has six pass deflections (third in the NFL). He’s also been effective in the run game and has 17 tackles (third on the Commanders).

Robertson, 28, has started every game and has been on the field for 99 percent of the defensive snaps. He’s been the lone bright spot in a struggling secondary.

This isn’t anything Robertson, his coaches and teammates didn’t expect. But it wasn’t always this way. Earlier in his career, he questioned whether he had what it took to stick in the NFL.

Robertson was never a Week 1 starter across four seasons with the Raiders. He started nine games from 2021 to 2022, but he was repeatedly benched and couldn’t carve out a consistent role. This time, he couldn’t block out the criticism he faced. It ate away at him.

Following his third season, Robertson isolated himself. He spent that offseason alone in Dallas. More than the physical elements of his game, he pushed himself to be more resilient mentally.

“It just came to a point where I had to go back to my roots,” Robertson said. “All of the negativity that I was seeing, I was like, ‘Just feed off of that. Don’t get offended by it. Use it as fuel.’ And that’s what I did. I built myself back together.”

[The Commanders signed] Robertson to a two-year, $16 million deal — partially because the coaching staff was confident he could help others in the secondary rise up.

“That’s what the coaching staff told me: ‘Look, we want you to come in here and be you,’” Robertson recalled. “‘We need guys like you. That energy and that the passion you play with is contagious, and we want guys to see that.’”

7 Commanders facing increasingly precarious situations after three games

Kaytron Allen – Commanders RB

An enormous amount of intrigue surrounded running back Kaytron Allen heading into the season. The sixth-round rookie came to the Washington Commanders with bold claims about making his presence felt early, but after a strong summer, his preseason performances left much to be desired.

Allen made the team and got some carries in the first two games. However, the Penn State product wasn’t utilized at all in Washington’s win over the Seattle Seahawks, which could mean he’s in the doghouse.

The No. 187 selection clattered into right guard Sam Cosmi against the Dallas Cowboys, resulting in a concussion and throat injury that has forced the veteran to miss two games. It may have been accidental, but the Commanders sent a message regardless.

It’ll be interesting to see what the future holds for Allen. But with Austin Ekeler now on board to go alongside Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White, it’s not looking especially promising.

2026 NFL trade deadline early look: Candidates to move, key teams, predictions

Daron Payne, DT, Washington Commanders

His contract voids at the end of the season, which will make him a free agent — unless the Commanders extend him first. If they do that, feel free to scratch him right off this list. But if they don’t, and if the Commanders aren’t in the NFC East race by midseason, their 2018 first-round pick could be of interest to teams looking to fill holes along their defensive lines.

If the Commanders aren’t tumbling out of contention by November, they could also be the type of team that’s looking to trade a veteran player for another, potentially dealing a guy who isn’t part of their future for a player they believe could be. Or maybe they could look to strengthen a different position. There are a lot of ways the season can still go in Washington, but it might need to stay active in order to keep its playoff hopes alive.

The Cowboys aren’t done trading

Dallas has only four picks left in next year’s draft — including nothing in the third, fifth or sixth rounds — as a result of deals for Quinnen Williams, Rashan Gary, George Pickens and Joey Porter Jr. And recent years have established the Cowboys as a far more disciplined team than they’re often given credit for. But something seems different about owner Jerry Jones this season, and the Porter deal is the most recent bit of evidence to support his bluster about his willingness and desperation to do whatever it takes to elevate this group.

If nothing else, maybe the Cowboys could trade away a backup player or two to help replenish that stash of picks. But another aggressive swing would not be a surprise.

5Qs, 5As with Bleeding Green Nation: How is Jalen Hurts faring with yet another new OC?

Q – Philly didn’t come close to defending their Super Bowl crown in 2025, given they lost in the Wild Card Round. Despite fielding one of the league’s top rosters, there’s still a lot of uncertainty about this team. How do you anticipate the rest of their season will play out?

A – The Eagles are 2-1 but they’re not exactly inspiring a ton of confidence right now. They’re not as strong in the trenches as they’ve been in the past, despite big investments in the lines. Their offense is overly reliant on the quarterback making plays instead of being a well-oiled machine. The defense is struggling to live up to lofty expectations.

Their winning record is disguising a team that’s looking like a below average group at this point in time:

Are they hopeless? Of course not. This team has earned some level of benefit of the doubt. They’ve never not made the playoffs since the Jalen Hurts/Nick Sirianni era began in 2021. They’re coming off back-to-back NFC East title wins, which previously hadn’t been accomplished by any team in this division since 2004.

In 2024, things were looking bleak for the Eagles after a 2-2 start. They got absolutely dominated by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 4 of that season … before then going on a massive run to win Super Bowl LIX.

Just because it happened then doesn’t mean they’re definitely going to be OK this year. It’s entirely possible they’re just not a very good team.

Blogging the Boys

Cowboys steal lockdown boundary corner

The Cowboys desperately need help on defense. The secondary is a hot mess, and they are banged up with recent injuries to Cobie Durant and Shavon Revel Jr., so adding a talented outside corner like Porter brings a huge sigh of relief.

To acquire Porter, the Cowboys will send a 2028 second-round pick as well as a 2027 sixth-round pick. Note the year on that second-rounder. While it appears rather cheap, it’s worth noting that Porter is in the final year of his rookie deal, meaning that unless the Cowboys work some type of extension, he’ll become an unrestricted free agent next offseason. This creates a lot of uncertainty when it comes to his future with the Cowboys. Will he be a one-year rental? Will the Joneses try to extend? Lots of questions remain.

But for now, he’s a member of the Cowboys and brings a lot to this cornerback group. Porter is an excellent boundary corner. He has top-notch press skills and thrives when he can get into the chest of the receiver. He has a knack for disrupting the timing of the receiver, making it tough for quarterbacks to sneak completions his way. He also has a reputation for showing up big in clutch moments, regularly shutting things down on third down and preventing big plays. The Cowboys are in desperate need of both of those things.

He has some weaknesses. He’s not the best tackler and can be wildly inconsistent when asked to come downhill in run support. His zone coverage ability is also not great, as he occasionally gets lost when he can’t lock in on his assignment. He can also get a little too handsy at times. And while he’s a regular pass contester, he doesn’t have the interception production you’d hope for.

Report: Cowboys will not be immediately extending Joey Porter Jr.

In case you haven’t been following along with Pittsburgh during Mike McCarthy’s first year guiding his hometown team, the main reason that Porter Jr. has been available has been due to contract standoffs with the club. Porter, represented by David Mulugheta for what it’s worth, has been seeking compensation that would, presumably, put him among the highest paid at his position. The Steelers and he clearly reached an impasse and he was traded away. Tale as old as time.

Typically when these things happen (a player seeking a contract is dealt) they are accompanied by a brand new deal. Think about when Dallas traded away Micah Parsons as an example. He immediately got the deal that he wanted from the Green Bay Packers.

It would appear that this will not be happening with the Cowboys and Joey Porter Jr., at least at first.

He is in the final year of his contract which isn’t ideal, but that is only true from the perspective of a long-term deal being the only desired outcome. The Cowboys could watch Porter Jr. walk in free agency and recoup a compensatory pick in 2028, likely a third-rounder. They could place the franchise tag on him like they did Pickens. They have shown that they have an ability to get creative.
